PREFACE.

passage, such points have been noticed. But, though the claims of exact scholarship have not
been disregarded, alterations in these respects have not generally been made in the interest of
mere grammatical accuracy. A great source of obscurity in the Authorised Version is the use of
different English words for one word of the original, even in the same context. In such cases,
one uniform rendering has frequently been adopted, with the result, not merely of clearing up the
context, but of suggesting an unexpected parallelism between different parts of the Bible.
(2) With regard to the Various Readings, it is necessary to remind the reader that the text
from which the Authorised Version of the New Testament is translated is substantially identical
with that of the first edition of the Greek text published by Hrasmus in 1516, an edition based
upon not more than five MSS., and those chosen almost at random without any regard to their
intrinsic value. The discovery of some of the most ancient and valuable MSS. of the New
Testament, and the systematic use of others, both ancient and valuable, which, though known in
Western Europe in the 16th century, were scarcely used, and, in general, a more comprehensive
study of MSS. and ancient Versions, has shewn that this * Received Text,” as it is called, labours
under manifold corruptions. A succession of scholars has now been at work, partly collecting
materials, and partly digesting and utilising the materials collected. Prominent among them are
the names of Lachmann, Tischendorf, Tregelles, and Westcott and Hort, who have made the
whole New Testament the subject of elaborate reconstructive criticism. Some other scholars
have paid special attention to the text of particular books, as Dr. B. Weiss in Germany to that
of the Gospels and the Epistle to the Romans, and Bishops Lightfoot and Ellicott in our own
country to some of the Pauline Epistles, Besides these, it was thought well in 1880 to note the
readings adopted in a carefully revised translation of the Gospels by the Rev. J. B. MsClellan.
As Mr. M°Clellan represents principles of criticism which were not entirely those of the dominant
school, it was thought that additional confidence would be felt where he was im agreement with
the other editors. : °
The Hebrew text of the Old Testament stands upon a somewhat different footing. The form
im which it appears in the printed Bibles is that in which it has been fixed by the Jews themselves
for centuries. But a close examination reveals the fact that, jealously guarded as it thus has
been, there must have been an earlier period in its transmission, during which errors and altera-
tions crept in. The existence of such errors may be easily shewn, without passing beyond the
limits of the Hebrew text itself, by a comparison of the corresponding chapters in the Books of
Samuel and Kings on the one hand, and in the Chronicles on the other. Of the MSS. which
have as yet been examined, but few date back as far as the 10th century «.p., and these few
contain only portions of the Bible. But the ancient Versions at once carry us back to a period
from 500 to 1000 years anterior to this: they thus reflect, with more or less exactness, a text far
older than that represented by the earliest Hebrew MSS. Certainly, to classify and account for
all the divergences which they exhibit is a problem of extreme complexity, and perhaps insoluble:
but, if used with tact and sobriety, the ancient Versions afford invaluable aid in restoring order
and sequence where the Hebrew, as we possess it, appears involved in much confusion, A com-
parison of the present edition with that of 1880, and indeed with the earlier Commentaries
generally, will, it is believed, make it probable that the gain from this source is still far from
exhausted.
Cases, however, occur in which a suspicion of corruption attaches to the text, which even a
comparison of the Versions does not avail to remove. Here, then, nothing remains but to make
a temperate use of critical emendation. However reluctant we may be to admit the principle
of conjecture, an exceptional application of it is justified in the case of the Old Testament
(1) by the long interval which elapsed between the composition of most of the books and the
earliest date to which we can trace them, and (2) by the nature of the Hebrew characters,
which, in every phase through which the alphabet has passed, are very liable to be confounded.
Purely arbitrary emendations are, of course, inadmissible; but there are many passages which
become at once intelligible on a slight alteration in the form of one or two of the letters.
Changes of the vowel-points are also occasionally of service, but these do not in the same sense
fall under the head of conjecture, for the vowel-points merely represent a valuable, but still

ABBREVIATIONS, Etc.
Aq.—Aquila, a Jewish proselyte of Sinope in Pontus ;
his work, which is in Greek and painfully lite-
ral, is only extant in the fragments of Origen’s
Hexapla. Date, about middle of second century
A.D.
Jer.—St. Jerome’s Latin translation of the Psalms,
made directly from the Hebrew. The Vulgate
yersion of the Psalms is St. Jerome’s revision of
the Old Latin Psalter, which was based upon the
Septuagint.
Jerus., Ps.-Jon.—The Jerusalem Targum (i.e. inter-
pretation, translation, viz. in Chaldee or West
Aramaic) of the Pentateuch. Hxtant in two
recensions; the one, sometimes called the Tar-
gum of Pseudo-Jonathan, entire, and belonging
to the seventh century A.D.; the other frag-
mentary, and considerably earlier.
Jos.—Josephus, Jewish historian (died A.D. 95).
Onk.—The Chaldee (rather, West Aramaic) Targum
or translation of the’ Pentateuch, ascribed to
Onkelos. Thrown into its present form about
end of third century A.D. on the basis of an
ancient Palestinian Targum, by learned men at
Babylon. Very literal, except in poetical pas-
sages. ;
Pesh.—The Peshitto, i.e. ‘simple’ or faithful; a
Syriac (tather, Hast Aramaic) version, made for
Christian readers from the Hebrew, though in-
fluenced frequently by Jewish exegesis, and in
parts (e.g. in the Psalms) by the Septuagint.
Date, not later than second or third century.
R.—Revised Version of 1885.
R marg.—Margin of do.
Saad.—Rabbi-Saadyah Gaon (died 942 a.p.). Arabic
translation of most of the Old Testament, of which,
however, only the Pentateuch, Song of Songs,
Isaiah, and parts of Job, Psalms, and Proverbs,
have been published.
Sam.—The Hebrew Pentateuch as read by the Sama-
ritans. In,character, its text agrees with that
used by the Septuagint.
Sept.—The Septuagint. An aggregate of Greck trans-
lations made in Egypt by Hellenistic Jews. The
oldest and best is that of the Pentateuch (third
century B.C.); the latest, those of the Hagio-
grapha (mostly finished before 130 B.c.). More
valuable for criticism of the text than for inter-
pretation.
Symm.—Symmachus, probably, a Hellenistic Jew.
Date, close of second century 4.D. More ele-
gant in style than Aquila; fragmentary.
Targ.—Various Targums, or Chaldee versions, par-
ticularly that of the books of Joshua, Judges,
Samuel, Kings, and the Prophets (except Daniel),
ascribed to Jonathan ben Uzziel. Thrown into
its present form in Babylon—probably some time
after the Targum of the Pentateuch (see ‘ Onk.’).

Nore 1. Notes of the form Vulg. (MSS.), Sept.
(Cod. Al.), mean that. the reading or rendering is not
found in the ordinary texts of the Vulgate or Sep-
tuagint, but is supported by particular MSS., or by
the MS. cited. The abbreviation MSS. is sometimes
used to indicate a small number of MSS.
2. (On notes of the form Heb. marg.) There is a
certain number of places in the Old Testament in
which Jewish tradition itself has introduced what
may be termed an ‘authorised correction’ of the
text, noting the alteration in the margin, and direct-
ing the reader to substitute it for what he finds in
the text. These marginal corrections are found in
all MSS. and Hebrew Bibles. They are by no means
always critically preferable; sometimes they merely
attempt to obviate an unusual, but quite defensible,
grammatical form.
3. When (l.) is appended to a Various Reading,
it means that the proposed correction differs from
the ordinary reading only in the form of one or two
letters, which may haye been mistaken by the scribe.
On the contrary, (pt.) or (pts.) signifies that the cor-
rection does not differ in the letters, but only in one
or more of the yowel-points attached to them.
4. The readings of the Hebrew MSS. are as a rule
cited from De Rossi’s Variae Lectiones Veterts Testa-
menti (Parma, 1784—1788), and his Scholia Critica
(Parma, 1798); those of the St. Petersburg MS. of
A.D. 916 (containing Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hzekiel, and
the 12 Minor Prophets) from the facsimile published
by Dr. Hermann Strack in 1876.
5. The Septuagint is cited, except where stated
otherwise, from Tischendorf’s edition; Dr. Swete’s
edition (vol. I. as far as 2 Kings) arriving too late to
be generally used: the variations: which it exhibits
from Tischendorf’s text, however, are rarely of a
character to affect quotations such as those in the
present volume. Lucian’s recension of the Septuagint,
published (as far as Esther) by Lagarde (Gottingen,
1883), is referred to as Sept. (Luc.). ‘The Peshitto
is cited from the edition of Dr. Lee, the Targums
from Walton, Berliner, and Lagarde, the Vulgate partly
from Heyse’s edition of the Codex Amiatinus, partly
from the Clementine text, and Aq. Symm. Theod.
from Dr. Field’s Oxford edition of the Hexapla.

At no hand. They trusted in him that hath the key of
David, opening, and no man_ shutting ; they prayed to
the Lord, the Father of our Lord, to the effect that St.
Augustine did; O let thy Scriptures be my pure delight ;
let me not be deceived in them, neither let me deceive by
them. In this confidence, and with thig devotion, did
they assemble together; not too many, lest one should
trouble another; and yet many, lest many things haply
might escape them. If you ask what they had before
them; truly it was the Hebrew text of the Old Testa-
ment, the Greek of the New. These are the two golden
pipes, or rather conduits, wherethrough the olivebranches
empty themselves into the gold. St. Augustine calleth
them precedent, or original, tongues ; St. Hierome, foun-
tains, The same St. Hierome afiirmeth, and Gratian
hath not spared to put it into his ‘decree, That as the
credit of the old books (he meaneth of the Old Testament)
ts to be tried by the Hebrew volumes ; so of the new by the
Greek tongue, he meaneth by the original Greek. If truth
be to be tried by these tongues, then whence should a
translation be made, but out of them? These tongues
therefore the Scriptures, we say, in thosg tongues) we
set before us to translate, being the tongues wherein
God was pleased to speak to his Church by_ his Prophets
and Apostles. Neither did we run oyer the work with
that poreny haste that the Septuagint did, if that be true
which is reported of them, that they finished it in seventy
two days; neither were we barred or hindered from going
over it again, haying once done it, like St. Hierome, if
that be true which himself reporteth, that he could no
sooner write any thing, but presently it was caught from |
him, and published, and he could not have leave to
mend it: neither, to be short, were we the first that
fell in hand with translating the Scripture into English,
| and consequently destitute of former helps, as it is writ-
ten of Origen, that he was the first in a manner, that
put his hand to write commentaries upon the Scriptures, _
and therefore no marvel if he overshot himself many
times. None of these things: The work hath not been
huddled up in seventy two days, but hath cost the work-
men, a slight as it seemeth, the pains of twice seyen times
seventy two days, and more. Matters of such, weight
and consequence are to be speeded with maturity: for
in a business of moment a man feareth not the blame
of conyenient slackness. Neither did we think much
to consult the translators or commentators, Chaldee,
Hebrew, Syrian, Greek, or Latin; no, nor the Spanish,
French, Italian, or Dutch ; neither did we disdain to re-
vise that which we had done, and to bring back to the
anvil that which we had hammered: but having and
using as great helps as were needful, and fearing no re-
proach for slowness, nor coveting praise for expedition
we have at length, through the good hand of the Lord
upon us, brought the work to that pass that you see.
Some peradventure would have no variety of senses
to be set in the margin, lest the authority of the Scrip-
tures for deciding of controversies by that shew of un-
certainty should somewhat be shaken. But we hold
their judgment not to be so sound in this point. For
though whatsoever things are necessary are mai est, aS
St. Chrysostome saith; and, as St. Augustine, in those
things that are plainly set down in the Scriptures all such
matters are found, that concern faith, hope, and charity:
Yet for all that it cannot be d sleds that partly to
exercise and whet our wits, partly to wean the curious
from lothing of them for their every where plainness,
partly also to stir up our devotion to crave the assistance
of God’s Spirit by prayer, and lastly, that we might be
forward to seek aid of our brethren by conference, and
never scorn those that be not in all respects so complete
as they should be, being to seek in many things our-
selves, it hath pleased God in his Divine Providence,
here and there to scatter words and sentences of that
difficulty and doubtfulness, not in. doctrinal points that
concern salvation, (for in such it hath been vouched
that the Scriptures are plain,) but in matters of less
moment, that fearfulness would better beseem us than
confidence, and if we will resolye, to resolve upon mo-
desty with St. Augustine, (though not in this same case
altogether, yet upon the same ground,) Melius est dubitare
de occultis, quam litigare de incertis: It is better to make
doubt of those things which are secret, than to strive
about those things that are uncertain. There be many
words in the Scriptures, which be never found there but
once, (having neither brother nor neighbour, as the
Hebrews speak,) so that we cannot be holpen by con-
ference of places. Again, there be many rare names of
certain birds, beasts, and precious stones, &c., concern-
ing which the Hebrews themselves are so divided among
themselves for judgment, that they may seem to have
defined this or that, rather because they would say some-
thing, than because they were sure of that which they
said, as St. Hierome somewhere saith of the Septuagint.
Now in such a case doth not a margin do well to ad-
monish the Reader to seek further, and not to conclude
or dogmatize upon this or that peremptorily ? For as it
is a fault of incredulity, to doubt of those things that
are evident; so to determine of such things as the
Spirit of God hath left (even in the judgment of the
judicious) questionable, can be no less than presumption.
Therefore as St. Augustine saith, that variety of trans-
lations is profitable for the finding out of the sense of
the Scriptures: so diversity of signification and sense
in the margin, where the text is not so clear, must needs
do good; yea, is necessary, as we are persuaded. We
know that Status Quintus expressly forbiddeth that any
variety of readings of their vulgar edition should be put

In the VARIORUM REFERENCE BIBLE, 1880, the familiar Reference Bible was combined
with a revised and enlarged Edition of the Queen’s Printers’ “varioruM BIBLE or the
Authorised Version edited with various Renderings and Readings from the best
Authorities, 1876,” owr object being—within the compass of a single portable volume of
moderate cost—to associate with the Authorised Version the surest results of the study of
the Sacred Text or of its Translation, and thus to enable the average English reader
to ascertain without labour the original import of the Sacred Writings, and to estimate
the authority by which proposed changes in the Authorised Version are supported.
In the Variorum foot-notes, which distinguish this Edition from all other Reference
Bibles, the method of the notes in the A.V. margin has been adopted but extended until. a
digest of the best accredited Various Readings and Renderings of the Teats, or, in other
words, a conspectus of the really tenable opinions upon difficult or imperfectly translated
‘passages in the Authorised Version—whether attributable to incorrectness in the Hebrew or
Greek Text used, or to inaccurate translation of a text correct in itself—was the result. The
Authorised Version and the chief: materials for its revision being thus presented at one
view comparison is made easy, but moreover the degree of authority attaching to each of
the selected Various Readings and Renderings is discriminated and (except where a
general consent can be alleged) authenticated by the names of the authorities by which
it is supported. So that even if compared with the Westminster Revision published in
1885, which work our Variorum Notes will be found to have largely assisted and untici-
pated, the VARIORUM REFERENCE BIBLE 7s of general and permanent use; for while that
Revision gives results only, this work indicates the places of the Authorised Version in
which the important changes are to be found, gives briefly and concisely the authority
for the changes adopted, and calls attention to the balance of opinion upon disputed
points.
To the general reader, the Variorum Notes will often render other note or comment
needless, and suggest the full meaning of a familiar passage.
To the clergyman, the teacher, and even the private student, who frequently cannot
consult an elaborate commentary, this summary of the results of an extensive literature
will shew at a glance the passages about which no question arises, and an outline of the
authorities that support each construction of the passages which are capable of different
interpretation.

EDITOR'S PREFACE:
(pee purpose of the present Selection is to put the ordinary English reader
in possession of the main results of modern research, so far as they tend
to throw a new and welcome light on the sacred records of our common faith.
The field of Oriental Archzology is a very wide one, and its boundaries are
being extended every day. The future is full of promise. ‘There is no reason
why the discoveries of the coming time should not equal or even eclipse the
greatest surprises of the past. Who can say what wonderful treasure-trove of
buried monuments and forgotten archives of men and nations, whose names
and memories barely survive in the fragmentary histories of the Old Testa-
ment, may not reward the fortunate explorers who are allowed to excavate
without let or hindrance the mounds in the neighbourhood of Damascus, or
the numberless other neglected sites of Babylonia, Syria, and the land beyond
Jordan P
In the meantime, whatever obstacles may intervene to prevent this desirable
consummation and crowning of past successes—whether the check be due to
the indifference and parsimony of civilized Governments, or to the caprices
and ill-will of Pashas and Sultans, or to the ignorance, fanaticism, and bar-
barism which characterize the populace of Eastern towns and the wandering
tribes of the desert—the harvest already reaped is of almost incalculable bulk,
and the gains of historical and theological science are far greater than can be
realized without a considerable effort of thought. The great national collec-
tions of Europe and even America are crowded with innumerable relics of the
old civilisations of Western Asia; a vast assemblage of the most diverse
materials for the political, social, religious, literary and artistic history of
antiquity. As yet, this mass of documents has hardly received more than
superficial examination. Thousands of Babylonian and Assyrian texts have
scarcely as yet been catalogued, much less copied and made accessible to
general study. But enough has been done to modify profoundly the point of
view from which both believers and sceptics have hitherto regarded the Old
Testament Scriptures. Never again will scornful incredulity dare to assert,
with Voltaire, that those Scriptures were an idle fabrication of medieval
monks. The Old Testament records no longer stand alone, supported only by
a few doubtful references in the Classics and by the uncritical narrative of
Josephus. Large portions of the sacred history can now be brought, and have
been already brought, to the test of strictly contemporary evidence. It has,
in fact, been proved abundantly by the ever-accumulating collateral testimonies
of the Assyrian, Babylonian, and Hgyptian remains, that the Old Testament
contains substantially true extracts from the annals of the Israelitish king-
doms, and many correct notices of foreign peoples and their relations to the
Chosen Race. Like the fragments cited by Eusebius and other ecclesiastical

EDITOR’S PREFACE,
writers from the lost histories of the Chaldean Berosus and the Egyptian
Manetho, which were formerly a favourite butt of literary scepticism, the
histories preserved in the Old Testament derive a marvellous amount of
confirmation from the monuments discovered and interpreted within the last
generation. Narratives recognized by scholars as dating from the times of
which they treat, for the most part stand the test of comparison with the new
documents to a degree that is highly satisfactory to an impartial judgment.
Where the statements of a Biblical writer differ from those of the contemporary
monuments as to matters of fact, the disagreement may usually be accounted
for by considerations of date, the imexactness of tradition, or the imperfect
nature of the sources accessible to the Jewish author.
It would be easy to multiply examples of the manifold service which Oriental
Archeology is now rendering to the Exegesis of Scripture and, therefore, to
Theology; but, for the present, J must be content to refer to the numerous
accurate, and beautiful reproductions of the principal monuments and the
explanatory notes relating to them, which practically constitute this work a
handbook to the Science of Biblical Archeology. It is hoped that the use of
it may at least convince the general reader that the sacred history no longer
hangs like a picture in the air, without visible background or solid terrestrial
surroundings; but is seen more and more to occupy a real and intelligible
place in the larger story of the nations, and is gradually falling into true
perspective as a part—unquestionably the most significant and essential part
—of the vast panorama of the fortunes of mankind.

INTRODUCTION TO THE ILLUSTRATIONS.
NHE aim of the following Introduction is to give the reader a general idea of the
various kinds of material afforded by the monuments for the illustration of
the Bible.
Most of the illustrations here given are drawn from the descriptive notes that
accompany the Plates. But occasionally some fresh material has been added, and if
the material so drawn from the body of the book is presented in anything like a new
setting—such repetition will, perhaps, be forgiven, while to some, at least, of the readers
of this volume it may even prove of service in helping to familiarise them with a few
of the precious contributions made, within comparatively recent years, by Oriental
Discovery and Research to Biblical Science.

of Manuscript Writing by means of which the Scriptures

1. The first ten plates of the following series exhibit the most important types of
ancient writing with which the monuments have made us familiar. Necessarily restricted
as this selection is, it will, nevertheless, enable the English reader to form some conception
of the range and variety of the material available for tracing in its various phases the
history of the development of an art essential to the progress of the higher civilisation.
It is a sufficiently striking fact, for instance, that even this small collection ranges in date
from the 5th millennium (Plate I.) to the 2nd century B.c. (Plate X.). A reference to
Plate IV. will put the reader in possession of some of the principal data for determining
the probable course of development followed by the ancient symbols, which resulted in
the formation of the Phosnicio-Hebrew alphabet. From this in turn were developed, as
is well known, the classical (Graeco-Roman) and modern Huropean alphabets, for illustra-
tions of which the reader is referred to the beautiful specimens of manuscript writing
reproduced in Plates XI.—XXIII., with the accompanying descriptions of the principal
biblical manuscripts written at various dates from the 4th to the 14th century a.p.
The first writing was pictorial and ideographic; that is to say, it represented things
directly by means of pictures or rude outlines, and the relations of things by a meta-
phorical use of the same means. Thus a young bird might, figuratively, represent a child,
and the ideas of generation and parturition might be signified by adding to the bird-
symbo! the character for knee, so that the Sumerian word mun. “to beget,” or “ bear,”
was represented in hieroglyphic writing by a combination of the two pictorial characters
bird and knee. Another excellent instance of this occurs in the inscription reproduced in
Plate I. Ifthe reader will look at the 13th line of the right-hand column of this document,
he will easily identify what is in reality a rough picture of a man turning his back (the
back is shown by the strongly marked backbone). ‘The idea conveyed by this symbol is
that of anger (to be angry): and the ideogram was read as ib, which in Sumerian meang
“anger,” “to be angry.”

INTRODUCTION
The two great hieroglyphic or pictorial systems of antiquity are, of course, the
Sumerian (Babylonian) and Hgyptian. (For the latter, compare the first part of the
inscription on the Rosetta Stone, Plate X. and cf. Plate LIX. There is also another
important system of hieroglyphic writing, viz., the Hittite, in Plates VIII., CIII., CIV.,
OCVL, CVII. Up to the present time this script unfortunately has not been deciphered.)
There is a growing consensus of opinion among scholars that the Egyptian system
is not of native origin, but was derived from the more ancient Sumerian. It should be
added that there is a mass of still accumulating evidence for the Babylonian origin of
the vast system of the Chinese characters.
In the arehaic system of Babylonian hieroglyphs we thus reach the ultimate source
of ancient writing. For it was from this system that the later arrow-headed (cuneiform)
script was undoubtedly derived (cp. columns 1 and 2 of Plate LV.) ; and it seems highly
probable that the Phoenician characters were borrowed not, as has commonly been held,
from the Egyptian hieratic (cp. Plate VIT.), but from the same primitive source (cp.
columns 1, 2, and 3 of Plate IV., and see below).
Tt remains to briefly trace the process by which an alphabet was developed from the
hieroglyphic script. The old pictorial writing was apparently the invention of the
Sumerians at a remote epoch. It is easy to see how, as the art of writing was developed
and diffused, the need for a simpler system would be felt (an obvious inconvenience
attaching to the hieroglyphic writing lies in the enormous number of characters it 1s
necessary to employ in it).
Asin Egypt this simplification was effected by largely replacing the ideograms by
phonetic characters; that is to say, symbols were used no longer merely to represent
ideas, but to express sounds (both systems existing side by side). The characters chosen
for phonetic purposes were selected from the ideographic symbols, and, im the first instance,
were used to express syllables (simple and compound). The syllabic value given to a
particular ideogram was determined by the phonetic value of the corresponding word
which (by usage) had become attached to it. An instance will, perhaps, make this clear.
A well-known Sumerian ideogram, an eight-rayed star, designates the sky, or the god of
the sky. The corresponding Sumerian word expressing these ideas is ana. Hence when
a syllabic value was given to the symbol, it became an. In phonetic writing, then, this
character denotes the syllable an wherever it occurs; and so with other symbols.
Such was the point of development reached by the Sumerian (Babylonian) writing ;
that is to say, it had resolved itseli into a syllabary, interspersed with ideograms, but had
not developed an alphabet proper. ‘This system of writing was adopted by the Semites,
who eventually came to predominate in the Euphrates Valley, and who spoke a language
far removed from the (Turanian) Sumerian, and nearly related to Hebrew and the
cognate tongues.
The Semitic language thus written is known as Assyrian.
The adoption by the Semitic Babylonians of the Sumerian system of writing (both
syllabic and ideographic) considerably increased the difficulties of reading the ancient
script. The old Sumerian ideograms became associated with the corresponding Semitic
words, and retained at the same time their original Sumerian verbal equivalents ; while
to the Sumerian phonetic characters new (Semitic) syllabic values were in some instances
added. ‘The difficulties attaching to the polyphonous character of the symbols, as thus
used, were keenly felt by the Assyrian scribes themselves, and various devices were
resorted to for overcoming them, which need not here be described.
It should not be forgotten that the Semitic Babylonians, as well as adopting the
Sumerian script, cultivated also the study of the Sumerian language and literature.
Under Semitic influence the Sumerian had become a dead language. Hence the study of

it was attended by difficulties, under stress of which a whole literature of grammars,
dictionaries, syllabaries, interlinear translations of the old texts, etc., grew up, which has
been of the greatest value to modern students of the two languages.
We have already traced the development of a phonetic system of writing (viz., the
syllabic) from the hieroglyphic, both systems (in Sumerian and Assyrian) existing side
by side. A highly developed example of a purely syllabic system may be seen in the
Cypriote, which, linguistically, is a dialect of Greek (cf. Plate IX. and the accompanying
description). The importance of this syllabic system lies in the fact that it occupies a
middle position between. pictorial and alphabetic writing. The transition from syllabic
to alphabetic writing (¢f. Plate LV.) is easy to understand. In fact, in Persian cuneiform
writing we actually find a purely alphabetic development from the Assyrio-Babylonian
system (similarly, too, ancient Egyptian, which probably started from a Babylonian basis,
“has already developed a set of some twenty-five strictly alphabetic signs, which it uses
in combination with pictorial syllabic symbols and determinatives”’).
In the ancient Phoenicio-Hebrew script (cf. Plates IX., V., and VI.), we come toa
real alphabet, free from syllabic or ideographic accompaniments. Since De Rougé, it has
been the fashion to assume that the Phoenician characters were borrowed from the
Egyptian hieratic (¢f. Plate VIT.). But such a theory is beset by grave objections, and
it is the deliberate opinion of the editor of the present work that the facts can only be
adequately explained by supposing that these characters were directly borrowed from the
Assyrio-Babylonian script.
2. A word should be said about the historical interest and importance of the following
inscriptions (Plates I.—X.).
Attention has already been called to the important inscription reproduced in Plate I.,
which is notable as illustrating the oldest known forms of the archaic Babylonian script
(circ. B.c. 4500-4000). The possible illustration it affords of the name Nod (Gen. 4. 16) is
detailed in the descriptive note (No. 1). It is also interesting as one of the most ancient
documents from the great temple of the sun at Sippara, which was restored long after-
wards by Nebuchadnezzar, and for its mention of the temple-shepherds and their
sacrifices of animals to “the Lord” (Bel = Baal), and of the metals, gold and copper, of
the maneh weight, and of the pitch or bitumen which flows from certain wells in
Babylonia and was from the earliest period used for building purposes (Gen. 11. 3).
One of the most interesting of the documents in this series, throwing, as it does, a
vivid light on contemporary life and thought, is the Letter in Egyptian hieratic of the
time of Moses and the Exodus, of which a full translation is given in the descriptive note
(No. 7). It is unnecessary to emphasise afresh here the historical importance of the
Inscription of Mesha, king of Moab (2 Kings 3. 4), and of the famous Siloam Inscription,
of which full translations appear in the descriptive notes (Nos. 5 and 6).
The Phoenician Inscription printed in No. 9 contains an interesting reference to the
month of Hthanim (i.e. the month of steady flowings). It is interesting to remember that
this name of the 7th month (=the post-Biblical Tisri) occurs once only in Biblical
Hebrew (1 Kings 8. 2).
The famous bilingual Rosetta. Stone, of which an illustration is given in Plate X.,
occupies an important place in the history of the decipherment of hieroglyphic writing.
It, in fact, furnished the key for unravelling the secrets enshrined in the monuments
of Kegypt (cf. the trilingual cylinder-seal of Darius, Plate CL. The great rock
inscription at Behistwn in Persia, written in Persian, Old Median, and Assyrian, in like
manner furnished Sir H. Rawlinson and others with the key to the decipherment of the
cuneiform writing).

It was after the quelling of Tidmat that Merodach’s creative labours began. These
are narrated in the fifth and following Tablets.
The fifth Tablet is unfortunately only a fragment. One section, however, remains,
relating the creation of the heavenly bodies, and the institution of the year and its

fourth day’s work given in Gen. 1. 14-19. Two lines narrating the creation of the moon,
and the assignment of its functions of distinguishing days and revealing the nightly
heavens may be quoted here :-—
Nannaru (= “The Shining One”) he made shine forth, made him overseer of night ;
He appointed him, a being of night, to determine days ;
Every month unfailingly with crescent-crown make division !
Of the sixth Tablet there are unhappily no certain, but some possible, remains. Deeply
interesting are the last two lines of one fragment, which possibly (though, owing to its
fractured condition, the decipherment is uncertain) refer to the creation of the first
human pair :—
[Then made] Niv-rat-azaa (é.e. Ia) two litt[le]
[Among the wh]ole of the moving things he made [them] mighty.
Comp. “And God said wnto them . . . . have dominion over the fish of the sea,
and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth wpon the earth”
(Gen. 1. 28).
With this should be compared also the following lines from what is probably the
closing tablet of the present series, where the creation of man is distinctly ascribed to Ia’s
son Merodach :—
To keep them (the vanquished demons) under,
He made mankind:
And the following, from another and older story of Creation :—
The goddess Aruru seed of man with his (Merodach’s) help did make (ef. Gen. 4, 1).
This last citation is taken from a poem which exhibits in a remarkable degree the

temples, is placed in the forefront of Merodach’s creative labours.
This religious feeling is again beautifully illustrated in the following fragment, which

Daily thy god thou shalt worship
With offering, word of mouth, due of [in]cense.
Towards thy god thou shalt have purity of heart :
That is the due of godhead,
Frayer, supplication, and a humble countenance.

The Deluge Tablet, containing the Chaldean story of the Flood (Plate XXXVILI),
ranks in importance with the Creation series. Here again the moral element is insisted
upon. The Deluge is a punishment for sin. The story is a fascinating one for the Biblical
student, and should be read in its entirety (cf. the translation of the chief part in No. 37).
The narrative, the affinity of which to the corresponding Biblical one is at once apparent,
forms the eleventh book of the great Chaldean Epic of Gilgamesh, or Nimrod. It is
related to Gilgamesh by his ancestor Ntth-napishtim (called also Atrahasis or Hasisatra,
i.e. “the very pious, wise one”; cp. Gen. 6.9: Noah was a righteous man, blameless in
his generation), who is the Chaldean Noah. Atrahasis narrates how, when a flood had
been decreed by the great gods on account of the wickedness rampant in the city of
Shurippak, which “was full of violence,” he had been directed to build a ship to hold
himself, his family, the craftsmen, and the animals. The ark is built, and the storm
descends, lasting six days and nights. As in the Biblical account, birds—a dove, swallow,
and raven—are sent forth, the last not returning. The ark rests on the mount of Nizir;
its inmates emerge; sacrifice is offered, and the gods agree not to punish mankind again
with a flood. Finally, Atrahasis and his wife are translated to the immortal land at the
mouth of the four rivers of Paradise, there to live like the gods (cp. the translation of
Enoch, Gen. 5. 24), The following extracts will serve to illustrate some of the points
of contact with the Biblical narrative already alluded to :-—
But when the seventh day was come,

Feeding, wading, croaking, returned not (cp. Gen. 8. 6-12).
The effect of Atrahasis’s sacrifice on the gods is thus described :—

The gods snuffed the pleasant odour,

Compare with this the language of Genesis: And the Lord smelled the sweet savour
(Gen. 8. 21), as well as the customary formula of Leviticus, which describes the offering
made by fire as a sweet savour to spree Jehovah.

It is interesting to note that the Babylonian story incidentally furnishes the explana-
tion of the Biblical name Noah. The Hebrew name is evidently abridged from the Nih-
napishtim (= Rest of Soul,” i.e. Tranquil-hearted) of the Epic, which is itself the
Semitic equivalent of the old Sumerian ideogram (GUS-zI—=KUSH-ZI, “rest of soul”).
Further illustrations of episodes in the great Epic of Gilgamesh (or Nimrod) are
given in Plates XXXVIII., XXXIX., and XLII. (cf. the accompanying descriptions).
One of the most interesting documents recovered from the Hast is the Ancient Babyionian
Map of the World, which is reproduced in Plate XXVII. This should be studied in
detail with the aid of the accompanying descriptive note. It throws a flood of light on
the state of geographical knowledge indicated in Gen. 2. 10-14.
Of the Babylonian seals here given, one of the most interesting is reproduced in Plate
XXVIII. This depicts the famous scene of the palm tree with pendent fruit, towards
which two seated figures are each stretching out a hand, while a serpent stands erect
behind one of them. It has been supposed that this might represent the Temptation
(Gen. 3). But it is highly doubtful, for the reasons given in the descriptive note.
Another valuable seal is exhibited in Plate CX. This is most important, as it seems to
solve once fer all the vexed question of the meaning of the divine title Shaddaz, rendered
“ Almighty” in the Authorised Version. The scene depicts the morning sun rising over
the mountains, and the god himself is designated “The Sun-god, the god Satum, i.e. the
god of the mountains (Satum=the Assyrian shaddé, “mountains”). The origin of the
Hebrew name Hl Shaddai (= Assyrian il shaddé, i.e. ‘god of the mountains”’) is signifi-
cant in the light of such a passage as Exod. 6. 2,3: And God spake unto Moses, and said
unto him, Iam Jehovah: and I appeared unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob as
God Almighty (El Shaddat). When we remember that Amos (4. 13) speaks of Jehovah
as treading wpon the high places of the ecrth, and that it is reported of the Syrians, in the
time of Ahab, that they spoke of Jehovah as a god of the hills, but not a god of the valleys
(1 Kings 20. 28, 28), it is surely not difficult to see in the divine title Hl Shaddai traces of
an ancient conception of God as the God of the mountains.

Something should be said also of the sacred trees, conventional illustrations of which
appear in Plates XX XI. and XXXII. The worship of a sacred tree, which is a common
feature in almost all ancient religions, flourished apparently in Babylonia, and especially
in Assyria, as well as among the other Semites (Arabs, Phoenicians, Canaanites, and
Jews). In the Old Testament, the worship of sacred trees (groves, or rather “ Asherahs”’)
is often spoken of, and prohibited (cf. Deut. 12.3: and ye shall . . . . burn their
Asherim with fire).
The trees are conventional representations of the palm, which was perhaps sacred, as
giving oracles by the motion or rustling of its leaves (like the laurel of Delphi).
It is interesting to notice that the ancient name of South Chaldea, Shumir (= Shinar,
Gen. 11. 2), may mean Palm-country. (Similarly, Jericho is called the city of palm trees,
Deut. 34. 3.) The palm tree which was probably found in large numbers on the settle-
ment of the Babylonians, in the Chaldean Plain, was early considered a benefactor both
to man and beast, and regarded as sacred.
Such was also the case with the early Arabs, among whom the palm tree was sacred
to the pre-Islamic goddess Athtar (i.e. Ishtar, or Ashtoreth), with the Phoenicians and
perhaps the early Hebrews (cf. Judges 4. 5).
Two other illustrations, which serve to throw light upon points in the historical

about 150 miles below the site of Babylon. Its situation on the borders of the desert
made it one of the first places in which the Semitic ancestors of the Hebrews would settle.
In fact it is certain that the Semites were settled here before B.c. 8800. The principal

Chaldea was invaded by the Elamites in 3.c. 2280, and the city of Ur, like most of
the cities of Chaldea, fell into the hands of the enemy. No doubt under the new rule,
which probably proved oppressive to them, large numbers of the Semites left the country.
Terah, with his family (including Abram), removed to Kharran (Gen. 11. 31). It is
curious that the city Kharran (the modern Haran) was, as the inscriptions show
and as is well-known from later Greek writers, like Ur, an ancient sanctuary of the
Moon-god.
Another illustration (see Plate LIII.) throws a welcome light upon the obscure
narrative embodied in Gen. 14. The inscribed cylinder, illustrated in the Plate, is from
Babylonia, and contains an important inscription of Babylonian and Hlamite kings. The
invasion of Chaldea by the HElamites (B.c. 2280) has already been spoken of. Their
supremacy in Babylonia lasted eighty years (from B.c. 2280—2200). The old Babylonian
capital Erech, having been destroyed, the Elamite viceroy (usually a member of the
reigning family) had his seat of government at Larsa: and the inscription before us is, in
fact, a votive memorial of Hriaku, king of Larsa (7.e. the Elamite viceroy), on behalf of
himself and his father Kudtir-Mabtg, the Elamite king, now ruler of Ur, Shumir, and
Accad. At some time during this period of eighty years, the invaders pushed on and
conquered Syriaand Palestine and retained the sovereignty of the latter for thirteen years
(Gen. 14. 4), Gen. 14 contains some account of this rule, the revolt, and the expedition
that followed to reconquer Southern Palestine. It is interesting to notice that Arioch,
king of Ellasar (Gen. 14. 9), corresponds to Hriiku, king of Larsa (the Elamite viceroy
mentioned above), while Amraphel, king of Shinar (i.e. Shumir, 8. Babylonia), is
probably to be identified with the great Babylonian king Hammurabi (a portrait and
inscription of whom are reproduced in Plate LII. Cf. also Plate CLI., where the names
of the four kings in cuneiform are reproduced). In Gen. 14, Hammurabi (Amraphel)
appears as a vassal king, fighting for his suzerain the king of Elam. In B.c. 2200 (no
doubt shortly after the events described in Gen. 14) Hammurabi revolted, and overthrew
the Elamite dominion in Babylonia. The importance of these data for students of the
Old Testament lies in the fact that upon them we can arrive approximately at the date
of Abram’s migration, which probably took place in the early part of the period of
Hlamite supremacy in Babylonia, t.e. between B.c. 2280 and B.c. 2255.
The historical narrative of Genesis now flows on into Egypt, and we naturally turn
for illustrations to the monuments of ‘that country rather than to those of Babylonia.
It is all the more surprising, therefore, to find ourselves confronted in this region with
documents in the Babylonian cuneiform writing. Yet such documents have recently
(1887) been unearthed in Egypt, at Tell el-Amarna (see Plate LXI.). Such a discovery
was quite unexpected. The Tell el-Amarna Tablets (which range in date from B.c. 1500
to B.c. 1450) are deeply interesting. They reveal the fact that, more than a century
before the Exodus, Babylonian writing was in universal use for the purposes of diplomacy
and commerce. Among the tablets are letters from Babylonia and Middanni (N. Mesopo-
tamia), as well as from Tyre, Sidon, Gebal, Askelon, Gaza, Lachish, and Jerusalem, to
(as well as letters from) the Egyptian kings Amenophis III. and the great Amenophis TV.
(Chu-en-aten ; see Plate LX., and accompanying description). The letters from Jerusa-
lem are of unusual interest. They are written to the king by Abdi-Hiba (servant of the
Good One). He complains of the advance of the Philistines and others against him,
Abdi-Hiba speaks of himself as the Pharaoh’s humble vassal. He states that he is king,
not by hereditary right; “nor from my father, nor from my mother, but by the King’s
strong arm am I king.”
The double name of Hebron (Hebron and Kirjath-Arba) is also explained in the
light of these inscriptions (see Description No. 50).

INTRODUCTION
The monarch to whom the greater part of the Tell el-Amarna correspondence is
addressed (Chu-en-aten, i.e. Amenophis IV.) is one of the most interesting figures in
Egyptian history. In his peace-loving disposition, and in the display of magnificence
made in the palace and temple which he built at his new capital (Chu-aten, i.e. Tell el-
Amarna), he resembled Solomon; while the hymns he wrote in honour of his god remind
us no less of David; and his earnest labours as a religious reformer, with their short-lived
results, suggest a comparison with Hezekiah and Josiah. Like Josiah (2 Kings 22. 3),
he, in the eighteenth year of his age, effected a radical change in the State religion. He,
in fact, adopted his Asiatic mother’s religion, the worship of the Aten—i.e. the sun—as
the lord and giver of life, to the entire exclusion of the polytheistic conceptions which had
hitherto prevailed in Egypt. At the same time, he assumed the name of Chu-en-aten
(=splendour of the solar disk), and founded a new capital at Chu-aten (Tell el-Amarna).
Chu-en-aten is supposed by some to be Joseph’s Pharaoh. But the more generally
received opinion is that Abraham, Joseph, and the other patriarchs entered Egypt when
Lower Egypt had fallen into the hands of foreign invaders from Asia, and was governed
by the Hyksos,* or Shepherd Kings, that is, about B.c. 2200 (see Plates LIV. and LVL.,
and accompanying descriptions). In fact, it seems probable that the Elamite invasion of
Chaldea in B.c. 2280, the (consequent) migration of Abram from Ur of the Chaldees to
Kharran and thence to Southern Palestine, and the Hyksos invasion of Lower Heypt
“may have been more or less contemporaneous, and perhaps connected events.”
The Hyksos kings ruled over Lower Egypt for some 500 years (according to Petrie
from 3B.c. 2098-1587). They resided at Zoan-Tanis (see No. LVIII.), at Memphis, and
also at Bubastis. It must be remembered that during this interval the native Hgyptian
kings exercised sovereignty in the south (in the new capital city of Thebes; see
Plate LXTV.). How obnoxious the “Shepherd” rulers must have been to them may
be seen from Gen. 46. 34: Hvery shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians.
It was no doubt at the court of an Asiatic Pharaoh that Joseph found a welcome;
and very probably it was under the Hyksos King Apepa (see portrait in Plate LVIL.), in
accordance with the tradition preserved in ancient writers, that he attained to distinction
in the Egyptian Court.
Certainly the manners and customs of the Hyksos period accord in a remarkable
way with the picture of the age of Joseph presented in the Book of Genesis. A striking
instance of this is given in the description to Plate LYVIII. By their expulsion of the
Hyksos conquerors (in B.c. 1587) the native Egyptian kings regained their authority over
the whole of Egypt; indeed, under Thothmes IIT. and succeeding monarchs of the
eighteenth dynasty the war of conquest was carried into Palestine and Syria (see p. 30).
Thus it came about that there arose a new king over Egypt which knew not Joseph
(Exod. 1. 8). The Pharaoh of the Oppression is usually identified with Rameses II.
(see Plates LXVII—LXX., LXXV., CXVI.), the great monarch of the nineteenth
dynasty, who reigned for 67 years (B.c. 1275-1208, according to Petrie). It was under ~
the son and successor of Rameses II. = Meneptah II., that the Exodus probably took
place. A portrait of this monarch is reproduced in Plate XC., which by great good
fortune, as well as an inscription of Meneptah (Plate XCI.), has recently (Feb. 1896) been
recovered by Petrie. The inscription contains the only known mention of the Israelites
in the Hgyptian monuments. “ The Israelites” (we read) ‘are destroyed; they have no
offspring” (cf. Exod. 1. 10-22, but see Description No. 91).
* Hyksos, according to the chronicler Manetho, is derived from the Egyptian hyk or hak, “ prince,”
and sos or shasu the usual term for the Arabian nomads (¢f. Plate C.). Hence, Hyksos = “ Prince of
the Bedéwis.”

TO THE ILLUSTRATIONS.
It has been possible to touch upon only a few of the more striking of the Hgyptian
illustrations included in the present collection (see Plates VIL, X., XX LIV = xXer
XCIV.—CIL., CXVI., CLII. (3)). These should, of course, be studied in detail with
the aid of the accompanying descriptive notes. But before we turn to the impor-
tant series of Assyrian historical inscriptions, it may be worth while to cite one
illustration, from Egyptian religious literature, of language which approaches some of
the higher expressions of Monotheism. The following extract is taken from a hymn
to the god Amun, or Amen, who was the chief god of the Theban pantheon,* and who,
from the rise of the eighteenth dynasty (about 1800 B.C.), was regarded as the national
god of Egypt (cf. the denunciations against this god in Nah.:3. 8; Jer. 46. 25). The
hymn reads :—
The One, Maker of all that is; the One, the only one, the Maker of beings; from whose eyes
mankind issued, from whose mouth are the gods; maker of grass for the cattle, (and) of fruitful
trees for men of future generations ; causing fish to live in the river, birds to fill the air; giving
breath to those in the egg; feeding the bird that flies ; giving food to she bird that perches, to the
creeping thing and the flying thing alike ; providing food for the rats in their holes ; feeding the
flying things on every tree.
Hail to Thee for all these things—the One, alone with many hands, lying awake while all men
sleep, to seek out the good of his creatures—Amun, sustainer of all things! (Cf. Pss. 104 and 121.)
A word should be said here also of the interesting Hittite remains, illustrations of
which are given in Plates VIII. and CIIL—CVII. The Hittite racial type (see Plate
LXII., coloured in the frontispiece) is noticeable as exhibiting Tartar characteristics
(¢.g., the plaiting of the hair in pigtails; see Plates OI., CII.). The type of face is distinct
from that presented by any other of the races of Western Asia. The monuments reveal
the fact that from about 1650 to 1850 8.c. the Hittite Empire in Western Asia was very
powerful, contending on equal terms with Assyria and Egypt. From their original
home, which seems to have been in the Taurus, north of the Gulf of Antioch, they pushed
northward, and westward as far as the neighbourhood of Smyrna. Southward they
advanced into and overran Syria and Palestine (in the time of Abram they had an
advanced post at Hebron, cf. Gen. 23. 2, 3, where the children of Heth is equivalent, of
course, to the Hittites; see Description No. 50).
‘Their power of offence was broken by Rameses IT. (x.c. 1275-1208) in the great: battle
of Kadesh in the Orontes Valley (see Plates LXVII., LXVIIL.). But the final ruin of
the Hittite Empire was not brought about till 714 B.c., when Sargon IT., king of Assyria,
stormed the Hittite capital city of Carchemish. Previously, as the interesting inscription
of Panammt shows, many of their strongholds had passed into the possession of the
Arameans (Syrians).
The series of Assyrian royal inscriptions, of which illustrations are given in Plates
CXV., CXXVI., CXXX., CXXXII., CXLIIL., is of the utmost importance for the
elucidation of the contemporary history of Israel. ‘They bring us face to face with some
of the chief personages in the great religious drama, which is the constant theme of the
eloquent warnings, exhortations, and promises of the Hebrew prophets.
It will not be possible to do anything like justice here, to the mass of illustrative
matter that is made available for the reader in the full descriptive notes that accompany
the Plates. ‘These should, of course, be studied in detail. Attention can only be drawn
(and that im the most cursory manner) to some of the more striking illustrations.

Plates CXXVI—CXXVIIL.), we meet with one of the earliest references to Israel. On

Nineteen districts of the city of Hamath, together with the towns round about them, which

Of the campaign of Sennacherib against Phcenicia and Palestine (including Judea

the city. Moreover, the tribute was sent after the king to Nineveh, not, as in the case of
the captured city of Lachish (see Plates CXXXV., OXXXVI.; and ef. 2 Kings 18. 13,
14; 19. 8), brought to him before the city.

No. 1.
HALF OF AN INSCRIBED LIMESTONE TABLET.
(Cire. B.c. 4500-4000.)
Tuts document, which was brought from the ruins of the great temple of the
Sun at Sippara in Southern Babylonia (ef. Nos. 52, 114, 145; by some identified with
Sepharvaim), is important as exhibiting the oldest known forms of the archaic Baby-
lonian writing, from which the cuneiform characters were in course of time developed.
It probably belongs to the period B.c. 4500-4000 (cf. No. 114). It appears to be a list
of offerings; or it may refer to the temple shepherds, and the flocks and herds in
their charge. Professor Hommel considers the town A-rpINNa, mentioned in the 18th
line, whose Assyrian name would be Nddu, to be identical with the Nod of Gen. 4. 16.
The tablet is now in Mr. Ball’s collection.
No. 2.
INSCRIBED STATUE OF GUDEA, KING OF CHALDEA.
(Cire. B.c. 3000 or 2800.)
Tus long inscription is in a somewhat later form of the archaic linear Babylonian
character. The language is the non-Semitic Sumerian. The statue and inscription
show the skill of the Chaldean sculptor as early as s.c. 3000. The stone is hard
diorite, which the inscription tells us was obtained from Magan, or the peninsula of
Sinai; a fact which seems to indicate the possibility of intercourse, even at so remote
a period, through this region, between Egypt and Chaldea. The inscription records
the building by. Gudea of the temple of his god, Ningirsu.
The statue is one of eight, some standing, others sitting figures, some under life-
size, and others over it, which were found by M. de Sarzee at Vell-Loh (see No. 40)
in 1881, and are now in the Louvre. All these statues have lost their heads; but
one of the two heads numbered 92, 93 may have belonged to one of them, as these
heads were found among them, in the central court of the palace. The statue here
reproduced is known as “Gudea the Architect,” the plan of a building and a graduated
rule being sculptured on the lap. The inscription opens thus :—
“Tn the House of Ninerrsu his King, the statue of Gupra, pontiff-king of Strauna, builder of
(the temple) E-Niynf. One ga of palm-wine, one ga of food, half a ga of grain (or meal) for
sprinkling (?), half a ga of pounded corn (?), as a continual offering he appointed. If a pontiff
king shall abrogate it, cena at nought the command of Ninairsu, may his own continual offe ring
in the House of Nivairsu be abroge ated (and) his own ordinances be done away !” (col. i. 1-20.)
Though the main topic is the building of “ H-Ninnt,” the temple of ‘ Ningirsu,”
the inscription throws some light on Gudea’s relations to other countries. Thus in
col. vy. 21 sqq. we read :—
“When he had built the House of Ninarrsv, Ninairsu his beloved King, spake, (and) opened
wide his (Gudea’s) way from the Upper Sea (¢.¢. the Persian Gulf) to the Lower Sea Ge the
Mediterranean).”
On Amanum (~ Amanus, N. of Lebanon), “the cedar mountain,’ he felled cedars
for the building of his temples, and fetched various kinds of stone from the mountains
of Marv, or Syria and Phoenicia. From Metucucua, or Ethiopia-Meroé, he brought

No. 3.
CLAY TABLETS INSCRIBED WITH EARLY HIEROGLYPHIC FORMS OF
CUNEIFORM CHARACTERS.
Tunse three fragments, the smallest of which came from Kuyungik or Nineveh, and
the two larger ones from Nimrtid or Calah, exhibit certain cuneiform characters side
by side with the antique hieroglyphic figures or rude outlines of objects, from which
they were slowly developed in the course of time and use. It is a curious fact that
the primitive picture-characters of Babylonia had already lost their original shapes long
before the time of Sargon I. (8800 B.c.); whereas the Egyptian hieroglyphs survived
unaltered throughout the whole course of Egyptian history (e.g. cf. No. 10).
Norr.—-The various modes of cuneiform writing, strictly so called, are well exemplified
in Nos. 25 (First Creation Tablet), 61 (Tell el-Amarna Tablet), 114 (Tablet from Sippara),
144 (Inscription of Nebuchadnezzar), and 147 (Cylinder of Nabonidus). It will be seen
that cuneiform type, of which No. 151 is a good specimen, does not perfectly represent
the ancient writing, but is a useful convention for the purposes of printing.
No. 4.
THE PHENICIO-HEBREW ALPHABET;
Snowine its origin from the old linear and primarily pictorial script of Shumir or
Shinar, rather than from the Egyptian hieratic character (cf. No. 7).
Since De Rougé started the theory, many scholars have held that the Egyptian
hieratic writing (No. 7) is the real basis of the Phoenician alphabet. It is, however,
impossible to see any likeness between some of the letters and their supposed Egyptian
prototypes; and the theory leaves the names of the letters—Aleph, Beth, Gimel, &c.—
totally unaccounted for, The late Dr. Mordtmann suggested, but was unable to establish -
the rival view, which is now held by Prof. Hommel and others. For completeness’
sake, our table gives both the Babylonian and the Egyptian hieratic forms.

HEBREW BIBLE: 9th century A.D.
No manuscript of the Hebrew Bible is very old, owing to the Jewish custom which
requires that so soon as a copy of the Scriptures is in any way damaged or defective,
as manuscripts are sure to become in course of time, it shall be put aside and used
no more. ‘The same rule applied to those which were found to have more than two
clerical errors on each page.
The older manuscripts are consequently relegated from time to time to receptacles
called “ Ghenizas”’ attached to the synagogues; and being then neglected they have
generally perished. From such a receptacle the manuscript of which a plate is here
given was rescued, and it is now in the British Museum (MS. Or. 4445). It contains
the Pentateuch, and is the oldest manuscript of any part of the Hebrew Bible at
present known to exist, having probably been written in the 9th century of our era.
The passage here photographed is ue end of Genesis and the beginning of Exodus
(Gen. 50. 283—EHxod. 2. 14).

furnished with vowel-points beneath the letters; the Massorah is without them here,
though in some parts of this manuscript, contrary. to the usual practice, it has them.
One sign of the age of the manuscript is the absence of the colon (:) which marks

THE GOSPEL OF PETER.
Iy this plate is shown a page of the only extant MS. of an early apocryphal Gospel,
which has a special interest from its very recent discovery. In the earliest ages there
were many narratives of our Lord’s life, in addition to the four which the Church
recognised as inspired (cf. Luke 1. 1). Some of these were modifications of the
Gospel narrative to suit the opinions of certain sects; and such was the Gospel
falsely attributed to Peter. It was probably written between a.p. 125-165, in the
interests of the sect of Docetz, who denied the reality of our Lord’s human body,
and consequently of his sufferings. Serapion, Bishop of Antioch in 190-201, found
it in use in some churches of his diocese, and at first allowed it to be read; but on
further investigation forbad it, saying that he found “that most of it belonged to
the right teaching of the Saviour, but some things were additions.” The book was
supposed to be entirely lost, but a MS. was found in Egypt in 1886, and published
in 1890, containing that part of it which relates to the Passion and Resurrection, as
well as portions of the Revelation of Peter and of the Book of Enoch. This manu-
script was probably written in the 6th or 7th century. The narrative shows a
knowledge of the four canonical Gospels; whether it also rests on independent tradi-
tion or other writings is a matter of dispute. The page here shown (very slightly
reduced) contains the final scene of the Passion—the darkness, the cry from the
cross (“My Power, my Power, thow hast forsaken me,” as it is here given), the
rending of the veil of the Temple, and the burial by Joseph.

THE PESHITTA SYRIAC VERSION.
(On this and other Versions, see Aips, pp. 11-13).
Or all the translations of the New Testament the Syriac is the most important for
textual purposes, owing to the very early date at which it was made. Syriac being
the language of Northern Syria, into which Christianity spread very early, a trans-

early Syriac Version, known as the Curetonian Syriac, from the name of the first
discoverer of a MS. of it; and the question of the relative antiquity of this and the
Peshitta is warmly disputed.* The MS. here represented is the oldest copy of the
Peshitta and the oldest dated Biblical MS. in existence, being dated a.p. 464. It is
now in the British Museum (Add. MS. 14425). It contains part of the Old Testament

part reproduced, 6; in. x 63 in.

Five different versions of the New Testament in the Coptic, or Egyptian, language

No. 24.
TINDALE’S BIBLE; printed A.D. 1525.
Wirn the invention of the printing press, the day of manuscript copies of the Bible
was over. Tindale’s Bible is the first English printed Bible; it is also the translation
which most influenced the style of the A.V., much of the splendid language of which
is taken from Tindale. Tindale issued two editions of the New Testament in 1525;
one in quarto form, the other in octavo. Of the octavo two copies exist, one at
Bristol and the other, which is imperfect, in St. Paul’s Cathedral. Of the quarto
only one copy is known, and that a mere fragment, containing only Matt. 1. 1—
22. 12, now in the British Museum. Half a page of this unique copy is here reproduced
containing the beginning of the Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5. 1-12). The language
of this shows that the “history of the Bible has now been oon to a stage well
within sight»of the A.V.

BABYLONIAN EPIC OF CREATION.
(Fragment of the First Tablet.)
Tue Assyrian Creation Tablets were found by the late George Smith at Kwyunyjik,
on the site of the ancient Nineveh, in a chamber of the ruined palace of Assur-bani-
pal, king of Assyria, B.c. 668-626. Their contents, however, are not of Assyrian
origin, the tablets having been copied from Babylonian originals for Assur-bani-pal’s ,
library (see No. 141). As duplicate copies of portions of them have been found in the
ruined temples of Borsippa and Sippara, we may reasonably suppose the composition
of the series to be at least as early as the great literary period 3.c. 2200-1800, when
the Deluge and other stories seem to have been first committed to writing.
There appear to have been seven tablets in the series, but very little is left of
several of them. The following is’a translation of the first, giving an account of the
birth of the gods from Apsti and TiAmat (Ocean and the Deep), before the creation
of heaven and earth :—
When aloft Heaven existed not,
And Earth below was not in being,
But eldest Ocean, the Sower of them (ie. of the gods),
And the primal (?) Deep, who was to bear them all,—

No. 27.
ANCIENT BABYLONIAN MAP OF THE WORLD.
: (7th or 8th cent. B.c.)
Tus unique document is a tablet of dark-brown clay, unhappily very much injured.
The two large concentric circles represent the Ocean-stream, which, according to the
ideas of antiquity, surrounded the earth (see Homer and Hesiod. Herodotus was the
first to doubt the theory: ii. 23). The cuneiform writing between these circles reads:
Nir Marratim, “ The Bitter (or Briny) Flood.”
The triangular projections from the outer circle, of which there seem to have
been seven when the tablet was intact, are marked as “islands”; and on the left
side of each, an inscription specifies its exact distance (from the nearer shore?). The
inscription to the left of the great hole on the top of the outer circle, to the
right, where one of these triangular projections once existed, reads: ‘“ Three KAs-BU
(i.e. six hours) distance”; with the strange addition, “where men do not see the
sun,” which reminds us of Homer’s Cimmerians (Odyss. 11. 14).
The two parallel lines, which run across the ground of the inner circle, represent
the River Euphrates; and the little rings on each side are the cities of the territory
through which it flows. At the top on the right (i.e. on the left bank of the river),
the word suapt, “east,” is written. The Euphrates cuts through the great city of
Babylon, the larger part of which lies on its left or eastern bank. Below, in the
south, the river enters the APPpARU or “marshes.”
The tablet. supplies an excellent illustration of the state of geographical knowledge
at the time. Cf. the four rivers of the Babylonian Paradise, Nos. 37
Gen: 2 (footnote ad fin.), 88; and see Professor Havrr’s paper Wo lag das
Paradies ? in Ueber Land und Meer, No. 15.

ARCHAIC BABYLONIAN SEALS, WITH MYTHOLOGICAL SUBJECTS.
(Cire. B.c. 3000-2000.)
Heropotus (i. 195) states that im his day every Babylonian wore a seal; and this, no
doubt, had been the case from time immemorial. The usual shape of such seals
is that of a small roller or cylinder, pierced lengthways. They are made of jasper,
haematite, diorite, rock crystal, lapis lazuli, basalt, agate, and other hard materials;
and are of considerable importance as illustrating the religious beliefs and ritual of
the ancient Babylonians. The usual subjects engraved on them are scenes from the
national Epic of Nimrod (Gishdubar; Gilgamesh, see No. 37), from the Legends
of Creation, and from the ordinary sacrificial worship. The names of the owners, of

Nos. 31, 32.
ASSYRIAN SACRED TREES WITH CHERUBIC FIGURES.
Tue worship of a sacred tree is common to almost all ancient religions. Among the
Arabs, Pheenicians, Canaanites, Jews (cf. the groves, or rather Asherahs, 1 Kings 14. 28 ;
2 Kings 17. 10), among the Hindoos, the Persians, and the Scandinavians, this form
of idolatry is found. It is therefore natural to find apparent traces of it in the
sculptures of Assyria and Babylonia. It appears to have been most prevalent in
Assyria during the Middle Empire, 8.c. 900-721; and the representations are found
at Nimrid (Calah, Gen. 10. 11), and Khorsébéd (Dor-Shargani, 7.c., “ Sargon’s Castle”),
but not at Nineveh.
Gen. 3.
The peculiar form of the tree may possibly be due to a conventional combina-
tion of three sacred trees, belonging to three ancient traditions.
According to an old Babylonian hymn in praise of the god Ha or Ia,
“Tn Eri-du a dark gish-kin tree grew,
On holy ground it sprang up.
Its appearance was that of gleaming lapis lazuli,
Lying in the deep” (é.e. seen under water).
The GisuKIn was, perhaps, a kind of palm (Chinese k’iung, kwang ?), or a conifer
(Chinese Kien ?); but it may rather have been a flowering shrub, such as the marsh
mallow (Chinese kin, Hibiscus syriacus). Black, white, and grey species are men-
tioned elsewhere. Ent-pvu, “Good City,” being the principal seat of the worship of Ia,
the tree was perhaps sacred as giving oracles by the motion or rustling of its leaves ;
like the oaks of Dodona, the laurel of Delos (Virgil Adn. 3, 91), and that of Delphi
(Hymn to Apollo, 390); ¢f.2 Sam. 5. 24, The “Teacher’s Oak” or “ Terebinth” (A.V.
plain of Moreh), Gen. 12. 6; “The Oak of the Diviners” (A.V. plain of Meonenim),
Judes 95 301; perhaps also Deborah’s Palm, and even the Burning Bush, may reflect
the same order of ancient ideas. The Arabs still believe the thorny bushes of the.
gharqad or box-thorn (a large species of Rhamuus), capable of uttering prophetic
words, and regard the samura, or Egyptian thorn, as sacred.
An Arab tradition states that the vine was the Forbidden Tree in the Garden
of Eden.. Cf. Gen. 9. 20.
The trees before us are conventional representations of the palm. On the settle-
ment of the Babylonians in the Plain of Shinar, or South Chaldea (Gen. 11. 2), they
probably found the Plain covered with palms. The character for palm, which was
read gi-shimmar and shanga, suggests that the name Shangar (Shinar), Shumir, may
mean Palm country. Cf. Deut. 34. 3. According to an Arab proverb, the palm has
a hundred uses beneficial to man. The inscriptions prove that at an early period it
supplied food, both for men and cattle, wood for building, fibre, and many other

Reference may perhaps be made to the palm tree of Deborah (Judg. 4. 5); and.

Nos. 33-36.
ASSYRIAN CHERUBIC FIGURES.
Guardians of Gates and Doorways.—The Guardian Genii were not unknown
to the Assyrians and Babylonians, although the designation Cherubim has not
yet been found in the inscriptions. It is, however, probably akin to the Assyrian
term karubi, “the mighty” (cf. Ps. 29. 1). At the doors of the royal palaces and
temples were placed winged human-headed lions and bulls, as also huge serpents,
These strange composite figures were known by the name of shédi (= Heb. shedim,
Deut. 32. 17, A.V. devils), and lamassi, and were placed at the entrance to public build-
ings to protect the royal pathway and to repel enemies. So the Cherubim
guard the way to the Tree of Life. Cf. also the two Cherubim over-
shadowing the Ark, Exod. 25.18; which were probably human-winged figures like
those which we see performing similar functions in Egyptian paintings. In Ps. 18. 10;
104. 3, a cherub appears as Jehovah’s steed or chariot; 7%.e., the storm-cloud borne
onward by the blast. ‘The Cherubim of Ezekiel’s vision (Ezek. 1 & 10) seem to
combine the principal Assyrian forms in one.

These figures are supposed to represent the ‘‘Scorpion Men” described in the

No. 36.—KEagle-headed Cherubic Figure.—The eagle-headed figures of the
Assyrian sculptures have been by many considered to be representations of the god
Nisroch (2 Kings 19. 37); but for this identification there is no ground whatever.
No such name as Nisroch is known in the inscriptions; and the most tenable
explanation is that Nisroch is a textual error, not for Nergal, as some have supposed,
because there was a temple of Nergal at Nineveh, but for the well-known Assyrio-
Babylonian deity Nuzku-Nebo (Halévy).
The monuments afford us some explanation of what the eagle-headed creatures

THE CHALDEAN STORY OF THE FLOOD AND THE CHALDEAN NOAH.
No. 37.The Deluge Tablet, of which there are several copies in the British
Museum, is one of the most important inscriptions yet discovered. It forms the
eleventh book of the Chaldean Epic of Gizeamesn, or Nimrod. It is introduced there
because the eleventh month of the Babylonian calendar, according to which the Epic
was arranged, was called “the Month of the Curse of Rain,” or “the Month of
Destruction,” corresponding to the Zodiacal sign of Aquarius.
The story is evidently older than the Epic into which it was woven; and is
therefore more ancient than s.c. 2200, the period at which the Epic is supposed to
have been drawn up. It is related to “Gilgamesh” by his ancestor NOu-napisurr *
(i.e. Rest of Soul), called also Atrahasis or Hasisatra (=the Greek Xisouthros), ‘the
very wise or reverent one,’ who is the Chaldean Noah.
The principal points of contact with the Hebrew account are :—
The Deluge is a punishment for sin. Atrahasis and his family are servants of
Ta, the god of the watery abyss. The other gods decree a flood. He is directed to
build a ship to hold himself, his family, and the craftsmen (who were under the
special protection of Ia), as well as the various kinds of animals. The ark is covered
with pitch without and within, and has a deck or covering. The rain lasted six days
and nights. The birds—a dove, swallow, and raven—are sent forth, and the last
returns not. The ark rests on the mount of Nizir. The rescued come forth from the
ark. Sacrifice is offered, and the gods gather round the altar smelling the sweet
savour. The gods agree not to punish mankind again with a flood. Finally the hero
and his wife are taken or translated to live like gods in the immortal land at the
mouth of the four rivers of Paradise.t Here we have an end nearly resembling that
of Enoch.
The chief part of this important text is translated here, Scripture parallels being
suggested in the margin.

TELL EL-AMARNA TABLETS.
In the year 1887 a remarkable discovery of clay tablets in the cunetform writing was
made in Egypt (see No. 60). The discovery of such documents in Egypt was quite
unexpected; but they are now found to supply an important chapter in Oriental
history. The tablets were found at Tell el-Amarna, the ruins of the city of Chu-en-
aten, built by Amenophis IV. after his adoption of the heretical creed of the worship
of the Aten or Solar disk (see No. 60). As there are some letters addressed to his
father, Amenophis III., among the tablets, the whole collection may be dated between
B.c. 1500-1450.
At this period, owing to the marriages of Amenophis III. with wives from
Babylonia and Middanni (N. Mesopotamia), the Egyptian court was crowded with
Asiatics, and correspondence with the Hast was carried on in the style of writing
then most used for diplomacy and commerce in Western Asia, namely, in the Baby-
lonian cuneiform. 1
Among the tablets from the city now in the British Museum, the Royal Museums
at Berlin, and at Gizeh (Cairo), are letters from Babylon and Mippannt, as well
as from Tyre, Sidon, Gebal, Askelon, Gaza, Lachish, and Jerusalem, showing the
universal use of the Babylonian writing at this period, more than a century before
the Exodus. The letters from Jerusalem are of great interest. They are written by
“ Appi-Hrpa,” i.e. Servant of the Good One, to the king, complaining of the advance
of the Philistines and others against him. Abdi-Hiba describes himself as the
Pharaoh’s vassal :
“Behold, this territory of Jerusalem—neither my father nor my mother gave it me; the
king’s mighty arm gave it me!”
Another letter begins :
“To the king, my Lord my Sun. Aspi-Hisa is thy slave. At the king my Lord’s feet
seven times and seven times I fall Behold, I am the king’s officer, and I bring
tribute to the king. Neither my father nor my mother, (but) the king’s mighty arm set me
up in my father’s house.” (Qf 2 Kings 28. 34.)
The tablet figured contains a letter from an unnamed king of Atasuia in
N. Syria to the king of Egypt. Compare the cuneiform letters to a governor of
Lachish described under No. 137.

THE HITTITES.
The Hittites, the Khittim or Bené Kheth of the Hebrews, and the Khetta of the
Egyptians, were a powerful confederation of tribes in North Syria and Asia Minor.
Their original home. seems to have been in the Taurus, north of the gulf of Antioch,
whence they pushed northward and westward as far as the neighbourhood of Smyrna.
Southward they overran Syria and Palestine, having an advanced post at Hebron in
the time of Abram (Gen. 23. 2, 38).
After the expulsion of the Hyksos or Shepherd Kings, completed by Ahmes
(Amosis), the founder of the 18th dynasty, Egypt—under Thothmes III., the greatest
king of that dynasty—established once more its suzerainty over all the petty princi-
palities of Canaan and Aram (A.V. Syria), as far as the Euphrates, and even beyond
it, for the Tell el-Amarna tablets contain despatches to the reigning Pharaoh
(cf. No. 61) from Mesopotamian princes. But as the dynasty became weakened by
internal dissensions (apparently the cause of the periodical fall of Egyptian dynasties),
the Khetta appear in the Orontes Valley (their advance is recorded in the Tell el-
Amarna tablets) as a power able to oppose Egypt, and even to ally itself with
Pharaoh on equal terms (¢f. No. 67). Their power from the 17th to the 14th cen-
turies B.c. was very great in Western Asia. In the Tell el-Amarna tablets, we
find them during the latter part of the 18th Heyptian dynasty advancing through
the Orontes Valley, and gradually obtaining possession of the regions of North cae
and the upper part of the valley of the igpimaies, Their chief centres, Carchemish,
on the principal ford of the Huphrates, and Kadesh, in the valley of the upper Orontes,
were not only commanding military posts, but also great emporia of trade.
On the rise of the 19th Egyptian dynasty about z.c. 1370, Seti I., its founder,
found that towards the close of the previous dynasty, almost all the Asiatic provinces
had been lost. ‘Then commenced a series of annual campaigns conducted with
unceasing vigour, and conspicuously by Rameses II. (Nos. 66, 67; cp. 2 Kings 23. 29).
In the north of Syria, the Egyptians had to encounter the opposition of a powerful
Hittite confederacy. Among the allies were Lycians, Teucrians, Dardanians, and
other peoples who had come eastward during the period of Hgypt’s weakness. In
the end, the offensive power of the Hittites was broken by the great battle of Kadesh,
in which Rameses II. defeated the confederation and their allies from Asia Minor
(see Nos. 68, 68a).
The Old Testament allusions to this warlike and commercial people are few.
The expedition of Hadadezer (2 Sam. 8. 3) may have been directed against the other
Hittite centre, Carchemish, for he had had wars with Tot, king of Hamath, which
seems, from its monuments, to have been (at any rate in later times) a Hittite city.
The confederacy may be meant by the Kings of the Hittites, and evidently
