A HITTITE PORTRAIT.
(Cire. B.c. 1300.)
Tuts head, from an inlaid tile from the palace of Rameses III. at Tell el-Yahudeh, in
Lower Egypt, gives us clearly the type of the race. The type of face is distinct from
that presented by any other of the races of Western Asia. The principal charac-
teristics are the straight nose and the receding forehead and chin; while the plaiting
of the hair in pigtails, Tartar fashion, is distinctly shown (cf. No. 101). The Egyptian
artists depict the Hittites as beardless and blackhaired and of yellowish-white com-
plexion, with a thin wirelike moustache (¢f. No. 102) and brown eyes, and with features,
low stature and thick limbs (cf. Nos. 105, 106), resembling those of the warriors upon
the Monuments of Hamah (Hamath) and Gerabis (Carchemish); their dress com-
prises a high conical cap, with the brim turned up in horn-shaped points, surmounted
by the crescent moon and the solar disk (apparently the emblems of the Hittite
Ashtoreth), and boots with upturned toes and long fingerless gloves. Such boots
and gloves are still worn by the mountaineers of Cappadocia, and indeed of
Asia Minor and Greece, for protection against snow and frost. From such data
it is inferred that the origmal home of the Khetta was in some lofty mountain
range, such as the Taurus. Archaic sculptures and inscriptions scattered through-
out Asia Minor are now termed “ Hittite,’ even including the famous figure on
Mount Sipylus, which the Greeks identified with the Niobe of their mythology but
Herodotus supposed to be a monument of the great Egyptian conqueror Sesostris
(i.e. Rameses II.), because they were found in 1879 to bear hieroglyphics corre-
sponding with those discovered by Burckhardt at Hamah (Hamath) in 1812,
and by Skene and George Smith at Gerdbis in the ruins of ancient Carchemish.
Many of these inscriptions are found in silver mines of the Taurus and Asia Minor;
a sign that the authors of these hieroglyphics worked these mines. See also Nos. 8;
103, 104-107, and Arps, pp. 82, 83.

GREAT HITTITE CAMPAIGN OF RAMESES II.
(The Battle of Kadesh and the King’s Return from the War.)
Ramzszs IT. was a valiant and able warrior, his greatest achievement being the victory
over the strong Hittite confederacy, which he won in the battle of Kadesh, on the
Orontes (see No. 66). This decisive engagement had great influence on the fortunes of
Egypt, and for a long period gave the Egyptians complete command over the rich
provinces of Syria.
The armies met in the narrowest part of the valley, near the city (see Nos. 68, 68a).
Here, after a hard-fought battle, the allies were defeated; but so strong was their
power that the Egyptian king was glad to conclude a treaty of peace with the king
of the Hittites, which was engraved on a plate of silver, and to take his daughter
to wife as part of the bargain. This treaty is the oldest whose terms are on record;
and the poem of Pentaur, describing the battle, inscribed.on the walls of the temple
of Karnak and elsewhere, is considered one of the most valuable historical memorials
of the Hgyptians.
In No. 67, Rameses IT. is represented returning from the war with his prisoners,
who are depicted by nations, and thus furnish the types of many foreigners.
In the first part of the great battle-scene, depicted on the temple wall at Karnak
(Nos. 68, 684), we see the giant form of the King of North and South, Usmr-mait-Ra,
i.e. Potent by the Law of Ra, Sormp-pn-Rx,* Chosen of Ra, RA-mmssu Mert AmuN,*
v.e. Rameses beloved of Amun, driving the chariots of the foe pell-mell into the river.

RAMESES II., THE PHARAOH OF THE OPPRESSION.
(B.c. 1840; Petrie, 1275-1208.)
A: piscovery made at Deir-el-Bahari in 1881 included the mummies of some of the
greatest of the Pharaohs. Among them was the body of the most famous of them
all, Rameses II., the supposed Pharaoh of Moses. This remarkable ruler held the
throne of Egypt for a period of sixty-seven years, and died at an age of over ninety
years. The face is of a highly intellectual type, and indicates great firmness; it is
altogether such as might be expected of a man who conquered the whole of Western
Asia, the famous “ Sesostris” of Herodotus.
Rameses II. was a lavish donor to the Egyptian temples, and especially to that
of the Theban Amun at Karnak (Nos. 64, 65), the greater portion of which was built
by him. In return for this support of the priesthood, the body of the old warrior
was removed from its tomb and hidden in the cave at Deir-el-Bahari when the priests
of Amun fled from Thebes before the advance of the Susian kings of the 22nd dynasty,
B.c, 900.

THE EXODUS.
Ramesses II., after his long reign, was succeeded by his son Meneptah, or Mer-en-
Ptah, i.e. beloved of Ptah, who had latterly been associated with him on the throne.
His father’s enormous expenditure and costly magnificence had impoverished the
realm, and left him an embarrassed heritage (cf. in Judah, the case of Solomon and
Rehoboam some centuries later). Of Meneptah’s reign we know but little; but an
inscription in the Temple of Amun, at Thebes (No. 64), seems to imply by the phrase
* Put away the dejected heart from thee,” that he was lacking in energy. During
his reign the Libyan tribes invaded the western portion of Lower Egypt. Probably
it was then that the watch over the Israelites was removed. On returning from
this expedition the Egyptian army pursued the Israelites. It is not to be expected
that we should find any Egyptian account of the disastrous result. 'The
“a: mai: Biblical narrative, however, does not state that the Pharaoh himself
perished in the Red Sea.
At the close of this dynasty, the Egyptian power once more became weak; and
probably this weakness enabled the Hebrew people to conquer the Canaanites, who
had been disabled by the terrible chastisements of Rameses II., and were disunited
among themselves.
In February 1896 Petrie explored the funeral temple of Meneptah at Thebes,
and had the great good fortune to unearth both the Statue (No. 90) and also the
Stele (No. 91).

Tue great Oriental Venus, under one or other of her names—Ishtar in Assyria, Ash-
téreth in Canaan, and Aphrodite amongst the Greeks—was common to all the religions
of Western Asia; it is, however, from Babylonia and Assyria that we obtain most
information regarding this widely prevalent form of worship.
The cultus of the goddess Ishtar is extremely complex in its character, owing to
the fact that in Assyria especially she was the goddess par excellence, and absorbed
the attributes and epithets of many other goddesses of the older creeds.
The various forms in which she appears there may, however, be thus distinguished :
she was the celestial goddess, the goddess of love, and the goddess of war.
In her celestial character the goddess represents, first, the crescent moon, and
is called the “Daughter of the Moon-god.” In this character she appears in the
legend of the descent of Ishtar into the under-world in search of her lover Tammuz,
ey Adonis; in this character, as Queen of Heaven, we find her worship
14; practised by the Hebrew women and rebuked by Hzekiel and Jere-
Jer.7.18&miah. The weeping for Tammuz, the Dumuzi of the Babylonians, was
bab ei oe great festival in Phoenicia, especially in later times in the glen of
Abaka, “the vale of weeping,” at the source of the Adonis river in the Lebanon.
Tammuz was the youthful summer ‘sun, the lover of the youthful moon, Ishtar, who
was killed by the cruel tusk of winter. It was in this celestial character that Ishtar
appeared as the “two-horned Ashtoreth” (cf. the name Ashteroth-Karnaim, 2.c. the
Ashtoreths of the two horns, Gen. 14. 5) with a crescent moon on her head (cf. the
Hittite cap, under No. 62). The cakes offered to the Queen of Heaven are often men*
tioned in the Babylonian religious texts. She was also the goddess of the planet Venus.
No. 112.—The second character of Ishtar, as the goddess of love and lust, is one
of which we have many examples in the Assyrian inscriptions. It was her special
character as the Ishtar of Erech. The story of her amours is told in the sixth
tablet of the Epic of Nimrod (No. 42); where, like the Greek Circe, Ishtar changes
her lovers into animals, by way of punishing them.
No. 113.—In her character of goddess of war, Ishtar is but little met with in the
Scriptures, being a distinctly Assyrian goddess, whose chief seat of worship was in
Arbela. In this form she is represented as armed with the bow.

CEDARS IN LEBANON.
Tus grove of cedars on Lebanon is that usually visited by travellers. The cedar is
indigenous on other mountains also of the Mediterranean, e.g. the Taurus and Atlas
ranges. Inscriptions record that the kings of Assyria and Babylonia, especially
Nebuchadnezzar II. (the great builder, see No. 144), drew their choicest timber from
Lebanon; cedarwood thence was also used in all three temples of the Jews, viz.,
Solomon’s (2 Chr. 2. 8), Zerubbabel’s (Ezra 3. 7), and Herod’s (so Josephus).

ROBINSON’S ARCH.
Rosrnson’s Aron, discovered by Prof. Robinson, consists of the springing of a bridge
in the S.W. angle of the Haram, part of the temple of Herod, but supposed by the
discoverer to be a survival of the temple of Solomon, whether the work of its founder

destruction and restoration that the Jewish temple underwent, especially the restora-

platform in which this arch occurs; indeed, authorities hold that the whole of the
western and southern substructures are Solomonic, and that the work of Herod can
be easily distinguished above them.

maritime range of Lebanon. Between the two ranges a broad valley (Merj Ayén)

No. 137——Mound of Tell el-Hesy, the site of the ancient Lachish—
The mound of Tell el-Hesy is situated a short distance north-east of Gaza. In 1888
digging was commenced here by Dr. Flinders Petrie on behalf of the Palestine
Exploration Fund, and has been subsequently continued by Mr. W. Bliss, who
named it ‘a mound of many cities.” The explorations led to the identification of the
site as that of Lachish, and this has been subsequently confirmed by the discovery
of an inscribed cuneiform letter to one of the governors of Lachish.
The excavations, carried downwards 60 feet from the top of the Tell, i.e. heap, to
the rocky platform of the original site (60 feet above the stream), revealed a regular
series of ruined cities one above the other, eight or nine in number. The uppermost
of these ruined cities belongs to the later Jewish period, representing the city destroyed
by Nebuchadnezzar, below which were the ruins of the city besieged by Sennacherib
in B.c. 701. Below this, again, were the ruins of an older town, probably of the
age of the Judges; and at a still greater depth the yet older settlement of the
pre-Israelite age of the Amorites. The ruins of this portion were very
hha i carefully explored, and show that the Amorite city was a fortress of
: great strength, walled up to heaven. The walls were over 20 feet thick
and built of mud-bricks sun-dried (¢f. Nos. 73-75). When such buildings fell into
ruins the roofs and upper portions of the walls resolved themselves into a mass of
crumbling earth, which effectually protected and preserved the lower portion of the
houses, as well as all but the most fragile of their contents. On these “heaps”
(of. Jer. 30. 18) of rubbish the subsequent inhabitants built their new city; and
so as city after city fell into decay it made a foundation for its successor, and
buried its own records, to be unearthed by explorers.* In the centre of this portion
Mr. Bliss found the remains of the residence of the governor, with a kind of
primitive barrack before it.
In one of the excavated chambers of this building was found a small clay tablet
in shape and style of writing resembling those found at Tell el-Amarna (No. 61). It con-
tained a letter written to the governor of Lachish, describing the revolt of a. certain
Zimripa and his ally Baya. Both these persons are known to us from the Tell
el-Amarna Tablets; and Zimrida, they inform us, was successful in hig revolt and
took possession of Lachish, but was subsequently slain by his soldiers in the gate
of the city. This tablet is most important, as it shows that the cuneiform writing
was in common use in Palestine about B.c. 1400; a century before the conquest by
the Israelites.

ASSYRIAN KINGS LION-HUNTING.
Tur old Egyptian and Assyrian kings were as proud of their feats in the chase as
in the battle field. In Gen. 10. 9 the legendary founder of the Babylonian monarchy is
called a mighty hunter before the Lord (cf. Nos. 42, 43, and 150),
No. 140.— Assur-Nasir-Pal (8.c. 885-860, cf. No. 115) Hunting the Lion.
Nos. 141, 142.—Assur-bani-pal, king of Assyria (circ. 668-626 2.c.), Hunting
the Lion, The same King Pouring a Drink-offering over his Trophies——The great
and noble Asnapper is certainly to be identified with Assur-bani-pal, the
ere % son of Esarhaddon, who reigned over Assyria with great splendour from
i B.C. 668-626. He probably, after the example of his grandfather, Sargon II.
(B.c. 722, cf. No. 133), had transplanted rebels from Shushan, Elam, Babylonia, and
other places to dwell in the cities of Samaria. ‘The expression used here, “great
and noble,” is a very remarkable one; as this monarch was certainly the most powerful
and magnificent of the kings of Assyria. In the early part of his reign he con-
quered Egypt, capturmg Memphis and Thebes; while in subsequent wars he reduced
Elam to a tributary state, and reconquered Babylonia after the revolt of his brother
Shamas-shum-ukin.
But Assur-bani-pal derives most honour as founder of the royal library which has
preserved to us so valuable a collection of the best Babylonian and Assyrian inscriptions.
This library contained many thousands of tablets, a great number of which have been
recovered by the explorations of Layard, Rassam, and Smith, and are now among the
treasures of the British Museum. The foundation of this library was due, not so much
to any love of literature on the part of the king, as to a political motive; that, namely,
of preventing the young Assyrians from going down to Babylon to be educated, where
treasonable ideas would be instilled into their minds by the priests of Babylon, who were
always in patriotic opposition to Assyria (cf. 1 Kin. 12. 27). The library was a direct
copy of the great library in the temple of Nebo, H-Zidda, at Borsippa (see Nos. 44,
144, 145), and was dedicated to that god. The king, however, claimed to be the
founder of it; and placed this colophon, as a sort of book plate, on all the tablets :—
“Palace of Assur-bani-pal, king of the world, king of Assyria, to whom Nebo and Tasmit
have given a broad ear (intelligence) ; who hath gotten a clear eye [and] the jewel of the scribe’s
mystery, an art which none among the kings who preceded me had acquired. The wisdom of
Nebo, even the contents of the inscriptions, as many as had been made, on [clay] tablets I
wrote, graved, examined (07, united, divided), and for my own reading laid up in my palace.”
The inscription in the field of the second sculpture (No. 142) reads :—
“TI am Assur-bani-pal, king of the world, king of Assyria, on whom Assur and Belit have
conferred exalted power. The lions that I killed—the strong bow of Ishtar, Lady of Battle, I
held upright over them; a drink-offering over them I poured; wine I offered over them.”

Tuts famous bas-relief of the Liberator of the captive Jews is the oldest known relic

GALILEE.
Tur Galilee of the Gospels comprised the Plain of Esdraelon, the parallel ranges of
Lower and the plateaux of Upper Galilee, and the basin of the Lake. The “ Way of
the Sea,” or Via Maris, a term applied to the route from Damascus and the Hast
‘to the Mediterranean, which varied somewhat at different periods, crossed the R. Jordan
above the Lake and traversed either Upper Galilee to Tyre or Sidon, or Lower Galilee
to Ptolemais (Accho, Acre). Another great route, from Bashan and Gilead and the
Decapolis, crossed the Jordan to Bethshan, and mounting the Valley of Jezreel crossed
the Plain to Megiddo and the passes of Manasseh, and led thence to Philistia and
Egypt. The abundant water-supply and fertility of Galilee had fostered a race of
active husbandmen, while the fishertes in its Lake supported a very numerous
population; Galilee therefore was full of busy life, native and foreign, commercial and
agricultural, when it became the scene of our Lord’s early life and of his ministry.
No. 155.—Nazareth (see Gosp. Harm., sec. 11).—Nazareth, where our Lord “was
brought up” (Luke 2. 39, 51 & 4, 16), lies in a basin on the edge of the most
southern of the parallel ranges of Lower Galilee (between which the traffic passed)
just above the plain of Esdraelon. Therefore, although somewhat secluded, it was not
out of the world.
The illustration suggests the local environment of our Lord’s early life. “ The
hills, paths, and well, the single natural fountain in Nazareth, all remain unchanged ”
(Tristram); a fig tree on the left, an olive. grove in the centre, and vineyards and
their buildings on the slope, exemplify the usual features of a Palestinian village.
No. 156.—Cana of Galilee, the hills of Galilee in the distance (see Gosp. Harm.,
secs. 19, 26, and John 21. 2).—As to the site of Cana, the scene of our Lord’s first
miracle, it is certain only that it was near Nazareth and on higher ground.
The illustration shows Kefr Kenna, one of the two supposed sites, 3} miles N.H.
of Nazareth, on one of the ranges of Lower Galilee, and on the direct highway from
Nazareth to the Lake of Gennesaret. It is a typical view, ruins included, of a mud-

No. 157.
JACOB'S WELL (John 4. 6).
See Gosp. Harm., sec. 24.
Av the head of the upland vale (or plain) now called Sahel Mukhna, and just outside
the narrow valley of Shechem, half an hour from the town, is the disused well
(7 feet 6 inches in diameter) traditionally sunk by Jacob (with labour immense for
those days, cf. the well is deep, John 4, 11) down to the mountain limestone and
carefully faced with masonry. ‘This is one of the very few spots in Palestine that
can be certainly identified with the life and words of our Lord.
Our view, photographed on the descent from Sychar (now ’Askar) down the
slope of Mount Ebal, shows the barren Mount Gerizim rising behind the well, its
brow crowned by the domed wely or Mohammedan shrine which marks the site of
the schismatic Samaritan Temple, founded by Manasseh 8.c. 332 and destroyed by
John Hyrcanus B.c. 129.
That summit—still an object of passionate veneration to the little sect of
Samaritans—was doubtless in view (“this mountain”) when our Lord, seated under
the arcades with which Roman builders had enclosed the well, first declared His
Messiahship, pronounced the doom of local worships, and proclaimed His universal
spiritual religion.
No. 158.
THE LAKE OF GALILEE, THE PLAIN OF GENNESARET AND ITS CITIES.
SITE OF CAPERNAUM.
See Gosp. Harm., secs. 19, 26, 27-34, 39-41, 44, 66, 67, 78.
Its “Sea” was the focus of the life of Galilee. The eastern shore was probably (as
now) almost uninhabited. But ruins and the narrative of Josephus testify that the
coast beneath the W. hills, a narrow strip, except in the N.W. corner where the Plain
ot Gennesaret opened out to a width of four miles, was, in Gospel times, an almost
unbroken ring of small towns. The plain and the hills, which rise 4,500 teet above
the Lake (the plain is 680 feet below sea-level), comprise varieties of climate which
permit the growth of trees from the sub-tropical palm (see the Illustration) to the hardy
walnut. This peculiarity, and the luxuriance of the vegetation of the plain excited
the admiration of Josephus (Wars, iii. 10. 8), who describes. the plain as an earthly
paradise where eternal spring reigns and the choicest fruits grow luxuriantly.
The fisheries, especially at the head of the Lake, were so productive that they
maintamed an independent and wealthy population; indeed, the pickled fish of Galilee
was known throughout the Roman, ¢.e. the civilized, world.
Town-walls, houses, synagogues, wharves and factories, fishing boats and nets,
must have lined the western shore, suggesting agriculture and fruit-growing, dyeing
and tanning, boat-building and fish-curing. Add to this the concourse of traders
native and foreign, the processions of camels and asses, evidence of the great carrying
trade along the Via Maris, which St. Matthew (4. 15) identifies with the way of the sea
in Tsa. 9. 1 (see “Galilee” above). With such facts in mind, we can understand the
rapidity with which crowds gathered around our Lord, and the impossibility of solitude
and almost of repose; and we can imagine the eddies and currents of human inter-
course in Galilee of the Gentiles (Gr. nations; Heb. Goyim) upon which our Lord
cast the bread of His teaching and example.
Four towns, Magdala, Bethsaida, Capernaum, Chorazin,* are conspicuous in the
history of our Lord’s ministry on the shores of the Lake; and it is notable that no
* Chorazin is now identified with Kerazeh, on the slope, more than two miles from the shore, between
Tell Hum and the Jordan. Some still place Capernaum at Khan Minyeh.

THE FORUM AT ROME.
Tue old forum or market-place of Rome—which is here shown with the results of
recent excavations—was, from the earliest times, the customary place of public
assemblies and judicial proceedings. In course of time, magnificent temples, basilicas
or law-courts, and other public buildings were erected all about it, the remains of
some of which are conspicuous in the illustration (see also No. 172). The Emperors
Cesar Augustus, Vespasian, Nerva, and Trajan, gave their names to other more
recent fora adjacent to the original one, adorning them with new temples, and
colonnades for business purposes. There can be little doubt that here, in the very
heart of Roman municipal life, St. Pau, was tried, in one of the great basilicas or
halls of justice, and condemned to death (May or June, a.p. 68).
No. 170.
“DIANA OF THE EPHESIANS.”
We give two figures of the Ephesian Artemis, the great Asiatic mother-goddess,
to whose worship the city of Ephesus was so devoted that on its coins it is styled
Nroxkorvs or “temple-keeper” (see Acts 19. 35, margin), as an official title of honour.
The statue, of the Roman Imperial period, is an example of a type which is common in
the Museums of Huropé. The small figure added thereto is from a diminutive specimen
in gold repoussé work belonging to the editor. The original image, which was
believed to have fallen down from heaven, had, perhaps, been fashioned out of an
aerolite or meteoric stone.
The Ephesian goddess was quite distinct from the old Latin Diana and the
Greek Artemis, both in attributes and worship. The many breasts, so conspicuous
on her statues, are totally alien to the idea of the virgin huntress Artemis; and
indicate that she is an old nature-goddess, the mother and sustainer of all things
that live. The same thing is suggested by the heads of animals, resembling bulls
and lions, with which her mummy-like body and the nimbus or aureole at the back
of her head are decorated. In short, she symbolizes the productive and nutritive
powers of mother earth; and is nearer akin to the Phrygian Cybele, and to the
old Babylonian Nand (Nanaea), Gula, or Beltis-Mylitta, the goddess of fertility and

birth, than to either Artemis or Diana. Like Cybele, she wears a mural crown. Her
priestesses, who were called melissai “bees,” were virgins, and her priests eunuchs; the
chief of the latter being the megabuzos (= “given to God,” Old Persian). ‘The temple,
which maintained a multitude of dependents, possessed large estates and rich revenues
from many sources. It was at once a place of worship, a museum of works of art
presented by votaries, an asylum or sanctuary of refuge, and a bank where royal and
private persons deposited their treasures for safety.
In 1863-1874 Mr. J. T. Wood excavated the site, and secured for the British
Museum portions of the fine columns, sculptured round the base with figures in high
relief, and fragments of the frieze. The building, which was reckoned one of the wonders
of the world, was of white marble, and roofed with tiles of the same material. It was
about 418 ft. long by 239 ft. broad, and was surrounded by a double row of columns,
100 in all, each about 56 ft. high. It was destroyed by the Goths, a.p. 262.

THE TRIUMPHAL ARCH OF TITUS,
Showing the spoils of the Temple of Jerusalem.
Tuts Arch, which stands in the Forum at Rome (No. 169), was built by the Senate and
people after the death of the Emperor Titus, to commemorate his conquest of Juda
and capture of Jerusalem, as general under his father, Vespasian, a.p. 70. On the
inner jambs are two fine reliefs, representing (1) the emperor in his triumphal chariot,
and (2), as shown in. our illustration, a group of men in festal array, wearing
laurel wreaths of victory, and. carrying in procession the spoils of the Temple of
Jerusalem, viz., the Table of Shewbread (cf. the description, Exod. 25. 23-80),
the two Silver Trumpets (Num. 10. 1-10), and the great six-branched Golden
Candlestick or Lampstand (Exod. 25. 31 sqq.); see Josephus, Jewish Wars, vii. 5. 5.
The last is said to have been dedicated in the Temple of Peace, where it remained
until carried off by the Vandal Genseric to Carthage, a.p. 455. Recovered by
Belisarius, it was finally deposited in the principal church of Jerusalem, a.p. 533.
Nothing is known of its further fate.

CHU-EN-ATEN, OR AKHU-EN-ATEN (= Splendour of the solar disk), ¢.é.
Amenophis IV., King of Egypt, his Queen, Nefer-titi, and three daughters,
throwing largess to subjects from a balcony of the palace at Chu-aten
(Tell el-Amarna).
Chu-en-dten is supposed by some to be Joseph’s Pharaoh, Brugsch fixes his accession at circ.
B.c. 1466; Petrie dates his reign B.C. 1383-1365. To him and his father, Amenophis III. the Tell
el-Amarna letters were mostly addressed (see No. 61).
In the picture the sun’s rays terminate in hands, which support the bodies and sustain the
crowns of the king and queen; while two of them hold the ankh or symbol of life to the nostrils of
the sovereigns (cf, Deut. 33. 2, 26, 27).

PITHOM :—WINNOWING AND STORING WHEAT IN GRANARIES, under the supervision of scribes
and stewards. (Cf. Gen. 44. 48, 56; Exod. 4. 11.)
In the lower scene the labourers are carrying the wheat in bushel-measures up a staircase to the roof of the granaries, and
pouring it into the chambers below, in the presence of the steward. The capacity of the chambers is marked in numerals on the
walls. Inthe upper scene some are winnowing with wooden shovels, and a scribe sits on a great heap of grain, noting the
number of bushels carried to the store-chambers. Before him is written, “The scribe of wheat measures, Tehuti-nefer.”

BRICK-MAKING IN EGYPT, under the supervision of taskmasters (Exod. 4. 14;5. 7-18),
From a series of wall-paintings in a tomb at Abd-el-Garnah, representing the foreign captives of Thothmes III. employed in building
the Temple of Amun at Thebes, Among the inscriptions these words occur: “'The taskmaster saith to the labourers ‘ The stick is in my
hand; be not idle!’”
Scene I.—Inscription : “Captives whom his Majesty carried away, building the Temple of his father Amun,” A man emptying a bucket
of mud; a taskmaster with stick looking on. Two men carrying loads of bricks, slung from yokes. A taskmaster with uplifted rod ;
two men carrying mud in vessels, and another with yoke and slings.
Scene II.—Here we see two men fetching water in large jars from a pond full of water-lilies; two others cutting off portions of
the clay; another carrying a load of it to the moulder, who is just turning a brick out of his wooden mould; another fixing his
cutter; and another settling the bricks in rows to dry, The inscription states that the work is “for the new building of the storehouse
of the god Amun of Apt in Thebes,’’

THE BIBLE:
[FS HAisTORY:
By Rev. H. B. SWETE, D.D., Regius Professor of Divinity, Cambridge.
| WVHAT is the Bible?
Under what conditions have its manifold elements been brought into their
present form? By what means has this collection of ancient documents reached our own age, and
what security have we that its contents are substantially identical with the originals? Lastly, by what
| process and in what sense has the Church been led to attach unique authority to this volume as an
inspired record of the Revelation of God ia
These and other kindred questions meet the thoughtful reader on the very threshold of Biblical study.
A full answer can only be gained by prolonged investigation, or from the scholarly and often inaccessible
labours of specialists.
The aim of the present brief introduction is to place before beginners and those
| whose opportunities do not allow more extended reading, a summary of the most important results
which have been reached by competent enquirers.
Tt will deal successively with (1) the titles of the Book ;
(2) the languages in which its contents were originally written ; (3) the divisions under which they have
| been grouped; (4) the history of their collection into the ‘‘Canon”’ of Holy Scripture; (5) the manner of
their transmission to
our own times; (6) the growth of Biblical versions and translations into the
vernacular; (7) the course which Biblical interpretation has followed. both among the Jews and in the
Christian Church; and lastly, (8) the unity which characterises the completed Canon notwithstanding
| the complexity of its parts, and the nature of its claim to a Divine authority.
UWS A
“The Scriptures ’—“ The Bible.”
Durine the gradual accretion of the writings which
compose our ‘‘ Bible,’ it was impossible that the
books should receive a collective name. ‘The suc-
cessive writers were scarcely conscious that they
were contributing to a treasury of sacred literature.
Harlier portions of the Bible are however recognised
by later writers as “‘ the Books”’ (Dan. 9. 2; Heb.) ;
the New Testament refers to the Hebrew Canon as
“the Scriptures,” or “ sacred writings ” (Matt. 22.
99; John 5. 39; 2 Tim. 8. 15), and in one passage
appears to place the writings of the Apostles in the
same category (2 Pet. 3. 2, 16). In the second
century a Christian omily (Ps.-Clem. 2 Cor. 14)
speaks of ‘‘ the Books (rd BiBAt&), and the Apostles ”’
in a manner which implies that they were regarded
as of co-ordinate authority. The fourth century
supplies more than one instance of the Greek O.T.
and the Greek N.'T. having been copied into a single
codex. St. Jerome (perhaps after 2 Macc. 2. 18)
called the entire Canon “‘the Divine Library,”
and by this name it was known to our Anglo-
Saxon forefathers, whilst ‘‘ Bibliotheca’? became
in the medieval Church the technical designation
for a complete MS. of both Testaments. Among
Greek writers it was usual to speak of the Old and
New Testaments, regarded in the light of a single
collection, as ‘the Books,’ and this collective use
of the title prevailed eventually in the West. In
the Latinity of the thirteenth century the neuter
plural was converted into a feminine singular, and
“the Books’? were thenceforth known as “the
Book.” Thus the Church arrived at a title for
Holy Scripture which impresses the reader with a
sense of its unity, almost to the exclusion of the his-
torical distinctness and intrinsic variety of its parts.
“Old Testament ’—“ New Testament.”
Earlier than the collective title of the entire
volume were the distinctive names of its two great
parts. Already in 2 Cor. 3. 14, the Book or the
Law is called “the Old Testament’? (“‘ Covenant,”
Gk.). The Law was itself a covenant (Bxod. 19. 5);
a book which contained it was a ‘‘ Book of the Cove-
nant’? (Exod. 24. 7); and by an easy extension the
name was at a later time given to the Pentateuch
(1 Macc. 1. 57; cf. 2 Kings 23.2). In contrast with
the Law the Gospel was called “the New Cove-
nant”? (Matt. 26. 28), and the name was in due
course applied to the Christian Scriptures. In
the early Latin Versions St. Paul’s “Old Cove-
nant’? became “vetus testamentum,”’ through a
misunderstanding of the Greek noun; and the
error affects to this day the names of both portions
of the Bible. In the West they were known from
the end of the second century as the “Old” and
“New? Testaments, and the names have survived,
notwithstanding a disposition on the part of Ter-
tullian, the father of Church Latin, to substitute
“Tnstrumenta’? (=documents) for “ Testaments.”
ORIGINAL LANGUAGHS.
I.—Hebrew and Chaldee.
Hrsrew, the language of the 0. T., belongs to a
family of languages known as “ Semitic,” because
chiefly spoken by descendants of Shem (Gen. 10.
21, ff.), and at various times prevalent in Western
Asia, from the Mediterranean to the Tigris, and
from the Armenian mountains to the Arabian Gulf.
The family divides itself into several branches,
Arabic, Aramaic, the Assyrian of the cuneiform

inscriptions, and Biblical Hebrew, with its next
of kin, the language of ancient Phoenicia. These
languages possess in common certain strongly-
marked peculiarities of grammar and syntax, such
as word-stems of three consonants, verbs of two
tenses, nouns of two genders, and in the structure
of the sentence a mere sequence of clauses.
The word ‘‘ Hebrew”’ occurs for the first time in
Gen. 14. 13, as a designation of Abram, either as a
descendant of Eber, or in the sense of immigrant,
one who had crossed the River Euphrates to settle in
Palestine. No O.T. writer applies it to the language
of Abram’s descendants, which is rather described
as “‘ Jewish”’ or “ Canaanitish’’ (2 Kings 18. 26, 28;
Neh. 13. 24; Isa. 19. 18); and when it appears in
this connexion in the N. T. (John 5. 2; 19. 20;
Acts 21. 40; 22.2; 26.14), the reference is to the
spoken dialect and not to the Hebrew of the O. T.
Josephus indeed uses it also for the latter; but the
Targums prefer to describe the language of the
Bible as ‘‘the sacred tongue.”’
A few portions of the later Books are written in
an Aramaic dialect known as ‘‘ Chaldee,”’ viz. Ezra
4, 8—6. 18; 7. 12-26; Dan. 2.4—7. 28; and a single
verse of Jer. (10. 11).
II.—Greek.
In the fourth century before Christ the East was
opened up to the influences of Greek civilisation by
the career of Alexander (d. 323 B.c.). Under his
successors, the Seleucidee and the Ptolemies, Syria
and Egypt received the language and culture of
Greece. Among the Jews the process was most
rapid at Alexandria, where a translation of the He-
brew Scriptures into Greek was in progress from
the middle of the third century (p. 11). In Judea,
under Antiochus Epiphanes (d. 164 B.c.), Greek in-
fluences received a check from the Maccabean reac-
tion; but the subsequent arrival in Palestine of the
Romans, and the rise of the Herod dynasty, revived
the spread of the Greek language; and in the days
of our Lord Greek was spoken together with
Aramaic, at least in the cities and by men of
business or education. The polyglott inscription
on the Cross points in this direction. In the pri-
mitive Church of Jerusalem a minority at least were
Greek-speaking or “‘ Hellenists’’ (Acts 6.1). Out-
side Palestine, the ‘‘ Dispersion,” not only at Alex-
andria and Cyrene, but in all the countries border-
ing on the Mediterranean, spoke Greek (cf. e.g.
Acts 21. 37, 39) and used the Greek Bible, whilst
their numerous “‘ proselytes’? were for the most
part of Greek birth or education. The Greek lan-
guage was at the time as prevalent throughout
the Roman Empire as French is now in Western
Europe, or Italian in the Levant, or as English is
not unlikely to become throughout the civilised
world. ‘Thus when the earliest Christian teachers
wrote their memoirs of the life of Christ, or ad-
THE BIBLE—ITS DIVISIONS.
)
dressed letters to mixed congregations at Ephesus,
Corinth, or Rome, it was natural that they should
employ Greek rather than Aramaic. It must not
be inferred that our Lord’s discourses were deli-
vered in Greek, or that Greek was the ordinary
vehicle of conversation between Himself and His
Galilean followers. In written monuments of the
New Faith the vernacular would have been mani-
festly inconvenient, and even in Palestine unneces-
sary. Much may be said in favour of the belief
that St. Matthew’s Gospel, which was designed for
Hebrew Christians, had an Aramaic original; but
the Greek Epistle to the Hebrews, notwithstanding
an early conjecture to the contrary, almost certainly
came from the writer’s pen in its present form.
The N. 1’. is therefore a Greek book. And yet it
must be understood that the Greek of St. Matthew
and St. Mark, St. James, St. Peter and St. John,
even of St. Luke and St. Paul, differs widely from
that of the classical writers of ancient Greece, and
to some extent from that of contemporary Greek
authors. The language of the N. T. is, in fact, a
variety of later Greek. The spoken Greek of Alex-
ander’s vast Empire was founded on the Attic
dialect, modified by a large infusion of provincial-
isms, and the resultant was known as the ‘‘ common
dialect.’’ This dialect. became in time the basis of
the literary style as it was used by foreigners.
When the “‘common”’ Greek was adopted by the
translators of the O.T. as the vehicle of Hebrew
thought, it was coloured by Semitic ideas and
phrases, by metaphors borrowed from the life
of the Hebrew race, and, above all, by religious
associations entirely alien to the conceptions of the
Greek mind. In the Greek O. T. this Hebrew ele-
ment is so strong as at times to overpower both
grammfér and sense, and the result is sometimes a
transliteration rather than a translation. A collec-
tion of original works, such as the Greek N. T., is
naturally less full of foreign forms, especially in
those portions of the book which are due to writers
who had learned Greek as a literary language. On
the other hand, it is perhaps in these writers (St.
Luke, St. Paul, and the author of the Epistle to the
Hebrews) that we find the largest proportion of new
Greek words and forms, and of Greek words used in
new senses required by the exigencies of the new
teaching. To these circumstances it is due that

THE CANON.
Tae Greek word kavév, canon (cp. English cane,
cannon) means a straight reed or rod, especially one
which has been graduated for the purpose of mea-
surement, a rule or standard. Warly Church writers
(e.g. Ivengeus) applied it to the traditional faith,
“the rule of truth.’ In the third century, Origen
spoke of the acknowledged Scriptures as ‘‘ canon-
ized,”’ 7.e., tried and approved by the Church’s rule;
and in this passive sense they were described, a
century later, as ‘‘the Canon.”’? But once allowed
as “‘canonical,’? the Sacred Books themselves be-
came a standard of truth, a canon in the active
meaning of the word. This meaning has long pre-
vailed; and by the Canon of Scripture we now
understand the written standards of Christianity,
including the pre-Christian Books which the Church
has inherited from the Jewish synagogue.
The history of the Canon falls into two parts, an-
swering to the two great divisions of the Christian
Bible, the Old Testament and the New.
The Canon of the Old Testament.

the steps by which the Canon of the Old Testament

giographa.”’ This arrangement suggests and cor-

The history of the transmission of the N. T.
Scriptures differs widely from that which has just
been passed under review. The text of the N.T.
rests upon the combined testimony of three streams
of documentary evidence—extant MSS. of the Greek
original, ancient versions, and “patristic”? quota-

Christian writers known as “‘ the Fathers.’’
1. Manuscripts.—The autographs of the N. T.

most part on thin leaves of papyrus (2 John 12;

sibly copies of O. T. Books), often by the hand of a
scribe to whom the inspired author dictated his
words (Rom. 16. 22), the original documents had
little value for men who lived in an age of Apostolic
teaching, and who could not anticipate their im-
portance to posterity. They served their immediate
purpose, were copied for transmission to. other |
Churches or for private study, and ere long perished
in the using.
All the copies of the first three centuries have
disappeared together with the autographs. The
violence of Diocletian, who in 303 A.p.—like a
second Antiochus Hpiphanes—ordered all the sacred
books to be burnt, enhanced the importance of the
N. Tl. Canon at the expense of the great majority of
its existing MSS. But enough survived to transmit

It remains to consider the history of the Greek
text of the N. T. since the invention of printing.
The honour of being the first to print the entire
N. T. in the original belongs to Cardinal Ximenes ;
it formed the fifth volume of his great Polyglott,
which passed through the press in 1514, but was
not published before 1520. Meanwhile, Erasmus
had published a Greek Testament at Basle, in 1516 ;
and the book was so welcome that before his death,
in 15386, it had gone through five editions. The
mantle of Hrasmus fell upon Robert Estienne
(Stephen), whose third edition (Paris, 1550) was
the first Greek Testament with anything like an
apparatus of various readings. Stephen’s work
was substantially reproduced by the famous Elzevir
press at Leyden; from a phrase in the preface to
the Elzevir edition of 1633 it has acquired the name
of the “‘ Received Text.’ This text seems to have
been in great part the basis of the Authorised
English Version of 1611, and has been adopted in
the majority of non-critical editions of the Greek
Testament. But it rests on very slender authority.
Stephen chiefly followed Erasmus; Hrasmus de-
pended on three or four cursives, subsequently
correcting his text by the Complutensian, which
also seems to have been based on a few compara-
tively late MSS. Stephen’s endeavour to bring
together a critical apparatus led to better results.
In England, his example was followed by Bishop
Brian Walton, in the great London Polyglott (1667) ;
by Bishop Fell, in his Greek Testament. of 1675;
and above all by Dr. John Mill, in his folio Greek
Testament of 1707.
Bentley issued proposals for the restoration of a
pure text, and hegan preparations, which led, how-
ever, to no immediate result. The task was taken
up by Germany in the person of J. A. Bengel, whose |
Greek Testament of 1734 for the first time departs
to some extent from the textus receptus. Matthai
followed in 1782 with a critical text: Griesbach
with the more important edition of 1796-1806, in
which the editor’s departures from the. Elzevir
text are distinguished by the use of smaller type.
At length, in 1720, the great |
Lachmann at last (1831-1850), abandoning the re-
ceived text altogether, drew his materials directly
from the uncial MSS. within his reach, making it
his aim to restore the text of the fourth century,
Tischendorf took up the work, and in eight editions
(1849-1872) endeavoured to bring up the text to the
level of the knowledge which his own researches
had so largely augmented. Meanwhile, Hngland
was returning to the task. Dr. Tregelles re-edited
the Greek Testament (1857-1872) mainly on Lach-
mann’s principle. Lastly, in 1881, there appeared
at Cambridge the joint work of Dr. Westcott and
Dr. Hort, with an introduction by the latter which
has produced little less than a revolution in the
science of N.T. criticism. Rejecting Lachmann’s
limit, Westcott and Hort made it their aim, as
Tregelles and Tischendorf had done, to obtain “ the
closest possible approximation to the Apostolic
text itself.” But in doing this they took up
afresh the project of Griesbach, and of Bengel
before him, to lay ‘‘a secure historical foundation
in the genealogical relations of the whole extant
documentary eyidence.”? Their investigations led
them to the conclusion, that in the third century
there existed at least three types of text, which they
distinguish as the Western, the Alexandrian, and
the Neutral. At the end of the fourth century a
fourth type appears, which exhibits a deliberate
blending of the three earlier texts. This mixed text

quently revised. (2) That of De Sacy, the Port-
Royalist, undertaken during his imprisonment in
the Bastile (1666-8). (8) Revisions of Olivetan’s
Bible, by Martin (1704) and by Osterwald (1724).
(4) The N. T. of Beausobre and L’Enfant, trans-
lated from the Greek (Amsterdam, 1718). (5) The
Bible of Geronde, a Roman Catholic translator,
who follows the Vulgate (1820-4).
There are thus many French Bibles, but the
French language yet waits for a national version.
It will doubtless be forthcoming as soon as the
nation manifests any general desire for a vernacular
Bible—a result hardly to be expected until the
Gallican Church has recovered her ancient liberties.
4. SpanisH.—In Spain, as in France, the Al-
bigenses seem to have anticipated the task of the
Biblical translator; and here, as elsewhere, partial
translations existed in MS. during the middle ages.
A version in the Catalan dialect was printed in
1478. In the next century two Spaniards, resident
abroad under Protestant influence, published ver-
sions of the Scriptures into their native tongue—
Enzina, who printed the N. T. at Antwerp in 1548,
and De Reyna, whose complete Spanish Bible ap-
peared at Basle in 1569. The Bible of De Reyna
was afterwards revised by De Valera (Amsterdam,
1602). Nor have the Roman Catholic clergy of
Spain been wanting in efforts to supply their coun-
try with a vernacular Bible. Padre Scio translated
the whole Bible from the Vulgate (1798), and
Bishop Amat, of Valencia, published an edition
with notes (Madrid, 1824). Another version was
printed in Mexico (1831-3).
5. Irantan.—A few portions of the Bible in
Italian are found in MSS. of the fourteenth and
fifteenth centuries. The first complete Italian
Bible was published at Venice, in 1471, by the
Benedictine, N. di Malermi. A second, by Antonio
Bruccioli (Venice, 1532), claimed to have been
translated from the original text. A third version,
professedly from the Vulgate and supplied with ex-
planatory notes,was the work of Ant. Martini, Arch-
bishop of Florence (Turin, 1769-79), and received

The above are but a few of the principal versions
of the Bible in the most important languages of

from the fact that the Report of the British and

Church, missionary enterprise has added largely to

BIBLICAL INTERPRETATION.
A Book which collects the literature of a thousand
| years, touches upon so many ancient, civilisations,
and treats of so many mysteries, clearly needs ex-
position. Both Jewish and Christian interpreters
have found in the exposition of the Bible an abun-
dant field for their learning, their ingenuity, or
their religious insight.
I—Jewish Interpretation.
To Ezra belongs the honour of having founded
| the long line of Jewish interpreters. Himself “a
ready scribe in the Law of Moses,’’ who “‘had set
his heart to seek the Law of the Lord and to do it,
and to téach in Israel statutes and judgments”’
(Ezra 7. 6, 10), his work was taken up by “ families
of scribes’? (1 Chron. 2. 55), organised bodies of
| men who devoted their lives to this end. The
Sopherim, or Scribes, were succeeded by other
schools of interpreters, the Tannaim (Teachers),
and the Amoraim (Speakers), each of which con-
tributed to the sum of Jewish exposition. With
the Sopherim arose the ‘‘ Chaldee paraphrases’’
or Targums (p. 11); with the Tannaim and
Amoraim respectively, the Mishna and the Gemara,
which make up the Talmud. The Talmud exists
in two forms, the Talmud of Jerusalem and the
Talmud of Babylon. The exegesis of the Talmud
falls under the heads of Halacha and Haggada.
Halacha consists of ritual and moral decisions based
upon the Law; Haggada is a maze of legend,
allegory, and hortatory matter founded on the
historical books.
The Midrashim, or commentaries (cf. 2 Chron.
24. 27, Heb.), form another body of Jewish expo-
sition, ranging from the second to the thirteenth
century after Christ. They deal with the literal
sense, the latent meaning, the illustration and
application of the text, and, like the Talmud, are
partly Haggadic, partly occupied with Halacha.
The Qabbala belongs to the history of theosophy
rather than of interpretation, playing (e.g.) with
the numerical values of the letters which compose
the words of a text, while it leaves the real difficulties
untouched.
Two later schools of Jewish O. T. interpretation
stand in marked contrast with the compilers of the
Talmud andthe Midrashim. (a) The Karaites, who
| date from the eighth century A.D., rejected oral
tradition, confining themselves to the plain meaning
of the written Law. (b) In the eleventh and twelfth
centuries a succession of eminent Hebrew expositors
began to treat the sacred text grammatically and
with a view to the literal sense. The most eminent
of these writers are R. Saadia, R. Salomo Isaaki
(abbreviated Rashi), Ibn Ezra, Maimonides, and the
Qimchis. Notwithstanding -reactions, this school
continues to bear fruit amongst educated Jews,
| many of whom incline to a liberal or even a rational-
istic interpretation of the Old Testament.
To the Christian student of the O. T. the most
| interesting period in this long history is that which
coincides with the lifetime of Christ and of the
Apostles. The earliest extant literature of Jewish
exposition is probably later than the Christian Era,
but its traditional character was already fixed when
our Lord preached His Sermon on the Mount. In
the ritual niceties of the Pharisees (e.g. Mark 7. 3-5)
we may see the germ of the Mishna; in the ‘‘ fables
and endless genealogies’? condemned by St. Paul
(1 Tim. 1. 4), the beginnings, of Haggadic and Kab-
palistic lore. The formalism and hair-splitting of
Jewish orthodoxy were already sufficiently marked
to throw into bold relief the freshness and power
of the new revelation (Matt..7. 28, 29). On the
other hand, the Sadducees, who denied the authority
of the oral tradition, missed altogether the deeper
truths of the written Law (Matt. 22. 29), and thus
were equally far from the teaching of Him who came
not to destroy the Law but to fulfil.
Besides these antagonistic schools of Palestine,
there existed at Alexandria in the time of Christ a
school of Jewish interpreters distinct from both,
and yet scarcely nearer to the Christian standpoint.
The Hellenists had learnt to interpret the O. T. in
the lightiof Greek culture. | Poets such as Ezekiel
of Alexandria rendered the Hxodus into. Homeric
verse; commentators like Aristobulus found in the
Pentateuch the origin of the Greek philosophy, a
result which they reached by abandoning the literal
truth of the Hebrew narrative. The system was
perfected by an Alexandrian Jew who was co-eval
with our Lord. According to Philo, the literal
sense of Scripture was addressed to the popular
understanding; the mystical, to the few of deeper
spiritual insight, Without denying the historical
truth of the narrative, he regards it as at least of
secondary importance, and the details as yaluable
only for their symbolism. The men and women of
the QO. T. are in Philo’s view characters rather than
persons; the countries and natural objects it men-
tions are treated as mere emblems of moral truths.
We are now prepared to turn to the history of
II.—Christian Interpretation.
The earliest examples of Christian interpretation
are to be found inthe N. I. The O. T. is largely
quoted by our Lord and His Apostles, and the
quotations, with the remarks they call forth, sutffi-
ciently indicate the line of interpretation which is
adopted. It is equally removed from the formality
of the Scribes, the rationalism of the Sadducees,
and the mysticism of the Alexandrians. ‘The Pha-
risees were rebuked by Christ as virtually set-
ting aside the Law by overlaying it with tradi-
tions, the Sadducees as ignorant of the Scriptures
which taught by implication the truths they over-
looked. lo the Apostles and their contemporaries,
guided by the teaching of the Master and by the Holy
Spirit, the O. T. is not merely a system of rules, ora
manual of national history, or a field for speculation.
They recognise the true inspiration of the Hebrew
Canon (2 Tim. 3.16; 2 Pet. 1. 21), and at the same
time its fragmentary and preparatory character
(Heb. 1.1). The Books of the O. 'T. are big with
thoughts and hopes greater than their writers could
comprehend (1 Pet. 1.10, 11). A particular passage

16 THE BIBLE—ITS INTERPRETATION.
of Scripture, personified as an organ of the Divine
Spirit, is said to foresee a future application of its
words to the Gospel'and the Church (Gal. 3. 8):
Moreover, the events of the history are sometimes sus-
ceptible of an interpretation which passes beyond the
letter: there are designed parallelisms between the
facts of the O. T’. and the facts of the New; and to
this extent St. Paul accepts the use of ‘allegory ”’
(Gal. 4, 24). But, above all, the O. T. is for
Christians a volume of practical teaching, inspiring
courage and hope, supplying needful correction and
discipline (Rom. 15. 4; 2, Tim. 8/16, 17). If in
this use of Scripture there are points of contact with
both the Rabbinical and the Alexandrian schools,
the method as a whole is original; and in its dis-
tinctly practical purpose it stands quite apart from
all the contemporary methods of interpretation,
The first great school of post-Apostolic Christian
interpretation arose at Alexandria at the end of the
second century. The Christian school of Alexan-
dria shared with its Jewish precursor the allegorical
treatment of the O. T. Scriptures. But inits hands
the method of Philo acquired new precision and
entered on new fields. To Clement of Alexandria
the esoteric treatment of Scripture approved itself,
not merely as offering points of contact with Greek
philosophy, but as satisfying the wants of a Chris-
tian gnosis. His greater successor Origen perfected
the system. As man consists of body, soul, and
spirit, so, Origen argued, Scripture must needs
have its own trichotomy—its triple sense—the
literal, the moral, and the spiritual; and the last
and highest is identified by him with the allegorical.
But in Origen’s hands allegory became the servant
of the highest truth; and it was largely in this form
that, from the third century to the thirteenth, the
spiritual teaching of Scripture gained acceptance,
especially in the Western Church. Moreover, he
may be regarded as the pioneer of the grammatical
and critical study of Holy Seripture. The remains
of the Hexapla bear witness to his zeal for ‘textual
purity ; his commentaries shew thati he refused to
indulge in allegorical interpretation until he had
first laid a firm basis in grammar and history.
Lastly, the homilies of Origen set the example of
the expository preaching which in ancient Christen-
dom supplied the place of the popular commentary,
and to which we owe some of our best materials for
the interpretation of the New Testament.
In the fourth century a second great school of
Christian interpretation arose at. Antioch, the capi-
tal of Syria. Its reputed founder was Diodore,
Bishop of Tarsus (d. 393) ; its chief representatives
were Theodore, Bishop. of Mopsuestia (d. 428), Theo-
doret (d. 457), and, best known to the West, St.
John Chrysostom. ‘The first is the commentator
proper, the second the annotator, the third the
homilist and Christian orator. With Origen, Theo-
dore based his interpretation on grammar and his-
tory; in strong contrast to Origen, he refused to
earry it beyond the literal, or at most the ethical,
sense. But opposition to the allegorical school
carried him much further. He gave up the directly
predictive character of O. T. prophecy, allowing to
only three or four of the Psalms a truly Messianic
character; the use of the Prophets by the writers of
the N. T’. was explained on the principle of accom-
modation, or by a providential analogy between the
historical settings of the two Covenants. These
peculiarities disappear in Chrysostom’s expository
preaching and in Theodoret’s notes; with the for-
mer the spirit of the Antiochene school shews itself
chiefly in the careful treatment of grammatical
questions, and in the practical and common-sense
treatment of the text, which thave given a perma-
nent value to his interpretation of the Gospels and
the Epistles of St. Paul.
Ancient Latin Christianity can hardly be said. to
have produced a, distinct school of Biblical interpre-
tation. From the days of Tertullian (d.¢. 220), Latin
writers continued to expend a vast amount of labour
on the exposition of Scripture. But as expositors
they laboured under great disadvantages. With one
brilliant exception they were practically ignorant of
Hebrew; with few exceptions they possessed little
or no knowledge of Greek. Jerome, the solitary
Hebraist of Western Christendom, is, as a com-
mentator, remarkable for acuteness and learning
rather than for judgment or good’ taste. A collec-
tion of terse and often useful notes on St. Paul’s
Epistles, once attributed to Jerome, is due to the
heresiarch Pelagius; a fuller commentary of con-
siderable merit was the work of an otherwise un-
known Hilary, who, from a mistaken identification
with St. Ambrose, is usually known as ‘the Am-
brosiaster.”” But the most prolific, and at the same
time the most important, expositor of the West is
St. Augustine of Hippo, whose sermons are a store-
house of materials for the spiritual and dogmatic
treatment of both Testaments. To Augustine’s
mind, “‘the New Testament lies hid in the Old,
and the Old lies open in the New’; he begins at
any Scripture which happens to have been read in
Church and preaches from it Jesus and the Christian
Faith. His weakness is a passion for allegorising,
which lands him at times in a fanciful or even im-
possible exposition; his strength lies in terse anti-
thesis, a wide experience of life, a depth of spiritual
insight seldom surpassed.
After the sixth century, independent. exposition
ceased generally both in Hast and West; its place
was taken by compilations culled from. earlier
writers, known as catenc and glosse.\ These collec-
tions are chiefly valuable).as preserving. to us frag-
ments of original works. which would otherwise
have altogether disappeared. In the middle ages
the stream of Latin interpretation received two new
contributions : the mysticism—of which St. Bernard
of Clairvaux (d. 1153) is the best representative—
and the dialecticism which fills the folios of the
Schoolmen. But patristic exposition is the back-
bone of the medizeval commentary—the exposition,
moreover, of Origen and of Augustine rather than
of the Antiochenes. An exception must be made
in the case of Nicholas de Lyra (d. 1340), whose
grammatical method, based, perhaps, on a study
of the liberal Jewish commentators of the eleventh
century (p. 15), was afterwards thought to have
prepared the way for the Reformation: “si Lyra
non lyrasset, Lutherus non saltasset.”’
With the sixteenth century, the interpretation of
Scripture took a new departure. It is enough to
mention the names of Hrasmus, Luther, and Calvin,
to shew the stride which Biblical study made in
fifty years. The revival of Greek and Hebrew learn-
ing opened to commentators new fields of labour;
the dissemination of printed texts, coupled with the
new and intense interest awakened by the study of
the Bible, supplied them with appreciative readers.
The period which followed the Reformation was too
much preoccupied with theological strife to sustain
this interest; yet the seventeenth and eighteenth
centuries yielded Biblical scholars of the first order
—in England, Walton and Lightfoot, Pearson and
Ussher, Mill and Lowth, Hammond and Whitby ;
and among Continental scholars, Grotius and Wet-
stein, and the great Bengel. The present age has

witnessed in Germany a vital struggle between a
| destructive rationalism and a rational orthodoxy,
with the general result that no period in the whole
history of the Church has been so fruitful in the
| scientific examination of every part of Holy Scrip-
| ture.

A. MOMENTOUS question remains to be answered.
Popular belief regards the Bible as an inspired Book
containing a revelation from God. On what grounds
does this opinion rest? Can it be maintained in
sense ? under what limitations ?
1. The reasonableness of the belief that a Reve-
Hebrew race, and the evidence which has led the
Christian world to recognise in Jesus Clirist the |
perfect manifestation of God are subjects anterior
to the question of Biblical Inspiration, and théir
treatment must be sought elsewhere. But assum-
ing the existence of a Revelation and its completion
in Christ, what is the relation of the Bible to the
Divine Word? Strictly speaking, the Book is not
the Revelation itself; nor does it claim to be this.
The Revelation was made in many ways—in visions,
through the living voice, in the history of the chosen
people, above all, in the Person and in the Life of
the Incarnate Word. The Bible is the history of
its progress, and the record of its teachings. It is
the documentary storehouse of the original facts
and doctrines of the Christian Faith. But viewed
from this point alone the Holy Scriptures possess a
claim upon the attention of Christians which is alto-
gether unique.
2. As we study this collection of documents, the
conviction grows upon us that it is bound together
by an inner unity which cannot be ascribed to acci-
dental causes. ‘The Bible is doubtless a ‘‘library,”’
but it is also a ‘‘book.” Externally, indeed, it
bears no traces of a common purpose or plan. Its
fragmentary histories describe experiences of life
as widely separated as the desert wanderings of a
nomad tribe in the days of the older Pharaohs, and
the journeyings of a Roman citizen along the high
roads of the Empire of the Cxsars. It expounds
systems as dissimilar as the Mosaic Law and the
Gospel of Christ. Nor has any attempt been made
to bring its units into a consecutive or even har-
monious whole. The two Testaments are separated
by a gulf of perhaps four centuries. There are four
memoirs of the life of Christ, three of which to a
great extent travel over the same ground. Even the
order_of the Books has been determined chiefly in
the course of their transmission; and in the case of
the O. 'T., the Hebrew order to this day differs from
that which is usual among Christians. Lastly, the
Bible contains no system of theology, or, unless
we except the Decalogue and the Sermon on the |
Mount, of ethics. In all these ways it seems to |
want the note of unity which might have been
expected on the supposition of a Divine super-
intendence. Yet a closer and more thoughtful
study reverses this conclusion. We see that the
character of the record corresponds with that of
the Revelation. If the voices of God came to men
of old time ‘‘in many portions and in many ways’
(Heb. 1. 1, Gk.), it is no surprise to find the Book
manifold. “‘It is precept upon precept, precept
upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here |

3. All this, however, amounts to little more than
the conviction that a providential superintendence
has been exercised in the collection and preservation
of the records of Revelation. ‘To affirm the Inspi-
ration of the Bible is another step, and one which
carries us much further. Yet no Christian can
doubt that in some special sense the Bible is an
inspired Book. The New Testament proclaims the
inspiration of the Old (2 Tim. 3. 16; 2 Pet. 1. 21).
The Christian Church has with one voice asserted
the inspiration of both Testaments. Nor is it easy
to see how this doctrine can be rejected without
rejecting the testimony of Christ Himself. His
recognition of the Hebrew Scriptures cannot in
fairness be explained as a mere concession to
popular belief (see Matt. 5. 18; 26. 54; Luke
16. 17; 24. 25-27, 45, 46; John 5. 39, 46). And
He promised His Apostles a supernatural guidance
which it is reasonable to believe was especially
realised in their written and permanent teaching
(John 14. 26; 16. 13-15).
But when we come to examine the nature and
extent of this inspiration, there is no such consensus
of authority for our guidance. Generally, we may
define inspiration as an operation of the Divine
| Spirit upon the spirit of man, by which the latter is
enabled to rise above its natural powers. Thus the
ancient prayers of the Church invite the inspiration

18 THE BIBLE—ITS UNITY AND INSPIRATION.
of the Holy Spirit on behalf of ordinary believers
for the conduct of the Christian life (e.g. the Collect
for the Fifth Sunday after Trinity). Was the inspira-
tion of the writers of Scripture of a similar kind,
affecting in their case the intellect rather than the |
will, but with them, as with others, varying in mea-
sure according to their needs, their desires, or their
use of the light vouchsafed ? Or was it in their case
of such a nature as to preclude the possibility of
error, uniform in its workings, independent of the
co-operation of the person inspired—such infact as
to render the sacred writer an infallible amanuensis
of the Spirit of God ?
It is remarkable that the ancient Church has for-
mulated no decision as to the nature of Biblical In-
spiration. Individual writers leaned sometimes to
the one view, sometimes to the other; but on the
whole Christian opinion, prior to the Reformation,
was content to recognise the human individuality of
the writers of Scripture and the Divine influence |
which wrought upon them, without attempting to |
define the spheres of the human and the Divine. The
Reformers of the sixteenth century were chiefly con-
cerned to maintain the supremacy and sufficiency |
of Seripture in matters of faith. The Anglican
Article (VI.) simply asserts that ‘ Holy Seripture
containeth all things necessary to salvation,” and |
Richard Hooker, while he affirms that ‘‘ what the
Scripture purposeth, the same in all points it doth
perform,’’ warns his Puritan opponents to “take
great heed lest in attributing unto Scripture more |
than it can have, the incredibility of that do
cause eyen those things which indeed it hath most |
abundantly to be less. reverently esteemed”
(H.-P. ii. 8.7)... The warning was not unnecessary,
as the scholasticism of the next century demon-
strated. In the eighteenth century a reaction was
led by Schleiermacher in Germany, and in England
by S. T. Coleridge, who endeavoured to modity the
prevalent views of Biblical Inspiration. ‘he former
regarded the inspiration of Seripture as commensu-
rate with its power of quickening and elevating the
religious consciousness of men; the latter held that
“itis the spirit of the Bible, and not the detached
words and sentences, that is infallible and abso-
lute.’’? Similar opinions have been expressed by
many of the teachers of our own age.
Probably no theory of Inspiration will ever satisfy
all the conditions of the case. In any attempt to
arrive at a solution two complementary truths must
receive full recognition. On the one hand it must
be remembered that the Divine Spirit works through
the natural faculties of men, and does not supersede,
although He heightens and corrects, their operation,
On the other hand any account of His action upon
the minds of the sacred writers will be inadequate,
which places their writings upon a level with the
works of human genius. To regard the Bible
merely as the noblest and best of ancient books
is to ignore at once its own repeated statements, and
the testimony of all Christian experience. Interpret,
the fact as we will, the Bible professes to be in a
manner peculiar to itself ‘‘inspired of God,”
and the claim is endorsed by the witness of the
be: Society, and by the facts of Christian
ife.

There is a term which has been used from Josephus

quent, describes (1) the advent of the Divine King

THE OLD TESTAMENT.
The Old Testament contains (1) an outline of prim-
sval history, followed by a sketch of the origin of
the covenant between God and the people of Israel,
and a statement of the principles involved in that
Covenant as affecting each of the contracting parties
—the promises given by God and the duties under-
taken by man, along with the laws laid down for the
better performance “of those duties (the Pentatewch) ;
(2) a series of histories giving an account of the
subsequent fortune of the Covenant people, with
especial reference to the degree in which they kept
or failed to keep their share in the Covenant, and
the consequent dealings of God with them (Joshua
—Nehemiah) ; (3) a number of literary productions
expressive of the principles involved in the Cove-
nant, in the shape of poems private and devotional,
or intended for liturgical use in public worship (the
Psalms) ; narrative or dramatic works, deriving
their interest from their connection with the heroes
of the Covenant race (Ruth, Jonah, Esther, Song of
Songs); collections of aphorisms and philosophic
utterances (Book of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes), and
the poetical treatment of deep religious problems
(Book of Job); (4) a series of works by the au-
thorised religious leaders of the people, who were
specially inspired to foretell future events and to
transmit the principles embodied in the original
Covenant, and to prepare the way for its final esta-
blishment on a new and broader foundation, and
with a new point of departure, no longer as a Cove-
nant between God and a single people, Israel, but
as a Covenant of grace and mercy vouchsafed by
God to all mankind (the Prophets).
The older Jewish classification is not quite co-
extensive with that which has just been given, but
may be illustrated by our Lord’s own words. In
Luke 24. 44 He gives us a three-fold division of the
sacred Scriptures, (1) the Law, (2) the Prophets,
(3) the Psalms. The first of these is known as the
Pentateuch, or Five Books of Moses ; the second was
divided by the Jews into (a) the former and (b) the
latter Prophets, i.e. (a) Joshua, Judges, Samuel,
and Kings (which were no doubt written by pro-
phetic men), and (b) Isaiah, Jeremiah, Bzekiel, and
the twelve Minor Prophets; the third group em-
braces all the other books not previously enume-
rated. This third division was known to the Jews
by the technical name Kethubim, in the Greek
Hagiographa or ‘‘ Scriptures,’ and is miscellaneous
in its character. Besides the Psalms, Proverbs, and
Job, it included the histories contained in Chro-
nicles, Hzra, and Nehemiah, and also the five
Megilloth or ‘‘ Rolls,” ¢.e. Canticles, Ruth, Lamen-
tations, Heclesiastes, and Hsther.
The Law and the Prophets (not the Psalms) were
divided by the Jews into Lessons; and it was one
of these which our Lord “‘ stood up to read”’ (Luke
4.16). In addition to this regular course, the five
Megilloth were recited at the principal feasts, Can-
ticles at the Passover, Ruth at the Feast of Weeks,
Lamentations in the month Ab (end of July), when
both temples are said to have been destroyed, Hecle-
siastes at the Feast of Tabernacles, and Hsther at
the Feast of Purim.
The writings of the Old Testament extend over a
period of at least 1,000 years. Almost the whole of
this literature is written in Hebrew, the ancient
language of Israel, which died out gradually after
the Captivity, being succeeded by Aramaic (a dialect
closely allied to the Hebrew), and partly also by
Greek. The following portions were written in
ReaD Jer. 10.11; Dan. 2.4—7.28; Hara 4. 8—
6.18; 7. 12-26.
The a ews of Palestine in the time of our Lord
reckoned in all 22 books, corresponding in number
to the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. In this
reckoning Ruth was taken with Judges, Lamenta-
tions with Jeremiah, and Nehemiah with Ezra; the
books of Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles were not
divided, and the twelve Minor Pr. ophets were treated
as a single volume. Our present list of 89 books is
the same as that which was current at Alexandria.
The Alexandrian Canon, like the Vulgate, also
included the books now known as the ApocRYPHA
(i.e. “‘hidden’’). ‘These books were so called either
because they were obscure in their origin or because
they were consigned by the judgment of the church
to comparative obscurity. They were, for the most
part, composed after the close of the Old Testament
Canon, and in the interval which separates it from
the New Testament. They were excluded from the
Canon because of their date, their non-Israelitish
origin, or on other religious grounds. They include
(1) spurious works attributed to Old Testament per-
sonages (Baruch, Letter of Manasseh, Esdras) ; (2)
spurious additions to the canonical books, such as
those introduced into Hsther and Daniel ; (8) his-
torical works belonging to the interval between the
Old and New Testament (Books of Maccabees) ; (4)
romances with a moral or religious tendency (Ju-
dith, Susanna, Tobit); (5) works of religious
philosophy, turning on the conception of Wisdom
(Ecclesiasticus, Wisdom of Solomon). None of
them are included in the Hebrew Bible.

Book of Joshua might be described as the Domes-

The title does not necessarily imply that the book
was written by Joshua, any more than in the case
of Ruth, Samuel, &c., though from chaps. 18. 9 and
24. 26, it seems that written records were made by
Joshua and his contemporaries. ‘The phrase “‘ unto
this day,’’ which occurs so frequently, indicates the
presence of notes later than the events narrated,
but in some eases at least certainly not much later.
Thus, in chap. 16. 10, we have a state of things which
had ceased to exist in the time of Solomon (1 Kings
9. 16). Some have seen in the Book of Joshua a
continuation of the Pentateuch, making that volume
strictly a Hexateuch. The Book of Psalms refers
to Joshua, e.g. Ps. 44. 2-4; 68. 18-15; 78. 54, 55;
114. 1-8; and so does Habakkuk, 3. 8-18. The book
probably covers about 25 or 30 years.
Special attention may be drawn to the circum-
stances connected with the crossing of the Jordan
through a temporary damming of the stream higher
up; to the prolongation of the day during the battle
against the five southern kings; to the double names
of many of the places, indicating that the record
was made in a transition period; and to the last
addresses of Joshua, in which he recapitulates the
past history of the people.

(chaps. 1—8. 4); (6) the main history (8. 5—16. 31);
and (c) a supplement (17—21). The main history
records in some detail six critical events in the his-

Midianites by Gideon (whose son Abimelech esta-

from the Ammonites by Jephthah, and the struggle
| of Samson with the Philistines. The supplement,
| referring to an earlier period, consists of two epi-
sodes, that of Micah and the Danites, and the
shameful deed of the men of Gibeah, which nearly

illustrates the fact that there was a growing weak-

to show by whom the book was written; but chap.
1. 21 was probably written before the 7th year of
David, 2 Sam. 5. 7; and chap. 17. 6, &c., per-
haps indicates acquaintance with Saul’s Kingship.
Samuel, therefore, may have compiled Judges; but
The first (1—12) includes the cross- |

much later. This verse may refer to the Philistine
captivity implied in chap. 18. 31, but is probably a

have occurred early in the history, because the
grandson of Moses (the probable reading, not Ma-
nasseh) is named (chap. 18. 30), and the grandson
of Aaron (20. 28). It is doubtful whether the rule
of the various judges recorded was consecutive or in
some cases contemporary ; if the former, we have in
| this book the history of some 410 years, which seems
borne out by chap. 11. 26 and Acts 13. 20 (where
the common reading is, however, incorrect) ; if the
latter, the period would be shorter. ‘This view is
| favoured by the genealogy of David (1 Chron. 2.
10-15) and of Zadok (1 Chron. 6. 4-8). . The chro-
nology of this book is one of the most difficult
questions in Biblical criticism. There can be little
doubt that Samson and Eli were contemporaries.
The history of Judges is referred to in many of
the later books of the Old Testament.
The relationship existing between the early chap-
ters of the book and some parts of the Book of
Joshua should be studied; also the providential
circumstances connected with the punishing of Is-
rael for their unfaithtulness, and the raising up of
saviours in their times of adversity. The song of
Deborah and Barak (chap. 5) and the speech of
Jephthah (chap. 11) call for special attention.
Ruth.—The book is so called because it relates
Ruth’s history, and accounts for her introduction
into the line of the Promised Seed as an ancestress
of David and of Christ (ep. also Tamar and Rahab).
The book does not follow Judges in the Heb., but
was so placed in the LXX. translation. The Tal-
mud ascribes it to Samuel. In its present form
it was clearly written after David became famous,
chap. 4. 22. The law contained in Deut. 25. 7-9,
which had already become modified in the time of
Ruth, seems to have been obsolete when her history
was written (chap. 4. 7).
The book specially illustrates the position and
responsibility of the Goel, i.e. the Kinsman, who is
also Redeemer of the inheritance. The references
to Rachel, Leah, and the house of Pharez, are to be
noticed.
Samuel.—The Books of Samuel are so called in
the Heb., but in the LXX. they are called the Ist
and 2nd Books of the Kings, though they only
contain the history of Saul and David. The name
of Samuel, however, is not more appropriate, inas-
much as his death is recorded in the 25th chapter
of the first book, the rest of the work being com-
pleted in all probability by Nathan or Gad. The
division between the Ist and 2nd Books of Samuel
is purely arbitrary, and indeed in the Heb. MSS.
the two books are one. They cover a period pro-
bably of about 130 years. ‘This period marks a
crisis in the history of Israel. The disorganization
which prevailed under the Judges reached a climax ;
the pure theocracy had apparently failed, and a mixed
theocracy was substituted for it by the appointment
of a king, who was to consider himself strictly as
God’s anointed vicegerent. The first king, Saul,
did not satisfy this condition, and the crown was
therefore transferred to David and his descendants.
The first book records the judgeship of Eli, the
early days of Samuel, and the destruction of Shiloh
by the Philistines (chaps. 1—4); the recovery of the
ark, and of some degree of prosperity under the
judgeship of Samuel (chaps. 5—8) ; the reign of Saul,
| with the youth and flight of David (chaps. 9—81).
