The second book describes the reign of David
(1) at Hebron for 7} years, in conflict with Ish-
bosheth (1—4) ; (2) in Jerusalem, for 33 years, as
undisputed monarch, victorious over his enemies,
though with his reign embittered by his own griev-
ous sin and by the “troubles in connection with his
sons Absalom and Amnon, and with Sheba the
Benjamite.
There is some difficulty about the chronology of
the reign of Saul, only the beginning and end of
which seem to be related (see Bases of “Chr ‘onology).
The sources of these books were probably the Book
of Jasher (2 Sam.1.18),the Psalms of David (2 Sam.
22. 1), the chronicles of king David (1 Chron.
27. 24), the Book of Samuel the seer, Nathan the
prophet, and Gad the seer (1 Chron. 29. 29; cp.
1 Sam. 10. 25). The text bears numerous marks of
corruption: see especially 1 Sam. 6. 19 (numbers) ;
13. 1 (numbers); 2 Sam. 5. 8; 21. 8 (Michal for
Merab); 24. 18 (cp. 1 Chron. 21. 12). The text
in the parallel sections of Chronicles should be
compared throughout.
The most notable chapter in the history of David
is 2 Sam. 7, which contains the original promise of
the MusstaH. It is referred to in the Psalms and
Prophets, and is the origin of the expression ‘‘ Son
of David’ in the New Testament.
The poetical sections in the Books are the song
of Hannah (1 Sam. 2), the lament of David over
Saul (2 Sam. 1), the song of David after being
delivered from his enemies (2 Sam. 22; see Ps. 18),
and the last words of David (2 Sam. 23).
Kings.—The Books of Kings (so called in Heb.)
are by the LXX. called the 3rd and 4th Books of
Kings. They are one in the Heb. MSS., and the
division is purely arbitrary. They contain the his-
tory of the Jewish nation from the closing years of
David till the end of the monarchy, and the depar-
ture to Babylon, a period of about 430 years. This
includes three periods:—(1) The undivided mon-
archy under Solomon, which, with the preceding
reign, marks the greatest height of power and
splendour in the Hebrew nation, though the causes
of disruption were already at w ork (l Kings i—11).
(2) The divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah, (a) at
first. hostile to each other, from Rehoboam to the
death of Asa, kings of Judah, and from Jeroboam to
the death of Omri, kings of Israel(1 Kings 12—16. 28),
(b) then allied under the dynasty of Omri in the
northern kingdom, and under Jehoshaphat and his
successors in the southern (1 Kings 16. 29—2 Kines
11. 20), and (c) finally, for the most part hostile again
under the dynasty of Jehu and succeeding kings in
the north, and under the kings from Joash onwards
in the south, to the taking of Samaria in B.c. 721,
which closed the regal history of the ten northern
and eastern tribes (2 Kings 12—17). (8) The sepa-
rate existence of the southern kingdom, assailed
successively by Egypt and Assyria and the Chaldean
king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar (who, having con-
quered Nineveh for his father, had absorbed the
Assyrian Kmpire), till the destruction of Jerusalem
by Nebuchadnezzar in B.c. 588 (2 Kings 18—25).
The Books of Kings supply us with the only
materials extant for the history of Israel, which
is passed over in the Chronicles in silence. The
latest event recorded, the accession of Evil-Mero-
dach, son of Nebuchadnezzar, takes us down to
561 B.c., but most of the book bears the marks of
being contemporary history. The Talmud and some
moderns have ascribed the final authorship of the
book to Jeremiah, perhaps not without some pro-
bability. The sources of Kings were the Book of
the Acts of Solomon (1 Kings 11. 41), the Book
of the Chronicles of the kings of Israel (1 Kings 14.
10, &.), and of Judah (1 Kings 14. 29, &.). In
addition to the history of the kingdoms of Judah
and Israel, we have also that of the prophets Hlijah
and Hlisha. The whole compilation is probably of
prophetic origin. For the chronology of these books,
see Bases of Chronology.
Special subjects for study in these books are the
structure and dedication of the Temple (1 Kings
6—9) ; the providential way in which God’s promise
to David was fulfilled (e.g. 1 Kings 11. 36); the
disruption of the kingdom (1 Kings 12) ; the political
relations of Israel with the outside nations, Egypt,
Syria, Assyria, and Babylon; and the special deliver-
ances of the people, frequently effected through the
intervention of the prophets, who are conspicuous
all through the period.
Chronicles.—The Books of Chronicles, like those
of Samuel and Kings, were one book in the Heb.
to the time of St. Jerome. Their original name is
the Acts of the Days or Times. In the LXX., it is
Paraleipomena, things omitted. 'The book was cer-
tainly completed after the Captivity : e.g. 1 Chron. 3
contains a genealogy of the descendants of Zerub-
babel. The writer made use of and quotes twelve
or fourteen authorities, which he mentions by
name. Writing after the Return, he was anxious
to represent the Law and the worship of the
restored Temple as the central bond of the nation,
hence its prominence in, and the generally Levitical
tone of, his narrative. According to the Jewish
tradition the Chronicles are the work of Hazara.
On comparing the history with that contained in
Samuel and Kings we observe many omissions:
e.g. David’s adultery with Bathsheba and murder
of her husband, the slaughter of the sons of Saul
at the demand of the Gibeonites, the rebellions of
Absalom and Adonijah, Solomon’s foreign wives
and idolatry; and many additions, chiefly religious
(e.g. Levitical details in the bringing of the ark to
Jerusalem, and at the consecration of the Temple,
the orders of the Levites and their distribution).
The writer of Chronicles does not concern himself
with the history of the Ten Tribes, no doubt for
the reason that, from his ecclesiastical point of
view, their separate political existence was indefen-
sible. ‘The book ends in the middle of a sentence,
which is continued in Hzra 1. 8; and the last
three verses of Chronicles are the same as the
first three of Ezra, thus showing that the books
were originally related, if not the work of one and
the same author.
The first portion of the book (1 Chron. 1—8) is
genealogical, tracing the pedigrees of the tribes,
especially Judah and Levi, from Adam downwards.
1 Chron. 9 gives us the names of the chief dwellers
in Jerusalem, apparently after the Return (ep.
Neh. 11). From 1 Chron. 10 and onwards we have
several sections of the history of David and his
line, abstracted either from Samuel and Kings or
from the materials from which these were com-
posed. There are also lists and records illustrating
the thorough organization of David’s kingdom.
(1 Chron. 23—27).
In 2 Chron. subjects of special interest will be
found in the reigns of Rehoboam (chap. 12), Abijah
Chee: 18), Asa (chaps. 14—16), Jehoshaphat (chaps. |
17—20), Amaziah (chap. 25), Ahaz (chap. 28), Heze- |.
kiah (chaps. 29—82), and Josiah (chap. 35). |
Ezra,—The Book of Ezra is really two books
thrown into one, and a gulf of about 56 or 57 years
separates the one from the other. The first part
(chaps. 1—6) relates (a) the history of the return

Zerubbabel prince of Judah and Jeshua the High

series of hindrances to the work of restoration,
caused for some years by the neighbouring tribes ;
(c) the final completion of the Temple, and re-
establishment of its services, in B.c. 516, the
prophets Haggai and Zechariah haying roused the
people from the despondency and sinful apathy
into which they had fallen and which God had
punished by drought and famine. The second part
(chaps. 7—LO) records Ezra’s own mission to Jeru-
salem under Artaxerxes Longimanus, in the years
458-457 B.C., with the reforms instituted by him,
especially in cases of intermarriage with foreign
wives. ‘hose who returned from exile were called
henceforward (from the tribe of Judah bearing the
most prominent part) Jews. The mass of the
12 tribes not availing themselves of the permission
to return formed ‘‘the Dispersion’’ (see James 1. 1).
Though scattered, we have no reason to call them
lost.”
It is to be noted that the passages, chaps. 4. 7—
6. 18 and 7. 12-26, are in the Aramaic dialect, which
is also to be found in some of the writings of
Daniel, who lived in the same age.
In the first part of the book special attention is
directed to the decree of Cyrus, which is regarded
as a fulfilment of Jeremiah’s prophecy. The con-
nection, ritual and genealogical, between the pre-
captivity and post-captivity period should be noted.
Ezra himself comes on the scene in the second
part, and writes in the first person. His priestly
descent, his learning in the law of Moses, and the
authority which he received from the Persian king,
enabled him to exercise a wholesome and much-
needed discipline in Jerusalem, where we find him,
12 years afterwards, in the time of Nehemiah.
Nehemiah was cup-bearer to Artaxerxes Longi-
manus, in Susa, and was evidently favoured and
respected by his master. He was undoubtedly the
writer or compiler of the book that bears his name.
It has four sections: chaps. 1—7 containing a nar-
rative of Nehemiah’s mission in 445-444 B.c., but
apparently completed 12 years later (chap. 5. 14) ; the
chief result of his mission is the rebuilding, in spite
of active opposition, of the walls of Jerusalem ;
chaps. 8—10 differ from the previous section in
being written in the third person (some have
thought this piece to be the work of Hzra); this
section records the joint work of Ezra and Nehe-
miah in the religious re-organization of the people ;
chaps. 11—12. 26 contain sundry lists of the princi-
pal men in the priesthood and in the laity. In the
last section (chaps. 12. 27—13) the author reverts
to the first person; and it was probably written by
Nehemiah about 430 B.c., a few notes being added
later. Another view is that Nehemiah wrote the
whole or greater part of sections 1 and 4, but that
the complete work was put together along with
Chronicles and Ezra by a somewhat later writer.
The internal evidence is as follows :—(1) Neh. 12. 23
(ep. v. 10), carries us down to about 350 B.c.; (2) Neh.
12. 22 (ep. again v. 10) brings the date to Alexander
the Great, in whose time Jaddua was high priest ;
(3) the title ‘‘ king of Persia”’ (Ezra 1.1, 2; 4.5, 7),
has been thought by some to presuppose the fall of
the Persian empire; and (4) Neh. 12. 46, 47, seems
to imply that ‘‘the days of Nehemiah’’ belonged to
the past.. But these inferences are uncertain.
Nehemiah was a man of marked character, and
possibly of royal blood. His prayer in the Ist
chapter indicates his knowledge, not only of the
Pentateuch, but also apparently of the 9th of Daniel.
The account of the repairs of the wall (chap. 3.)
is the most important topographical record we
possess. In the 7th chapter we have a long extract
from the Book of Hzra containing ‘‘a register of
the genealogy of them that came up at the first.”
The reading of the Book of the Law of Moses by
Ezra (chap. 8) is followed by a prayer abounding
in verbal quotations from the Jaw (chap. 9). ‘There
is a remarkable relationship between the list of
those who dwelt in Jerusalem (chap. 11) and the
list contained in 1 Chron. 9, though authorities
are undecided as to their identity.
During Nehemiah’s absence from Jerusalem,
444-432, having been recalled to Susa, various
abuses grew up amongst the people; and the 18th
chapter records his efforts to rectify them. ‘There
was laxity as to the tithes and offerings, profana-
tion of the Sabbath, and a defiling of the covenant
of the priesthood through mixed marriages. These
things are also referred to by Nehemiah’s contem-
porary Malachi, with whose writings this chapter
should be compared.
Esther.—The Book of Esther is one of the five
Megilloth, or Rolls, and is read at the Feast of
Purim, of which it recounts the origin. The date
and authorship of the book are uncertain. It is
commonly supposed that Ahasuerus is the Persian
Xerxes, whose character fitly corresponds with the
description given of him in the book. He reigned
from 485 to 465 B.c., 7.e. between the age of Ze-
rubbabel and that of Ezra. Hsther is a, Persian
name meaning ‘‘ Star,’ but the Queen’s Hebrew
name is Hadassah, which signifies ‘‘ Myrtle.’? She
was a descendant of Kish, and thus related to the
family of Saul. It has often been remarked that
the name of God does not occur in the book, neither
is there any direct reference to religion—unless fast-
ing be so called—though the doctrine of a providen-
tial arrangement of events is presupposed through-
out. It is probably on this ground that it was one
of the last to be admitted into the Jewish Canon.
The Greek translation inserts prayers and various
religious expressions.
Esther is introduced as the niece and adopted
daughter of Mordecai. She becomes the favourite
wife of the Persian king. Some years afterwards
Haman, in his spite against Mordecai, stirs up
hatred against all the Jews in the empire, and lots
are cast to find a lucky day on which to destroy
them. This providentially delays the execution of
the plan for a year. When the crisis comes, the
plot is brought before the king by Hsther, and a
previous good deed of Mordecai is also recalled to
his memory. The result is that Mordecai is re-
warded, Haman hanged, and the Jews are permitted
to defend themselves.
THE POETICAL BOOKS.
Job.—The Book of Job is remarkable as differing
from all other books of the Bible in having no re-
ference to the Covenant People or their history.
Its origin and date are matters of much obscurity,
about which very opposite opinions have been held :
some regarding the book as older than the Penta-
teuch, and others as later than the Captivity. The
name occurs nowhere else in Scripture, being ety-
mologically distinct from ‘‘Job’’ Gen. 46. 18, and
“ Jobab”’ Gen. 36. 38, with which it has frequently
been confounded and identified. Hzekiel was fami-

The argument of the Book of Job is one of

the world, more especially with reference to the
sufferings of good men. ‘The appearance of Satan
as the minister of permitted physical evil is to be
noticed; also the similarity of style between the
utterances in this book and the ‘‘parables” of
Balaam. The poetical descriptions contained in
the book are unequalled elsewhere.

Psalms,—The Hebrew name for the Book of
Psalms is Tehillim, which means praises, whilst
the word translated Psalm in all passages where
the word occurs in the Old Testament is quite
different and signifies a song, or perhaps music,
the word Psalm being the Greek rendering of it.
The Book of Psalms is divided by the Hebrews
into five sections, like the Law of Moses, whether
for that reason or for any other is not known.
The first section consists of Pss. 1—41, the second
of Pss. 42—72, the third of Pss. 73—89, the fourth
of Pss. 90—106, and the fifth of Pss. 107—150. Hach
| portion concludes with a Doxology, the first three
sections having the additional words ‘‘ Amen and
Amen,”’ and the last two ‘“‘ Hallelujah,” which is
not found in the others. As the Psalms approach
their close, the Doxologies of praise and thanks-
giving increase in volume and intensity.
All the Psalms have superscriptions, with the
exception of 34, which are called in the Talmud
orphan Psalms. The authority of the titles is
however doubtful, both on account of the difficulty
of harmonising them in many cases with the con-
tents of the Psalms, and also because of the
variations in the Hebrew, and in the Septuagint
and Syriac Versions. No less than 73 are ascribed
in the Hebrew to David, 12 to Asaph, one of the
leaders of his choir (1 Chron. 6. 39, &e.), 11 to the
sons of Korah, one each to Heman, Hthan, and
Jeduthun, who were probably among the number of
David’s singers, two (Pss. 72 and 127) to Solomon,
and one (Ps. 90) to Moses. In the LXX. Pgs.
137, 188, and 146—148, are ascribed to the pro-
phets Jeremiah, Hzekiel, Haggai, and Zechariah.

down to times after the Captivity, while some

buted to the age of the Maccabees.

Proverbs.—The Book of Proverbs is known in |
Heb. by its first word, a form of the word mashal,
| which often signifies a proverbial utterance. The |
book is not however contined to ‘‘ proverbs’’ in the
modern sense, but contains also connected poetical
pieces of some length. It falls naturally into four
parts.
The first nine chapters are on true wisdom.
They illustrate the folly of a godless life, and
enforce the duty of walking in the fear of the Lord.
They are attributed to Solomon, and there is no
reason to doubt that they express the true charac- |
teristics of that wisdom with which he was specially
gifted.
Chaps. 10—24 are a collection of isolated sentences
or proverbs, contrasting the right and wrong ways
of living. They are also ascribed to Solomon,
though not necessarily all originated by him.
Chaps. 25—29 are called the Proverbs of Solomon,
which the men of Hezekiah copied out (07 removed).
This is an interesting testimony to the literary
character of the age of Hezekiah. It would appear
that over and above the previous collection there
were many sayings current which were attributed
to Solomon, and these were preserved in an
authoritative form by the men of Hezekiah.
An appendix follows consisting of the words of
Agur (¢hap. 80), the words of king Lemuel, whose

THE PROPHETS.
Isaiah (salvation of Jehovah), is pre-eminent
among the Literary Prophets, of whom we reckon
A greater and 12 less. If we calculate his prophetic
life from two years before the death of Uzziah (chap.
6. 1) to the 3rd year of Manasseh (in whose reign,
according to a tradition, he was sawn asunder in the
trunk of a mulberry tree), it must have extended
from about 760 to 695 B.c. ; and the combined reigns
of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah give us a period of
more than 60 years, so that evenif he did not survive
Hezekiah, he must have lived to a great age. We
know nothing of his personal history, except the
name of his ‘father, the fact that he was married
(chap. 8. 3), and had two or more children (chaps.
7. 3,16 & 8. 3,18). There is also a tradition that
Amoz and Amaziah were brothers; and if so, Isaiah
and Uzziah were cousins. It is possible that the
prophecies are not in all cases arranged in order of
time, and it would seem that Isaiah was solemnly
called to his office in the last year of Uzziah (chap.
6.1). The Book of Isaiah naturally divides itself
into two parts, which are separated by the his-
torical chapters (36—39). It has been supposed by
many modern critics that the second part is by an
unknown writer, who lived a century and a half
later, towards the end of the Captivity and at
Babylon—mainly because the scene seems to be
wholly laid in a time when the return from captivity
is accomplished, Cyrus being mentioned by name;
and on similar grounds the authorship of Isaiah has
been denied also in the case of chaps. 13; 14. 1-28;
21. 1-10; 25—27; 34; 35. Arguments from style
and language have been used on both sides of the
controversy. One of the main arguments for the
Isaianic authorship of the disputed passages is the
literary relation which they present to the writings
of Zephaniah and Jeremiah (ep. e.g. Isa. 47. 8, 10
with Zeph. 2.15; Isa. 44. 12-15; 41.7; 46.7 with
Jer. 10. 1-16, &c.). It cannot be said that the
traditional view of the book as entirely the work of
Isaiah has been disproved or need be abandoned.
Isaiah’s chief characteristic is his manysidedness.
He excels in various styles, and combines the moral
qualities of several less eminent prophets (especially
Amos and Hosea). He deepened the prophetic idea
of the Day of the Lord, and gave a new turn to the
current expectations of the Messiah. He is the
first to hint at the Virgin Birth (7. 14) ; and while
describing the glories of the Messianic Kingdom
(9. 1-7) and its beneficent effects (11. 1-9; 60. 15-22 ;
61. 1, 3) he also gives to the ‘“‘ servant of Jehovah ”
a peculiar character of mildness (42. 1), and speaks
of him as making atonement for sin by humiliation,
suffering, and death (53) ; moreover he looks forward
in a striking manner to the ultimate inclusion of the
Gentiles in the family of God (11. 10-16; 19. 28-25;
42.6; 49. 6, 22, 23; 60. 1-16). These remarkable
anticipations of Christianity have obtained for
Isaiah the name of the Evangelical Prophet.

THE PROPHETS.
The Minor Prophets are so called from the
smaller bulk of their writings, which form a, single
volume in the Hebrew. They are twelve in num-
ber, and extend over a period of about 400 years,
nearly equal to that from Chaucer to Wordsworth.
We may arrange them roughly in chronological
order, according to three stages in Israel’s history,
thus :—
I. The period from Uzziah to Hezekiah, which
covers the downfall of the Ten Tribes and
the preservation of Judah. This includes
Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, and
Micah, all of whom probably committed
their prophecies to writing before the
greater part of Isaiah was written.
Il. The period leading up to the captivity of |
Judah. This includes Nahum, Habakkuk,
and Zephaniah, all of whom show acquaint-
ance with Isaiah’s writings.
III. The period of the Restoration. This includes
Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.
In studying these short books it must be borne
in mind that we have only such a selection from
the oral addresses of the prophets as God ordered
them to put down in writing. This accounts for
their brevity. Contrast the case of Jeremiah, who
had to write all that God had spoken to him (Jer.
36. 2).

latter part the prophet reviews the past history of

and strength in God, notwithstanding any calamities
that may befall the nation or himself.

THE APOCRYPHAL BOOKS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT.
The books commonly known by the name of the
Apocrypha are those books which, though not found
in the Hebrew canon, are attached to the ancient
Greek and Latin versions. Scholars are by no
means agreed as to the real explanation of the name
Apocrypha, t.e., hidden or concealed; but whatever
may be its precise technical meaning, the expression
is used by ancient writers to denote books inferior
in authority to the writings included in the canon.
It is, however, certain that none of these books
were admitted into the Hebrew canon, and the testi-
mony of Josephus to that fact is clear and unmis-
takeable. Many of these books, however, were
widely known in the early Christian Church, and
some even occasionally quoted as if of equal au-
thority with the canonical writings. The distine-
tion, however, so concisely drawn by Jerome between
the canonical Scriptures as of authority, and those
Scriptures of inferior authority, which might be
privately “‘read for example of life and instruction
of manners,”’

3. The Book of Tobit, or Tobiah, or Tobias, was
originally written in Hebrew or Aramaic (Chaldee).
It is extant in several versions—Greek, Latin, He-
brew, and Aramaic. All these are, however, trans-

existing Hebrew texts are from the Aramaic, and

women. ‘The smoke arising from the heart and

Raphael, the angel, gives an untrue account of him-
self in order to conceal for a time his real nature.
But, with all these drawbacks, there is much good
moral teaching in the book, and, though uncanonical,
it was much thought of by some of the earliest
Fathers of the Church. The story is of course
unhistorical, but probably worked up on the basis
of historical facts. The thanksgiving of Tobit in
chap. 13 is fine. The book seems to have’ been
written to encourage benevolence and almsgiving,
to urge the burial of the corpses of those slain by
| arbitrary tyrants, to promote sound doctrine on the
sanctity of marriage, and probably to encourage
marriage within the family circle.

| tions are cut off from the book itself, and form a
| Separate set of additional chapters.
They are all
much later than the original story, and are deprived
| of all coherence when arranged m a separate book.
They contain (a) The dream of Mordecai (chap. 11.
1-12), placed incoherently after (b) The exposition
of the dream, which is chap. 10. 4-13. This is
followed by (c) an enlarged account (chap. 12. 1-6)
of The conspiracy of the two ewnuchs recorded in
Esther 2, 21-23, (d) The royal decree drawn up by
Haman (chap, 13. 1-7), (e) A prayer of Mordecai
(chap. 18. 8-18), (f) Prayer of Esther (chap. 14.
1-19), (g) an enlarged account of Hsther’s interview
with the king (chap. 15), (h) The edict in favour of
the Jews (chap. 16).
The dream of Mordecai and the conspiracy of the
eunuchs (a and c) given in chaps. 11. 2—12. 6 is in
the LXX. placed before Hsther 1. 1, while the
exposition (b) appears at the end of the book im the
LXX., at chap. 10. 4 ff. The royal decree (d) is in
the LX X. after chap. 3.18; the prayers of Mordecai
and Hsther (e and f) after chap. 4. 17, The addi-
tions in (g) come in the LXX. after chap. 5. 1, 2,
and the edict of Mordecai after chap. 8. 12. Large
additions here and there are made in the Vulgate
version, which may be seen translated in Churton’s
edition of the Apocrypha referred to in No. 2.
Several of these ‘‘additions’? were known to Jose-
phus, and have been included by him in his history.
6. The Book of Wisdom, or the Wisdom of
Solomon, is a book of great value.» The author
speaks in the person of Solomon, but the work is
no forgery. The readers of the book at the time it
was produced must have known that the mask of
Solomon was put on only with the special purpose,
probably, of opposing the freethinking views of the
young Alexandrian school, which were founded on a
misunderstanding of passages in the Book of Hecle-
siastes, Chap. 2, in particular, is almost an anti-
Keclesiastes. The writer, who probably wrote
between 150-100 B.c. (some say as late as 50 B.c.),
was an Alexandrian Jew. The doctrine of immor-
tality is strongly taught in the book; that. of the
resurrection nowhere appears. Chap. 2. 12-20 has
often been regarded as a prophecy of Christ; it is,
however, a description of the righteous as a class.
The book has been of late fancifully assigned to
Apollos. It is remarkable that, though much of
Israelitish history is alluded to in the book, no pro-
per name occurs in it from first to last. The idea of
the writer was to depict the godly as wise in all their
varied relations; the ungodly, in every condition
and at every period, as the fools.
7. The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach,
or Ecclesiasticus; styled by the latter'name by
Jerome and Ruffinus, probably because it’ was an
ecclesiastical reading-book, read in some churches,
Its date (notwithstanding the apparent preciseness
of the date afforded in the prologue to the work,
and in chap. 50) is somewhat uncertain, though the
best critics generally suppose that the work was
translated into Greek, and edited with additions by
Jesus the Son of Sirach (Ben Sira, as he is usually
termed by Jewish writers) from a work of his grand-
father Jesus, about 132 B.c. Ben Sira seems to
have been acquainted with the LXX. version. His
proverbs were held in great esteem by the Jews,
though the book was not regarded as canonical.
Some forty verses of the Hebrew original are pre-
served here and there in the Jerusalem and Baby-
lonian Talmuds. Some other sayings of Ben Sira
are extant in Chaldee (Aramaic), and some in
Hebrew and Chaldee. ‘The work, which is pre-
ceded by two prologues, one from ‘an uncertain
author’? and another by Ben Sira, mainly consists
of a collection of proverbs and sayings of value, both
from a moral and doctrinal pomt of view (chaps.
1—43), followed by a valuable appendix “‘in praise
of the righteous’? (44—50. 26), concluding with a

8,9. The Book of Baruch, as it appears in the
Hnglish version of the Apocrypha, consists of three
distinct parts, disconnected with one another, and
written by three different authors. I.—Chaps. 1—
3. 8 contain a penitent prayer, professedly written
by Baruch in Babylon and sent to the Jews in
Jerusalem, in the fifth year prior to the destruc-
tion of Jerusalem, in’ the name of those who
had been carried away into exile. The prayer
is evidently ‘grounded on that in Dan. 9. The
opening chapter contains a number of _his-
torical inaccuracies. This portion may have been
composed some time after the Maccabéan period.
There are evident signs of its having been trans-
Jated from a Hebrew original. No critic of mark
ascribes it to Baruch. Some suppose it to have
been composed ‘after the siege by Titus, ‘in which
case the names Nebuchadnezzar and Balthasar
stand for Vespasian and Titus. But the earlier date
is the more probable. II.—Chaps. 3. 9—5. are
probably a later work, and contain some fine pas-
sages (chap. 3. 35-87 has been often regarded as a
prophecy of Christ). The original of this portion
may have been Hebrew, but the proofs are not
quite decisive. It was probably written somewhat
prior to the Christian era. IIT.—The Epistle of
Jeremiah, given in chap. 6. This portion profess-
edly consists of a letter written by Jeremiah to the
exiles in Babylon, warning them against’ idolatry.
The original of this little book is Greek. It has no
connection with the former chapters, but was pro-
pably written in Egypt, and is a cutting exposure
of idolatry. It is formally referred to in 2 Mac. 2. 2.
The chapter is in the LXX. properly treated as a
separate book, and follows the Lamentations of
Jeremiah. -The Vulgate has improperly attached it
to the Book of Baruch.
10, 11, 12. The next three books in the English
Apocrypha consist of certain additions to the Book
of Daniel found in the LXX. yersion. (a) The
Song of the Three Children, preceded by the
prayer of Azariah, occurs in the LXX. and Vulgate
at chap. 3. 24-90. It was not improbably composed

of Susanna, in the Vulgate, occurs Dan, 13.) «ln
the LX xX. it formed a separate book, with a title of

some of the versions, It is of no historical value,

Greek is probably the original. (c) The story of
Bel and the Dragon. In the LXX. it is also a
separate book entitled, “‘ From the Prophecy of
Habakkuk son of Jesus of the tribe of Levi.” It

13. The Prayer of Manasses' was not regarded
by the Council of Trent as canonical, and in most
editions of the Vulgate comes after the New Testa-
ment; with 3rd and 4th Esdras, as being apocryphal.
Tt is a prayer of some beauty, but not altogether

THE BIBLE—THE APOCRYPHAL BOOKS.
14. The First Book of the Maccabees.—There
are four books, entitled respectively, First, Second,
Third, and Fourth Books of the Maccabees, all writ-
ten by: different authors. The first two only have
found a place in the Vulgate, and consequently are
reckoned among the apocryphal books mentioned in
Article VI. of the Church of England. The First
Book is a most valuable historical work, and was
composed shortly after the death of John Hyrkanus
(chap. 16. 24) in 105 B.c. Other critics place it as
early as 125 Bic. Jerome and Origen both bear
witness to the existence of a Hebrew original of the
work, which has long since been lost. It contains
the history of the Jews in Palestine from the com-
mencement of the reign of Antiochus Epiphanes
(175 B.c.) to the death of Simon (185 B.c.), giving
an account of the heroic deeds of Judas, Jonathan,
and Simon, the three Maccabee brothers. The Greek
translation of the book was used by Josephus.
15. The Second Book of the Maccabees is
composed of several documents, loosely joined to-
gether. I.—Chaps. 1—2. 18 contain two docu-
ments: (a) a letter from the Jews of Jerusalem to
their brethren in Egypt, respecting the Feast of the
Dedication (chaps. 1. 1-9)... This purports to have
been written 124 B.c., and is probably translated
from a Hebrew original, but is generally regarded
as spurious. (b). Chaps. 1. 10—2. 18, another letter,
written also to the Egyptian Jews on a similar
subject, which gives an account of the death of
Antiochus Epiphanes, and records divers marvels.
It probably had a Hebrew original, but is also
spurious, although it does not follow that all its
history is untrue. II.—The second portion of the
book, chap. 2. 18 to the end, is of some, though not
of very great historical value. | It professes to be
abridged from the history of Jason of Cyrene, of
whom nothing more is known. It relates the his-
tory from the times of Seleucus IV., Philopater,
176.B.c., and closes with the victory obtained_ by
Judas Maccabeus over Nicanor. The book does
not appear. to have been used by Josephus. Its
original language is Hellenistic Greek, and it was
probably composed in Hgypt. The history it con-
tains (chaps. 6, 7) of the martyrdoms of the Jews
in the time of Antiochus Hpiphanes is of great
interest. It seems probably referred to in Heb.
11. 35, 36, and was highly esteemed in the early
Christian Church.
16. The Third Book of the Maccabees does
not form one of the books generally known under
the title of the Apocrypha, though early writers
have so classified it. Its canonicity is maintained
by none. The title is a misnomer, because it relates
events which occurred earlier than that. period, in
222-205 B.c., connected with the victories of Pto-
lemy LV., Philopater, of Egypt, and his attempt to
profane the Temple. Its unhistorical character has*
been maintained by mamy critics, who. have sup-
posed that it is an historical fiction really referring
to later times; .but, as Churton ‘has fairly argued.
its partial historical character is proved by its
agreement with Polybius, in the account given of
the battle of Raphia, It contains, however, many
fabulous histories. It is first mentioned in the
Apostolic Canons.85, but its mention there is sup-
posed by some to be an interpolation. | The book is
translated into English in Churton’s work, together
with the book following, viz. :—

18. Other Apocryphal Writings of the Old
Testament.— Among these may be mentioned
(1) Lhe Psalter of Solomon, consisting of eighteen
Greek psalms, strongly suggestive of a Hebrew
original, composed shortly before the Christian era,
| which give a picture of the revived hopes of the
pious Jews at that period. These psalms allude to
the profanation of the Temple by Pompey, and
| the death of that conqueror on the sands of
Egypt. The seventeenth psalm of this collection
speaks of Messiah and His kingdom. . (2) The Book
of Jubilees, or the Little Genesis; (3) The Book of
Enoch; (4) The Asswmption of Moses; (5) The
Ascension of Isaiah; (6) The Apocalypse of Baruch;
(7) The Sibylline Oracles. Several of these are of
peculiar interest. The Book of Enoch and the
Ascension of Isaiah have been translated from the

THE NEW TESTAMENT.
The New Testament, or Covenant, derives its
name from Luke 22. 20 (cp. 1 Cor. 11. 25; Heb.
9. 15-22; in other passages the reading is doubtful),
where our Lord speaks of Himself as concluding a
“new covenant”’ (A. V. testament) by His death.
The more common figure in the Gospels is that of
the “ kingdom of heaven’’ (St. Matthew), or ‘‘ king-
dom of God” (St. Mark and St. Luke), which He
came to found: the theocratic kingdom of the Old:
Testament becomes the Messianic kingdom of the
New. The New Testament contains at once the
history and conditions of this covenant or kingdom.
It is, however, differently composed from the Old:
Testament. It does indeed begin with a group of
histories (the Gospels and. Acts), but its doctrinal
teaching is conveyed no longer by prophecies or
psalms, but by a series of letters from the leaders
of the Church addressed to a number of different
Christian communities. This is a natural conse-
quence of the fact that Christianity ceased to be
confined to a single territory and people, and be-
came a missionary religion with outposts scattered
throughout the -world: --The: instruction put on
paper for the use of these outlying communities
has become the permanent law of Christians. - Of
the whole body of Hpistles thus collected, thirteen
are by the hand of a single writer, the Apostle St.
Paul; one, though anonymous, has been attributed
to him, probably without sufficient reason (Hebrews),
The remaining seven are classed together as the
Catholic or General Epistles... They are so ‘called
because the longest and most important of them
were addressed, not like'the majority of St. Paul’s
Hpistles to a particular Church or individual, but to
a number of churches. The larger Epistles all being
of this character, were distinguished from St. Paul’s
by the name Catholic or General; and the: two
smaller Epistles of St. John came to be classed
with them, though the name was not strictly appli-
cable to them. » In later usage the name “Catholic,”
pplied to a writing, was almost equivalent to ‘‘ca-
wonical.’? The New Testament closes with a work
which is only partially paralleled in the Old Testa-
ment, though it has several more complete counter-
parts among the Apocryphal writings—an ‘f Apoca-
| lypse,”? or description under symbolic forms’ of the
| final triumph of the Messianic kingdom.
But in order-to understand the organic growth of
the New Testament literature, it is necessary to look
upon it in another light. Divine Providence acts
through human means and by steps that can be to
some extent traced. Christianity sprang) out of
Judaism. , It fulfilled the. hopes raised by the Old
Testament, but it fulfilled them in a way that no
Israelite expected, and gave to them at the same
time an entirely new development. Hence it was
not surprising that the Jews as a body refused to
embrace Christianity, and that those who did em-
brace it were some time before they could reconcile
themselves to all its principles and consequences.
Christ came as the Jewish Messiah, but His work on
earth was utterly different from what it was expected
that the Messiah’s work would be. Even the Aypos-
tles: themselves were overwhelmed by its seemingly
disastrous close. Only the startling miracle of the
Resurrection awoke them to a sense of its true
significance, and that not all at once, but in part by
slow degrees. The Resurrection ‘proved that, in
spite of the ignominy and apparent failure of the
Cross, Jesus was still the Messiah, and it followed
necessarily from this that the Messianic kingdom
was not what they had imagined. But at first
the Apostles remained true Jews, attending the
Temple services and observing the rites and ordi-
nances of Judaism. The first marked step in
the way of separation from these was made
through the Hellenistic or foreign Jews. One
of their leaders, the Deacon Stephen, fearlessly
proclaimed the insufficiency and dissolution of the
Mosaic system. His death, and the ‘persecution
which followed, served only to spread the doctrines
for which he died. One of his fellow deacons,
St. Philip, and even St. Peter himself, began to
extend their preaching to Samaritans and prose-
lytes. Meantime a purely Hellenist (if not actually
Gentile—a point which depends upon the reading
of Acts’ 11. 20) Church was founded at Antioch.
Here a new character appeared upon the scene.
Saul of Tarsus, one of Stephen’s persecutors, now
a Christian, undertakes a mission journey to Cyprus
and the south of Asia Minor, in which he is per-
sistently repelled by the Jews, but meets with
success among the Gentiles. This raised the ques-
tion of principle definitely, and a formal conference
was’ held -at~ Jerusalem under the presidency of
St. James to decide it. As the result of this the
right of Gentiles to admission into the Church, as
such, was conceded; nor was their right materially
qualified by the restrictive conditions applied to
the Churches hitherto founded. From henceforth
St. Paul: preached boldly among the Gentiles, un-
deterred by the plots and intrigues of the extreme
Judaizing « party, who dogged his footsteps and
Hawarted him at every turn. In his intercourse
with the Gentile Churches: he formulates the
doctrines which he himself had been taught by
special revelation (Gal.1.11-17). Not only is Jesus
the Messiah, but His death, so far from being a
failure, alters the whole relations of God to: man.
Faith in Christ crucified is henceforth the great

motive power. In this way man may obtain
righteousness and salvation, which were impossible
to him under the régime of ‘legal observance. The
Gentile who believes is no whit behind the Jew;
and circumcision is not only unnecessary, but posi-
tively harmful to him as the badge of a slavery from
which he has been delivered. ‘This is the root-idea
of St. Paul’s teaching; and this again he developes
in opposition to the various perversions which
rapidly grew up in the Church through contact
with the strange off-shoots of Jewish and Gentile
philosophy which were then current. The work
that he began was continued after his death. The
Gospel of St. Luke, and in a still more marked way
the Gospel and Epistles of St. John, bring to the
front that higher unity in which Ji ewish and Gentile
Christianity are reconciled; while the KHpistle to
the Hebrews at an earlier date had shown how the
types and shadows of the Law became realities in
the Gospel.
The other Apostles give different aspects of the
new Christian faith. Of these St. Peter in his two
Epistles comes nearest to St. Paul. St. James con-
fines himself more to the simple teaching of a pure
Christian morality, presenting Christianity not in
its profounder theological aspects, but as the
“royal law ’’ of love ; while St. John, in his earlier
stage, as a genuine “‘son of thunder,” fulminates
against the “backslidings of the Churches of Asia,
and, like a second Daniel, revives the forms of
Apocalyptic vision.

THE BIBLE—THE GOSPELS.
THE GOSPELS.
The Gospels of St. Matthew, St. Mark, and
St. Luke are frequently classed together as the
“Synoptic Gospels,” from a Greek word meaning
capable of being seen at once, or of being arranged
in parallel columns. This name is given to them
from the amount of common matter found in all
three. Some think that this large common element
in them represents the oral teaching of the Apostles
during the time that they lived together in Palestine.
Others believe that this oral teaching had been
already committed to writing by St. Mark at the
time when the other two Gospels were written, and
that St. Mark’s Gospel lay before the other two
Evangelists. These two appear to be the most
probable of many theories of the relation of the
first three Gospels to each other. The first two
| Gospels were probably written before, and the third
not very long after, the destruction of Jerusalem.
The fourth Gospel was thought at a very early date
to be intended as supplementary to the other three,
and this would certainly seem to have been one of
the objects (though hardly perhaps the main object)
present to the mind of the writer. It was the latest
written of the four. Recent discoveries and investi-
gations have made it certain that all four Gospels
were current before the middle of the second century.
| Indeed, at a date little later than this, a harmony
of them appears to have been published under the
name of ‘‘ Diatessaron,” or ‘‘ Four-fold Gospel,’’ by
Tatian, a disciple of Justin Martyr. About this
time the Gospels seem to have been translated into
Latin, soon afterwards into Syriac, and then into
the Egyptian dialects. By the end of the century
they occupy a position very similar to that which
we now describe as ‘‘ Canonical.’’ But the strongest
evidence for the truth of the Gospel narrative is to
be found in the Gospels themselves. It is impos-
sible to separate the miraculous from the non-
miraculous portions, even if it were possible to
| explain Christianity without miracles. The narra-
tive taken as it stands forms a consistent and
coherent whole, and explains the facts so as nothing
else can explain them.
It has been usual to assign to the four Evange-
lists the symbolic figures described in Rev. 4. 7. Of
| the different modes of distributing these the best
is perhaps that of St. Augustine, who assigns to
| St. Matthew the Lion, as representing the royal
dignity of Christ; to St. Mark the Man, as pour-
| traying most carefully His human nature; to St.
| Luke the Ox, as the sacrificial victim; to St. John
the soaring Hagle, which pierces the clouds and
gazes directly upon the sun. The more common
order gives to St. Mark the Lion, and to St. Matthew
the Man.
_ St. Matthew.—Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, who
lived in the early part of the 2nd century, relates
that ‘‘ Matthew composed the oracles in the Hebrew
{i.e. the later Hebrew, or Aramaic] tongue, and
every one interpreted them as he was able.’’ Valu-
able as this statement is, both on account of its date
and from the fact that Papias seems to have got his
| information from persons who had been in contact
with St. Matthew himself, there are several points
in it which are still matter of much obscurity. It
has been proved that the word translated “‘ oracles ”’
| may refer to the whole Gospel as we now have it,
| including both discourse and narratives; but there
| are still some who think that Papias is speaking of
a collection of discourses only, which at an early
date became united with a body of narratives re-
sembling, if not identical with, our present Gospel
of St. Mark. TIrenseus, the celebrated bishop of
Lyons, who wrote about 180 A.p., also says that
the Gospel was originally written in Hebrew, and
adds that it was written ‘“‘ while Peter and Paul
were preaching at Rome and founding [7.e. organiz-
ing] the Church.’? This would be about 64-67 A.D.
The earliest witnesses concur in stating that He-
brew, or Aramaic, was the original language of the
Gospel; but, if so, it must have been very soon
translated into Greek. After the taking of Jeru-
salem in A.D. 70, the number of Hebrew-speaking
Christians bore a small proportion to those who
spoke Greek. Hence the Greek form of the Gospel
survived, while the Hebrew form fell out of use.
It is a further question of much intricacy, what
was the relation of St. Matthew’s original Hebrew
Gospel to a so-called ‘“‘ Gospel according to the
Hebrews’? which was current in the 2nd century,
and of which fragments have come down to us.
These fragments, in their present shape, cannot
be, though they may perhaps be based upon, the
original Gospel of St. Matthew.
Of St. Matthew himself little is known. His call
is described in Matt. 9. 9; from which it would
appear that he had been a collector of customs at
Capernaum. The call of Levi the son of Alpheus
is described in very similar terms, and at a corre-
sponding place in the narrative, by St. Mark and
St. Luke (Mark 2. 18, &e.; Luke 5. 27, &c.); so
that the inference lies near at hand, that, like
St. Jude and St. Paul, St. Matthew also bore two
names, the second, ‘‘ Matthew” (=‘‘ Gift of God’’),
being assumed after his conversion. He appears to
have remained at Jerusalem until the general dis-
persion of the Church there on the outbreak of the
Jewish war; and, according to Eusebius, it was just
at this time, when about to ‘‘ go forth to other
nations,’’ that he wrote his Gospel, and left it as
a legacy to his fellow-countrymen whora he was

St. John.—The Gospel of St. John is one of

eyéwitness of the events, (4)an Apostle, and (5),

St. John. John was the son of Zebedee and Sa-
lome, and probably the younger brother of James.
His family were well-to-do fishermen on the ‘Sea of

He received his final and public call on the Sea of

St. John was the disciple ‘‘whom Jesus’ loved,”

intimacy with our Lord (Mark 5. 387; Matt.17. 1;

On the final dispersion of the Apostles (A.D. 65 or

The Acts.—The Acts of the Apostles is the
natural link between the Gospels, which record our
Lord’s life, and the Epistles which shew the result

canonical acceptance of this bock dates from the

St. Paul’s companions has been worked into the
narrative, will not bear examination. But of all
the companions of St. Paul, St. Luke is the one
who best satisfies the conditions of the problem ;
and he is named as the author of the book by an
unwavering tradition. Sowrces of the Book.—The
close relation of St. Luke to St, Paul naturally
gave him access to excellent materials, especially in
that part of the history in which St. Paul was con-

nized. Among the multitudes who flocked to Rome
from the East there would certainly be some
Christians, and, if we may judge from the greetings
in chap. 16, probably not a few converts of St. Paul
himself, It is possible, too, that some of the
Roman pilgrims who were present on the day of
Pentecost may have carried back with them the
seeds of the Gospel. In this way loose collections
of Christians would gather together, some from
the Jewish synagogues, others from the Gentile
population. The latter seem to have been more
numerous. And it may be inferred from the list
of; names in the last chapter that they belonged
chiefly to the middle and lower classes—freedmen
and slaves. That St. Paul should write to them in
Greek rather than Latin is consistent with the fact
that Greek was very largely spoken among these
classes. Thus it, would appear that the Church at
Rome was a Greek-speaking Church until the
middle of the 8rd century. The Apostle takes the
opportunity of writing to a Church of so much. im-
portance, which he had not yet seen, to set forth
the broad outlines of the Christian scheme in its
application at once to Jew and Gentile, and in all
its profound significance as a new dispensation de-
signed by God to effect that in which previous
systems had failed, viz., to open out a way to
righteousness and salvation for men. ‘he way is
faith in Christ’s death, and sanctification through
His in-dwelling Spirit. Incidentally also the Apostle
discusses the problem which could not but force
itself upon a thinking Jew, the setting aside of the
exclusive privileges of his countrymen, and their
apparent rejection to make room for the Gentile.

There is a close resemblance between the Hpistle
to the Hphesians and that to the Colossians, due
apparently to the fact that they were both written
and despatched at the same time. This resemblance
extends not only to the ideas, but to the expression
which in several places (e.g. Eph. 17 Col. 1.14;
Eph. 1. 10 = Col. 1. 20; Eph. 3. 9 = Col. 1. 25, 26)
is repeated almost verbatim. But though the same
ideas run through both Hpistles, they are regarded
from different points of view. In the Ephesians
the Church is the primary object, and the thought
passes upwards to Christ as the Head of the Church.
In the Colossians Christ is the primary object, and
the thought passes downwards to the Church as the
body of Christ.
Philippians.—Philippi, the scene of the famous
battle (B.c. 42) which ‘decided the fate of the
Roman Republic, occupied a position of importance
on the great military road which connected Rome
with the East. St. Paul arrived here with Luke
and Silas upon his second missionary journey, and
after a short but eventful stay (Acts 16. 12-40) left
behind him the nucleus of a Church, which he
visited again in going and returning from Corinth
(Acts 20. 1-6). The Philippians were especially
forward in contributing to his support (2 Cor. 11.9;
Phil. 4, 15, 16, 18). The Hpistle was in any case
written during the Roman imprisonment, A.D. 61-64,
but opinions differ as to whether it was written in
the earlier or the later portion of that imprison-
ment. The frequent similarity both in thought and
expression to the Romans is an argument for placing
the two Epistles as near to each other as possible ;
and at the same time the other group of Epistles
(Ephesians, Colossians, and Philemon) seems. to
shew signs of a later origin. We shall, therefore,
probably not be far wrong if we suppose that this
Kpistle was written about the autumn of A.D. 61.
It is decidedly personal in its character, and reflects
vividly the alternations of feeling in the Apostle’s
mind as he looks upon the circumstances of his
own imprisonment or upon those of the Philippian
Church. For himself he awaits tranquilly either
event—for ‘‘to live is Christ, and to die gain.”
For them he is grateful for their alms, and speaks
warmly in their praise. The one drawback is a
certain tendency to party-spirit in the households
of Huodia and Syntyche. The whole tone of the
Hpistle is buoyant and cheerful. It has been rightly
observed that the keynote is given in the often-
recurring word “Rejoice.” In its structure it is
broken and unsystematic, and it seems to have
been originally intended to end at the beginning |
of chap. 3.

taking his stand upon the doctrine of the Person
of Christ. He shows how Christ is the one
Mediator between God and Man, so excluding
angel-worship; and that assimilation to Him is
the one great source of sanctification, so excluding
asceticism and ceremonialism.

James.—There can be little doubt that the author
of this Epistle is not, as a few writers have sup-

the James whom we find presiding at the Con-

most prominent figure in that Church in Acts 21.
Keclesiastical tradition describes him as the first
‘bishop’ of Jerusalem; and it adds that he was
distinguished from the other Apostles by his strict
ascetic life and by his scrupulous observance of the
Jewish law and attendance at the Temple worship.
In ‘this way he obtained the respect of the unbe-
lieving Jews as well as of Christians, though he fell
a victim to the more bigoted party about 62, 68 A.D.
St. Paul in Gal. 1. 19 speaks of him by another
designation as ‘‘ James, the Lord’s brother.’’? This
has given rise to much discussion. The ancient
Church regarded St. James as either the son of
Joseph and Mary, or the son of Joseph by a former
marriage. Jerome, however, throws out a new
hypothesis which has obtained wide acceptance, that
the James who wrote this Hpistle is identical with
James ‘‘the Less’’ (or rather ‘‘the little,”’ i.e. in
stature) and James the son of Alphzeus (who in his
turn is identified with the Clopas of John 19. 25),
thus making him a cousin of our Lord. This view
does, indeed, fall in with many of the indications,
but is at the same time exposed to many difficulties,
more especially the statement of John 7. 5, that the
brethren of Jesus still did not believe on Him at a
date after the appointment of the Twelve Apostles,
and that of Acts 1.14, where they are treated as
forming a class by themselves apart from the
Twelve. It is difficult to reconcile this with the
supposition that St. James was one of those origi-
nally appointed by our Lord, St. James was the
acknowledged head of the Jewish party in the
Church, though there is abundant evidence to show
that he gave no countenance to its extreme section.
It was not, however, unnatural that his teaching
should be wrested into seeming opposition to the
freer Gentile Christianity of St. Paul. For in-
stance, he contends that Abraham was justified by
works, where St. Paul contends—and from the very
same quotation (Gen. 15. 6)—that he was justified
by faith: But, in fact, St. James and St. Paul are
attacking, not each other, but the Pharisaic ortho-
doxy whether of Jew or Christian. They attack it
from different sides. St. James says, Show that
your belief is real by its fruits. St. Paul says, See
that you give to right action a deeper personal basis
and motive. Faith is used in different senses; in
the one case of mere head belief, in the other of
heartfelt devotion. The passage Gen. 15. 6 appears
to have been a common topic of discussion in the
Rabbinical schools. The general tenor of St, James’s
Epistle is that of an earnest practical morality, re-
lated to the teaching of St. Paul much as the wise
maxims of the Book of Proverbs are related to the
prophetic visions and profound insight of Tsaiah.
It is to be observed that the word ‘‘ wisdom”? is one
of the keynotes of the Hpistle (1. 5-8; 3. 13-18).
A number of parallels have been pointed out be-

Apocalypse might have been written by another John,
not the Evangelist, as indeed there was a tradition
that two Johns had lived and been buried at Ephe-
sus. he difference which Dionysius observed is a
fact, and some writers, even in modern times, have
had recourse to the same supposition to account for
it. Another explanation, however, which seems to
| be sufficient, is that the Apocalypse was written by
| St. John soon after his arrival in Asia Minor from
Palestine, under the immediate stimulus of the ex-
citement caused by the approaching destruction of
Jerusalem, while the Gospel and Epistles were
written in a ripe and calm old age, after some
20 years of residence in a Greek city. It has been
thought, too, that when the internal indications of
date come to be examined, they point clearly to the
| reign of Galba, the successor of Nero, and to the
year 69 A.D. (the “‘seven heads” of chaps. 18, 17=
the first seven Roman Emperors, the fifth in 17. 10
=Nero, and the ‘‘ number of the beast’’ in 18. 18=
NERON or NERO CAISAR). But these indica-
tions, attractive as they may seem, come into direct
conflict with the external testimony, which is quite
| clear to the effect that the exile of St. John to
| Patmos took place in the 14th year of Domitian,
A.D. 95. How these difficulties are to be resolved
is as yet uncertain; it will be observed, however,
that they consist not so much in the absence of
evidence as in the very abundance of it, and in the
necessity of fitting a number of highly complex phe-
nomena into a fixed scheme.
A like uncertainty rests upon the interpretation of
the book. , There are three schools: (1) the Praeter-
ists, who see in it a series of ideal visions conjured up
in the mind of St. John by the movements attend-

| Futurists, who would throw the description forward
and expect its fulfilment at the end of the world;
(3) the Historical school, who hold that the fulfil-
ment is being gradually accomplished in the course
of human history. It is perhaps possible to accept
the first of these views to the extent of supposing
| that the Apostle has clothed his description of the
Messianic triumph in forms borrowed from the events
of his own time, and yet to believe that no ‘“‘ word
that goeth forth’’ from the Lord shall return to Him
void. The imagery of the Prophets, especially Hze-
kiel, enters largely into the book.

A HARMONY OF THE FOUR GOSPELS,
WITH THE PLACES WHERE THEH EVENTS APPEAR TO HAVE OCCURRED.
REVISED BY THE
Rey. 8S. G. GREEN, D.D., Co-editor of the Revised English Bible.
The general expectation of the Messiah—the impatience of the Roman sovereignty, fostered by the bold and turbulent doctrines of Judas the Galilean—the extra-
ordinary exzitement of the more fanatical part of the people, which led them to crowd round the banner of each successive adventurer, who either assumed or might
assume that character—the rigid prudence of the chief priests, lest the slightest indication of revolt should compromise the safety of the city and the Temple, and expose
the whole nation to the jealous resentment of the Roman governor—these circumstances of the times sufficiently account for the reception which such a teacher as Jesus
of Nazareth met with in Jerusalem. Appearing, as he did, with doctrines so alarming to the authority of the priesthood—so full of disappointment to the fanatic
populace—so repugnant to the national pride, as implying the dissolution of the Mosaic constitution, and the establishment of a new and more comprehensive faith—
and, above all, openly assuming the mysterious title, the Son of God—it excites less astonishment than sorrow and commiseration, that the passions of such a people
should at once take arms, and proceed to the most awful violence against a Teacher, whose tenets were so much too pure and spiritual for their comprehension, whose
character was so remote from their pre-conceived notions of the expected Messiah. Milman’s ‘‘ History of the Jews,” Book 12, p. 123.

By THE Rey. R. B. GIRDLESTONE, M.A., Hon. Canon of Christ Church, Oxford.
| A CONSIDERABLE proportion of the Bible—perhaps a
third—is of the nature of Poetry, though it is not
usually printed in poetic form. The Oriental mind
| is naturally more poetic than the Western, and has
| a strong tendency to figurative style, which i is one of
the ordinary characteristics of poetry. There is a
| strong poetic ring in the most ancient literatures of
the world, and we naturally look for it in’the Bible.
We must not, however, expect the measured and
resonant lines which ordinarily express poetic feeling
amongst ourselves. .Hebrew poetry has, strictly
speaking, neither rhyme nor metre. It is, however,
to a large extent rhythmical, and is more concise,
pointed, and allusive than prose. Its peculiar feature
lies in the sense rather than in the sound, and consists
| in the balancing of sentences and thoughts, either
in the way of Parallelism, or of Progression, or of
Contrast.
It is not always easy to determine the boundary
line between’ Biblical poetry and prose. There is
prosaic poetry in Scripture, and there is poetic prose:
In fact, with regard to the poetry of all lands, we
can more easily say what it does than what it is. It
elevates, it stirs, it kindles emotion, it thrills, it
deepens, it evokes echoes, it draws. out harmonies
between the soul and the world, and between the
creature and the Creator, ‘‘'The poet’s words spread
their invisible arms through time and space; and
when generations and countries, and even religions,
have gone away, still stand m unwearying freshness
and truth.’? (See Wordsworth’s Pref. to Vol. 1 of his
Works.) The Biblical poet is essentially a theologian.
He touches the springs of life, and recognises the
Divine beneath the human. Without professing to
be a philosopher, he is one really, for he is in contact
with the One Being, with whom is the secret of the
universe.
We proceed to point out some characteristics of
Hebrew poetry. The Parallelism, which is its ordinary
feature, may be seen in such a passage as Num. 23.

From the top of the rocks I see him,
And from the hills I behold him:
Lo, the people shall dwell alone,
And shall not be reckoned among the nations.
Who can count the dust of Jacob,
And the number of the fourth part of Israel?
Let me die the death of the righteous,
And let my last end be like his!
The Inferential or Progressive style is specially
| instructive, as it often suggests a line of argument
| which it does not work out.
Thus, Ps. 119. 78 :—
Thy hands have made me and fashioned me:
Give me understanding, that I may learn thy com-
mandments.
The Contrasted style may be illustrated from the
closing words of the Song of Deborah (Judg. 5
31) :—
So let all thine enemies perish, O Lorp:
But let them that love him be as the sun when he
goeth forth in his might.
The Refrain is frequently used by the Hebrew
We find it in the Lament of Dav id over Saul,
where there is the thrice repeated, ‘* How are the
; and in the 46th Psalm, when, twice
we meet with the words,—
The Lorp of Hosts is with us;
The God of Jacob is our refuge.
Tn the 136th Psalm the Refrain becomes a liturgical
response, ‘* For His mercy endureth for ever.’’ Occa-
over,
sionally the terms of the Refrain are slightly varied,
as in Pgs. 42 and 43, which contain, three times,—
Why art thou cast down, O my soul?
And why art thou disquieted within me?
Hope thou in God:
For I shall yet praise him for the help of his
countenance.
The variations in such cases are frequently put
down to errors of copyists; but this is quite unneces-
sary, as a more complete study of Hebrew poetry
will show that the writers had a strong tendency to
deliberate variation.
One of the characteristics of the Hebrew poet is
his Irony. This is often shown in his skilful method
of putting words into the mouth of some actor in the
scene. ‘Thus in the Song of Moses (Ex. 15. 9, 10) :—
The enemy said,
“TI will pursue, I will overtake,
I will divide the spoil;
My lust shall be satisfied upon them;
will draw my sword,
My hand shall destroy them.’
Thou didst blow with thy wind,
The sea covered them:
They sank as lead in the mighty waters.
Similarly in the Song of Deborah, the mother of
Sisera is depicted at her lattice questioning as to the
delay ; and in the answer of the wise women there is
a fine instance of suppressed irony, followed by a brief
and allusive summing up of the enemies’ fall.
The rapidity of Transition in these passages amounts
almost to abruptness. There are many similar cases,
and there are also frequent instances of Transition
from person to person, which becomes perplexing to
a careless reader. Thus in Isa. 52 and 58 the Righteous
Servant is generally spoken of in the third person,
but once in the second person; and God is spoken
of in the third person (53. 6), in the second person
(53. 10), and in the first (53. 12). These changes of
person are sometimes imagined to be slips of copyists;
but they are deliberate, “and must be regarded as
characteristic of the Hebrew style.
The tendency to the Concrete and Figurative may
be illustrated freely from Hosea, one of the most
poetical of the Old Testament writers. The last
chapter presents an excellent example :—
I will be as the dew unto Israel:
He shall grow as the lily,
And cast forth his roots as Lebanon.
His branches shall spread, 4
And his beauty shall be as the olive tree,
And his smell as Lebanon.
One secret of the vividness of the poetic style in
Scripture is the frequent use of the Question. Thus,
in the 114th Psalm :—
What ailed thee, O thou sea, that thon fleddest ?
Thou Jordan, that thou wast driven back?
Ye mountains, that ye skipped like rams?
And ye little hills, like lambs?
The most remarkable series of Questions is that
contained in Amos 3. 8-8, where there are nine
questions within the compass of six verses. Another
series, unique as well as suggestive, is to be found
in the 38th and three following chapters of Job,
where the ignorance of man is forcibly displayed in
his inability to give answers to the questions of God
concerning Nature.
The Poetry of the Bible may be classified according
to its subject-matter. Riddles, proverbs, blessings,
thanksgivings, and prophecies generally tended to-

68 HEBREW POETRY.
wards poetic structure. Thus, Samson’s enigma,
and also its solution, both have a poetic ring :—
Out of the eater came forth meat,
And out of the strong came forth sweetness.
What is sweeter than honey?
And what is stronger than a lion?
So with the prediction concerning Rebekah’s children
in Gen. 25. .23:—
Two nations are in thy womb,
And two manner of people shall be separated from
thy bowels;
And the one people shall be stronger than the other
people ;
And the elder shall serve the younger.
Jacob’s blessing of his twelve sons is all poetry,
so is Moses’ blessing of the tribes. The national
song contained in Deut. 32 is poetry as well as pro-
phecy. The Dirge over Saul, contained in 2 Sam. 1, is
a striking specimen of a Hebrew lyric. The Book of
Proverbs can hardly be called poetry, though at
times very near it. Some of the Psalms are’ sen-
tentious and proverbial ; but most of them, especially
the songs of praise and of aspiration, are highly
poetic. They exhibit, at times, a peculiar feature,
which Mr. Isaac Taylor called attention to in his
“ Spirit of the Hebrew Poetry,’’ viz., the juxtaposition
of apparently inconsistent attributes of God. One
instance which he quotes will suffice to illustrate this
point, It is to be found in the 147th Psalm :—
The Lorp doth build up Jerusalem:
He gathereth together the outcasts of Israel.
He healeth the broken in heart,
And bindeth up their wounds.
He telleth the number of the stars;
He calleth them all by their names,
Great is our Lord, and of great power:
His understanding is infinite.
The Lorp lifteth up the meek:
He casteth the wicked down to the ground.
As one reads these lines one is impressed with the
power, tenderness, infinity, and providence of the God
of Israel, What philosophical treatise could produce
so deep and vivid an impression? And this leads to
another consideration. The songs of praise, contained
in the Psalms and elsewhere, consist largely in the
setting forth of the attributes of God; this is the
very best form which the utterance of praise can
take, and it is here that Inspiration was specially
needed by the singer, both to suggest truth and to
guard from error. An instance of this may be seen
in the Song of Hannah. ‘The occasion was a simple
one—the birth of a child; yet the Spirit lifts the
singer up above the ordinary condition of thought in
order to make her the mouthpiece of deep truths.
The Song (1 Sam. 2) opens thus :—
My heart rejoiceth in the Lorn,
Mine horn is exalted in the Lorp:
My mouth is enlarged over mine enemies;
Because I rejoice in thy salvation.
There is none holy as the Lorp:
For there is none beside thee:
Neither is there any rock like our God.
Even if the Song had gone no further, we should
have been struck with the introduction of the word
‘ salvation,’’ and with the reference to God’s holiness
and eternal strength, for the circumstances of the
case seem hardly sufficient in themselves to call for
such an utterance. But a little further the singer pro-
ceeds thus :—
The bows of the mighty men are broken,
* And they that stumbled are girded with strength.
They that were full have hired out themselves for bread ;
And they that were hungry ceased:
So that the barren hath born seven,
And she that hath many children is waxed feeble.
This would be gross exaggeration if regarded simply
as a poetical version of what had actually occurred ;
and the ‘critic’? who would dismiss the Song as a
late invention might be justified. But where it is
read as the work of one ‘‘rapt’’ by the Holy Spirit,
it becomes a revelation of great and eternal truths.
This becomes more clear as the Song proceeds :—
The Lorp killeth, and maketh alive:
He bringeth down to the grave, and bringeth up.
The Lorp maketh poor, and maketh rich:
He bringeth low, and lifteth up.
* * *
* * *
He will keep the feet of his saints,
And the wicked shall be silent in darkness;
For by strength shall no man prevail.
The adversaries of the Lorp shall be broken to pieces;
Out of heaven shall he thunder upon them:
The Lorp shall judge the ends of the earth;
And he shall give strength unto his king,
And exalt the horn of his anointed.
The closing lines are, perhaps, the most remarkable,
because they introduce the Messianic element, and
that, in anticipation of the Kingly period. <A critic
dealing with the matter on purely secular grounds
rejects the Song as a whole, or, at any rate, the last
part of it, as a late invention. But the devout
student of Biblical poetry, believing, with St. James,
that ‘ known unto God are all his works from the be-
ginning of the world,” reads these startling words as
the utterance of the Eternal Spirit, and reckons them
among the distinct predictions of the Messianic dis-
pensation. It is not surprising, on this understand-
ing of the Song, to find it quoted verbally in the
Psalms and Proverbs, and to discover its outline
reproduced in the Magnificat.
The Prophetic element of Scripture is largely com-
bined with the poetic. The mind being lifted out of
itself, seemed to become specially fertile in figurative
language, specially concise in allusions, specially
abrupt in transitions. There is a grandeur, a sub-
limity, in some of the Apocalyptic poetry of the Old
Testament, as, for instance, in the account of the
manifestation of God, in Hab. 3, or in the denun-
ciations on Babylon, Egypt, and Tyre, in Isaiah,
Jeremiah, and Hzekiel.
It remains briefly to point out the parts of the
Old Testament which are distinctly poetical, It is
the fashion to talk of Genesis 1 as the ‘‘ Creation
poem’’; but, from a literary point of view, this is
a complete mistake. The chapter is plain prose,
and contains none of the marks of Hebrew poetry.
Putting aside the blessings and songs contained in
Gen. 49, Ex. 14, Deut. 32 and 33, and a few short
fragments, there is nothing to be called poetry till
we reach the Songs of Deborah (Judg. 5), of Hannah
(1 Sam. 2), and of David (2 Sam. 1). Thus, we
reach Dayid’s Song of Deliverance (2 Sam. 22) and
his ‘last words’? (2 Sam. 22), and the message of
Isaiah (2 Kin. 19). We now reach the Book of Job,
which is a dramatic poem in a prosaic framework.
The Psalms may be called Israel’s hymn-book.
Ecclesiastes is mainly prose, but its proverbial
chapters (e.g., chap. 7) tend to a poetic form. The
Canticles are unique, and have a dramatic character.
Isaiah is almost all poetry; but Jeremiah consists
largely of sermons, though the book contains some
poetic chapters (see chaps. 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12-16, 20,
23, 25, 30, and 46-51). The Book of Lamentations
is poetic, and the first four chapters are acrostic,
following the order of the alphabet, as is the case
with some of the Psalms (e.g., 111, 112, and 119)
and Prov. 31. 10-31. Ezekiel may be called poetic
prose, with occasional flashes of real poetry, ¢.9.;
chap. 32. Hosea is highly poetical; Joel, fairly;
Amos, hardly at all. Jonah is prose all but the
hymn, which is really a selection taken from the
Psalms. Micah sometimes rises to true poetic
style. Nahum is sublime in parts, so is Habakkuk.
Zephaniah is also poetic; but the remaining three
prophets, who belong to the post-Captivity period,
write in prose, except fragments in Zech. 9 and 11,

THE ETHNOLOGY OF THE BIBLE.
By THE Rev. A. H. SAYCE, M.A., Queen’s College, Oxford.
Tux ethnological knowledge displayed in the Bibli-
cal books varies with their age. The geographical
horizon of the Jews became gradually widened, new
tribes and races appeared upon the scene, and infor-
mation was. collected from the merchants of Pho-
nicia or the literature of Egypt and Babylonia. The
ethnology of the Bible, therefore, naturally falls into
four periods :—(1) the Patriarchal ; (2) the Davidic ;
(8) that of the Exile; and (4) that of the New Tes-
tament. Great light has been thrown upon it by
Egyptian and Assyrian research; the first period
being chiefly illustrated by the monuments of
Egypt, the next two periods by the monuments of
Assyria. But we must first ascertain what indica-
tions may be found in the Bible itself of the origin
and ethnological relations of the peoples with whom
the Hebrews were brought into contact, and then
consider how far these have been confirmed or
modified by modern discovery. In such a subject
it is difficult to draw a hard and fast line between
what is ethnological and what is geographical; our
only means for determining the blodd-relationship
of some particular people often consists in its geo-
graphical position and local names. Other means
will be language, history, tradition, and (where
attainable) moral and physical characteristics.
We must remember, however, that language and
race are not convertible terms, A race may adopt a
foreign language even without intermarriage, and
where intermarriages take place, such an occurrence
is far from uncommon. Of this, the modern Jews
are a good instance in point. The fact that two
nationalities speak the same language only proves
that they have been at some time or other in social
contact, while diversity of language does not neces-
sarily imply diversity of race. At most, linguistic
agreement or diversity raises a presumption in
favour of racial agreement or diversity.
Languages are classed (1) according to the way in
which they express the relations of grammar, and
(2) according to their descent from a common
parent-tongue. In Hurope and Western Asia we
find examples both of inflectional and of aggluti-
native languages. An inflectional language is one
in which the grammatical relations of words in a
sentence are denoted by terminations which have
no independent existence apart from the words to
whick they are attached, or else by the change of
vowels or consonants within the words themselves.
French, or German, ot Latin are familiar examples
of inflectional tongues. An agglutinative language
is one in which the relations of grammar are ex-
pressed by affixing one word to another. In English,
for instance, man’s, men, book-s, love-d would be
illustrations’ of inflection; there-in, there-to, of
agglutination. In Europe and Western Asia there
are two leading inflectional families of speech, the
Aryan or Indo-European, to which Latin, Greek,
Persian, Sanskrit, Keltic, Slavonic, German, Eng-
lish, and most modern European languages belong ;
and the Semitic, which comprises Hebrew, Pho-
nician, Aramaic, Arabic, Assyrian, and Ethiopic ;
while there are at least two agglutinative families
of speech, the Turanian or Finno-Tatar, com-
prising Finnic, Hungarian, Tatar, Turkish, Mongol,
and other tongues; and the Dravidian of Western
India, of which Tamil is the chief dialect. There
is also another inflectional family of speech known
as Alarodian, once spoken throughout the Armenian
highlands, of which Georgian is now the chief repre-
sentative. In the Caucasus we find the remains of
several distinct families of speech which have else-
where disappeared. A family of speech, it must be
remembered, is a group of cognate languages which
can all be traced back to a single parent-tongue.
Western Asia, with which the ethnology of the
Bible is mainly concerned, may be regarded as a
square, bounded on the north by the Black Sea and
the Caucasus, on the south by the Indian Ocean, on
the east by the Caspian, the Persian Gulf, and the
intervening mountainous country, and on the west
by the Mediterranean and Red Sea. LHgypt is
attached to the western side of the square by the
isthmus of Suez, the promontory of Asia Minor
lying opposite to it, with the Greek islands of the
Aiigean Sea beyond. The square is further divided
by the two great rivers, Euphrates and Tigris, which
rise near each other in the mountains of Armenia,
and after flowing in a parallel direction towards the
south, fall into the Persian Gulf at the same spot.
Armenia and Asia Minor are high tablelands, inter-
sected by lofty chains of mountains, of which the
Taurus, Masius, and Niphates raiges may be con-
sidered the chief, and sloping upwards to the peaks
of the Caucasus. The mountains of Armenia ex-
tend to the south-east along the southern shore of
the Caspian, where they enclose Media Rhagiana,
the home of the Medes, and then, taking a bend,
run southwards to the Persian Gulf, and so form
the highlands of Elam and Persia on the east of
Babylonia. The plain of Babylonia enclosed be-
tween the Tigris and Euphrates is low and fertile ;
Mesopotamia, however, its northern continuation,
is a limestone plateau of moderate elevation. On
the west the spurs of the Taurus range, under the
names of Amanus, Bargylus, and Lebanon, and of
Anti-Lebanon and Hermon, stretch southward along
the shores of the Mediterranean, and constitute the
mountainous region of, Syria proper and Phoenicia.
The Jordan rises on the south-western slopes of
Anti-Lebanon or Hermon, and after flowing through
the Sea of Galilee or Lake Tiberias, falls into the
Dead Sea. The angle enclosed between the moun-
tains of Syria and Palestine on the one side, and the
Euphrates on the other, is flat and barren, and was
known to the ancients as Arabia Petreea. This
stony desert extends far into the heart of Arabia ;
indeed, it is only on the coastlands of the latter
country that mountains and rivers are to be found,
and more especially in the south, the Saba and
Himyar of early writers, the Arabia Felix of the
Romans, the Yemen of modern geographers. The
peninsula of Sinai at the head of the Red Sea is also
mountainous, but bare and barren, like the coast of

the Nile flows at a little distance inland, fertilis-
