V. Science, Literature, and Art.
It is difficult to trace Egyptian influence upon the
Israelites in either one of these respects. It is
otherwise as regards Assyria and Babylonia. The
dial of Ahaz points to his acquaintance with Baby-
lonian science, and we may gather from Prov. 25. 1
that HEZEKIAH established a library where scribes
were employed in copying and editing old books,
like the libraries with their staff of scribes and
copyists found in every great Babylonian and
Assyrian city. Though papyrus or parchment was
generally used for writing purposes, in Jer. 32. 10,
11 we seem to have a reference to a contract in-
scribed in the Assyrian manner on a clay tablet,
and, after the signatures of the witnesses, covered
by an outer coating of clay, on which the heads of
the contract were written, with a docket of papyrus
attached to it by a string. In art, the Israelites
were the pupils of the Pheenicians (see 1 Kings
mainly borrowed and adapted from Assyria and
Babylonia. Thus the devices of cherubs, palm-
trees, pomegranates, lions, and the like in Sono-
Mon’s TEMPLE were Phoenico- Assyrian, and the
architectural details of the Temple itself have been
traced back to Phoenicia and Assyria. Babylonia
was the original home of the column as used in
Western Asia and Europe, as also of seas or reser-
voirs in temples: 1 Kings 7. 23. The cherubs seen
by Ezekiel (10) ) resemble those of Assyrian art, and
the Assyrian and Babylonian gods were carried
about in arks. The ‘pattern’? of the altar at
Damascus, again, which Anaz ordered to be imi-
tated in the Temple at Jerusalem (2 Kings 16. 10,
11), was no doubt Assyrian. Just as the Phosnicians
borrowed the Egyptian sphinx, so also did they
borrow the Assyro-Babylonian cherub; but whereas
the sphinx was not represented among the Israel-
ites, probably on account of its idolatrous connec-
tion, the cherub was freely introduced into the
decoration of the Temple. ‘To the Phceenicians the
Israelites also owed their alphabet, which had been
adapted from the Hgyptian hieroglyphiecs by the
Pheenicians of the Delta at a very early date.
What influence the Phoenicians may have had upon
Hebrew literature it is impossible to say, but when
we remember that Kirjath-sepher, “‘ the book town,”’
(Josh. 15. 15; Judg. 1.11) was among the places
conquered by the Israelites upon their entrance into
Canaan, and that Phoenician literature, more espe-
cially historical literature, went back to a period
anterior to that of Hiram and David, we are justi-
fied in believing that some influence it must have
had. At all events, Josephus, quoting from Menan-
der of Hphesus and Dius, asserts that Solomon and
Hiram propounded riddles to one another on-the
penalty of paying a fine if they were not guessed,
and that Hiram was unable to solve the riddles of
Solomon until a Tyrian named Abdemon came to
his aid.

we gather that cir. B.c. 2280 the Hlamites invaded
Babylonia, captured Ur and Erech, and expelled
the Semites. The Elamite was the roling element,
but had the Guti, the Goim or “ nations’? of Gen.
14. 1 (see Var. note), for allies. An inscribed stone
of a king of Guti of the period exists (B.M.), but his
name is obliterated.

Other inscriptions of this period are bricks and
cylinders of Kudur Mabug, f father of Hria-kw or
Arioch, who claims the title of ‘‘ Lord of Syria”
(B.M.), as Kudur Lagamar, i.e. Chedorlaomer,
might have done (Gen. TA. 4). The most important
record is a contract dated in the year when ‘‘ Kham-
murabi”’ the king gloriously marched and overthrew
Eriakw and the Lord of Kiam (B.M.), who may have
been ‘‘ Chedorlaomer, king of Hlam”’ (Gen. 14. 1).
Migration of Terah, i.e. from Ur of the Chal-
dees to Haran, 7.e. Charran (Gen. 11. 31; Acts 7. 4).
A. eylinder from Ur inscribed by Nabonidus, and
another of the king from Sippara (B.M.) recording the
restoration of the temple of the Moon-god in Kharran,
show the close relation between the two towns,
and this may explain the first step in the migration
of Abram the Hebrew (Gen. 14. 13). The contract
tablets also show the high degree of development of
trade amongst the Semites of Babylonia, and are an
important comment on the incident of the purchase
of the Cave of Machpelah (Gen. 23. 17-20), the
wording of these verses corresponding exactly to
that of the tablets of sales of laud at this epoch.
Period of the Patriarchs.—A gap in the se-
quence of the monumental evidence has recently
been filled by the most astonishing discovery in
Kgypt of a remarkable series of inscriptions known
as The Tel-el Amarna Tablets (B.M., Blk., and Ber-
lin ?), which supply also most important details as
to the state of Palestine during the two centuries
preceding its conquest by the children of Israel.
These
royal city founded by
tablets were discovered in the ruins of the
Khu-en-aten, i.e. Ameno-
phis [V. of Manetho. This king, whose reign may
be placed about B.c. 1500, married an Asiatic wife,
Ti, daughter of Tushrata, king of Mitani, i.e. Aram-
Naharaim, and, owing to these relationships, he
carried on a close communication, by correspondence,
with the court of his father-in-law, and with the
other courts of Western Asia. These letters are
written in a peculiar style of cuneiform writing,
and contain letters and reports from scribes or con-
suls at Gaza, Zidon, and the cities of Northern
Syria, which throw a most important light on the
geography of Palestine. In one of the tablets (Blk.)
mention is made of Gaza, Hebron, Keilah (1 Sam.
23. 1) and a city of Uru-salim, which can be no other
than the Jebusite fortress, mentioned even at this
early period under its later name. These tablets,
moreover, show the great importance of Hebron and
the reason why it became the centre of rule in
Southern Palestine. Its name is clearly derived
from the word Khabiri=“‘allies,’’ and therefore it
probably was as the centre of four allied tribes that
it obtained its name of Kirjath-Arba, “‘ the village
of the four’? (Josh. 14. 15). The lists of products
sent to Egypt, recorded in these tablets, show the
wealth of Canaan prior to the Hebrew conquest.
The Time of Joseph.—Almost all scholars ad-
mit that the time of Joseph’s rule in Egypt belongs
to the period of the Shepherd Kings in Hgypt (Gen.
46. 34), i.e. of the subjection of Lower Egypt to its
Hyksos conquerors. Indeed, tradition marks Apept
as the special Pharaoh under whom Joseph rose to
power. Monuments of special interest in relation to
this period are, the fine stone head of a Hyksos king
—a head revealing all the characteristics of a foreign
race—and a fine statue of a Hyksos king, both found
recently at Bubastis (B.M.); Sphinwes from Tanis
or Zoan, of a very Asiatic character, and a curious
altar, presenting a marked contrast to true Hgyptian
Ww ie and the sepulchral tablet of Baba, an Egyp-
tian nobleman, found at El-Kab in Southern Egypt
(Blk.). This man lived a good and benevolent lite
oe the latter years preceding the rise of the
18th dynasty, and therefore probably during the
period of Joseph’s rule. This inscription contains
a direct reference to a contemporary famine, viz.
‘“ When the famine arose, lasting many years, I
distributed corn to the city each year of famine.’
Many smaller monuments in the British and other
Museums throw great light on the Life and Times
of Joseph.
Shortly after the time of Joseph a war broke out
in Egypt, and resulted in the expulsion of the foreign-
ers; the details of this war (which must have afflicted
the Israelites) are found in the inscription (at Thebes)
of Aahmes, a sailor who gained great glory under
the last native king of the 18th dynasty, Ra-seknen.
Period of the Oppression.—In the mound of
Tel-el-Maskhuta, near ‘Iel-el-Kebir, M. Naville, act-
| ing for the Egyptian Exploration Fund in 1880,
found the ruins of Pithom,
“the treasure city’
(Exod. 1. 11), -which also was ‘called Succoth (Exod.
12. 37), and was, therefore, the first station on the
route of the Exodus. Here were strong treasure
houses, with massive walls of sun-baked_ bricks,
some with and some without straw (Hxod. 5. 7).
The bricks are stamped with the cartouche of
Rameses IT., whom we must now identify with the
Pharaoh of the oppression.
From this city several monuments of interest have
come to the British Museum. Among the monu-
ments from Pithom, one of the chief is the statue
of the Recorder of ’Pithom (B.M.).
Canaan before Joshua,—Lists of geographical
names, engraved by Thothmes ITI. on the walls of
the temple at Karnak, supply (arranged in groups)
the names of over 100 of the principal cities of
Canaan.* Moreover, the papyrus of the ‘‘ Travels
of a Mohar’’ (messenger) in Syria, made during the
latter part of the reign of Rameses IT., records his
journey from Egypt to Aleppo, passing Gebal, Bey-
rout, Sidon, and other important cities.
THE HEBREW NATION IN CANAAN.
Hittite Monuments.—During the period between
the rise of the 18th dynasty in Egypt, 7.e. B.c. 1600,
and the end of the 19th, the archeology of the
parts of Western Asia most in contact with the
Israelites is represented by the curious monuments
of the Hittite people. We so find the Hittites at
Hebron (Gen. 23. 3), and the association of this
eity with Zoan (Num. 138. 22) may connect them
with the Hyksos conquerors of Lower Ngypt.
Amongst these recovered monuments are the in-
scribed stones from Hamath (Constantinople Mu-
seum), written in a curious hieroglyphic character
(casts in B.M.), and monuments from Carchemish,
Berejik, Mar: ash, &c. (B.M.), and from various parts
of Asia Minor (Berlin). It has been ascertained
that the Hittite empire extended from Carchemish,
on the Euphrates, to the shores of the A!gean Sea.
The Hittites were a very warlike people (2 Kings
7. 6), trading in horses (1 Kings 28. 29), The king-
dom of Hamath, one of the Hittite confederate
states, was that nearest to the Israelites, and the
alliance formed by David (LXX.) seems to have
lasted until the power of the kingdom in the Orontes
valley was broken by the Assyrians (2 Kings 14, 28).

The power of the Hittites is shown by the Treaty
between them and Rameses II., preserved upon the
walls of Karnak and in the Sallier Papyrus (B.M.).
Their language is as yet unknown, but some clue
is afforded by the silver boss of Tarkutimme, which
bears an inscription both in Hittite and cuneiform
characters (cast in B.M.), but the ethnic type of |
face is certainly Mongol or Tartar.

Synchronisms.—The synchronisms between the |
historical books of the Old Testament and the |
monuments are first established by the famous
Stele of Shalmaneser II., discovered at Kurkh, on
the Tigris, near Diarbek’r (B.M.). In about B.c. 854
the Hittite kings under Sangara, king of Carcha-
nish, the Syrians of Damascus under Ben-hadad IT.,
or Hadad-idri, and Akhabu, king of Sirlai or
Israel, combined to oppose Shalmaneser, but the
allies were defeated in a great battle at Karkar
on the Orontes. This is in harmony with Scripture,
for Ahab, after the battle of Aphek, concluded an
alliance with Syria, which resulted in the restora-
tion to Israel of cities which had been lost, and of a
trading quarter in Damascus (1 Kings 20. 34).
Tribute of Jehu to Assyria. — The important
fact that Jehu was a tributary of Shalmaneser IT.
is recorded on an Obelisk of black-basalt (B.M.), the
Israelitish embassy being represented, with the fol-
lowing inscription :—‘‘ The tribute of Jehu son of
Omri, bars of silver, bars of gold, a golden bowl,
a golden ladle, golden goblets, golden pitchers, bars
of lead, a staff for the hand of the king, and spear
shaft I received,”’ *
A pavement slab found at Nimroud proves that
this tribute was paid in the year B.c. 842, after the
defeat of Hazael, king of Damascus (2 Kings 8. 15
& 9. 2). The next inscription in importance is
(B.M.) a mural slab of Rimmon-Nirari (8.c. 810-
781), who mentions his conquest of Tyre, Sidon, the
land of Omri (Samaria), and the land of Palastar
(Philistia).
After a break in our monumental series of about
55 years, t.e. until the rise of the new Assyrian em-
pire under Tiglath-Pileser II, (8.c. 745), an impor-
tant series of inscriptions follow. The Pavement
Slabs, from Nimroud, give details of the overthrow
of analliance between Judah under Azariah (Uzziah)
and Hamath under Yahu-bihdi (2 Kings 14, 28, but
see Var. note) in B.c. 743. At this time Arpad was
captured by Assyria (2 Kings 18. 34). In these in-
scriptions Menahem of Samaria and Rezon of Da-
mascus are named. In 2 Kings 15.19, the Assyrian
king is called Pul, a variation of name now explained
by a most valuable inscription (B.M.) known as the
Babylonian Chronicle, which has the name Pulw
(the Poros of Ptolemy’s Canon), in correspondence
to the Tiglath-Pileser of the Assyrian Canon.
Later inscriptions of the same series record the re-
volt of Pekah, and the installation of Hoshea by
the Assyrian king.t From the Chronicle inscrip-
tion we learn that Tiglath-Pileser died in Tebet
(December), B.c. 727, whereupon Ulula (the Bulasos
of Ptolemy) seized the throne, and proclaimed him-
self as Shalmaneser IV.,8.c. 727. We have as yet
no inscriptions of this king. It was he who besieged
Samaria (2 Kings 17. 5), and whose reign terminated
in a revolt headed by Sargon the Tartan.

Sargon ascended the throne on the 12th day of
Tebet, B.c. 722, and captured Samaria early in that
| year (2 Kings 17.6). The most important inscrip-
| tions of Sargon are those from Khorsabad, near

sieged, I captured, 27,280 of its inhabitants I carried
| away; 50 chariots of them I took....my viceroy I
placed over them; the tribute of the former king I
imposed upon them.’’? Other monuments of Sargon
are the Barrel Cylinder (B.M.), Cyprus Monolith
(Berlin), and a large pair of Winged Bulls (B.M.),
Another most important inscription of Sargon is
upon a terra cotta cylinder in the British Museum,
which records the siege of Ashdod in B.c. 711. In
B.c, 712, the embassy to Hezekiah from Merodach-
baladan (2 Kings 20. 6) arrived at Jerusalem,
and the proceedings for revolt were arranged. In
B.c. 711 Sargon marched against Ashdod (Isa. 20),
and after its capture overran “‘the wide land of
Judea,” as well as Hdom, Moab, and Philistia. This
monument throws especial light upon the descrip-
tions of the siege by Isaiah (10-11). Sargon was
assassinated in his palace on the 12th of Ab (July),
B.C. 705, and his son Sennacherib succeeded him.
Sennacherib. — The British Museum is ex-
tremely rich in memorials of this great king. The
first and most important is the Taylor Cylinder,
a large hexagon terra cotta cylinder, which records
the Siege of Jerusalem (2 Kings 18.18). This event
is also recorded on the Winged Bulls from the
king’s palace, and on a large slab in the Museum at
Constantinople. We may also assign the fine series
of sculptured slabs (B. M.) representing the Siege
of Lakish to this series. The Jewish type of face
is certainly clearly shown here, and so marked is it
that we may connect these sculptures with a series
in the Koywnjik Room, representing a siege, which
there is strong reason to identify with that of
Jerusalem, A remarkable point in connection with
these sculptures is the deliberate mutilation of the
face of Sennacherib, to mark the hatred of the
king after his murder. From the Babylonian
Chronicle we learn the date of this murder: “ On
the 20th day of the month Tebet (December, B.¢.
681), Sennacherib king of Assyria, by his own son
in insurrection, was slain’? (2 Kings 19. 37). This
insurrection is referred to in a cylinder inscription
of Esar-haddon (B.M.), where he states that after
the battle in which he defeated his brothers there
‘vose from the host the cry, This is our king.”
From the death of Sennacherib and the accession
of Esar-haddon the information is chiefly derived
from the Babylonian Chronicle, and the chief points
of contact with the Bible are the Ethiopian revolt
in Hgypt under Tirhakah (2 Kings 19. 9), in B.c. 675,
and followed three years later, in B.c. 671, by the
| invasion of Egypt and the capture of Memphis, and
the defeat of Tirhakah. Esar-haddon died on the
10th day of Marchesvan (Oct.), B.c. 668, and was
succeeded by his son Assurbanipal, the Sardana-
palus of the Greeks, who ascended the throne as
viceroy shortly before his father’s death, who is
probably the Asnapper of the Bible (Hzra 4. 10).
The reign of this king was the highest period of the
Assyrian civilisation, and is probably the period |
against which the prophet Nahum pours out his |
denunciations. Assurbanipal resumed the Hgyptian
wars of his father, and in his second war, in B.C. 660,
captured Thebes from Urdamani or Rud-Ammon,
the successor of Tirhakah. The capture of Thebes,
the No Amon of the Bible (Nahum 3. 8), is de-

of Assurbanipal (B.M.), who states :—‘‘ Urdamani |
fled alone and entered No, his royal city. In a |
march of a month and ten days they advanced....
into the midst of No, that town in its entire extent |
they captured.’? It is evidently to this capture that |
the prophet refers. The monuments of Assurbanipal
are more plentiful than those of any other Assyrian |
king, consisting of several inscribed terra cotta cylin- |
ders from Nineveh, and tablets; also some hundreds
of tablets from the Royal Library (B.M.), and a |
magnificent series of sculptures in the best style of
Assyrian art (B.M.), especially those representing
the Lion Hunt (B.M.). The reign of Assurbanipal
was followed by a rapid decline of the empire, owing
to the disruption in the royal party. The most im-
portant records of this period are a series of rough
tablets (B.M.) recording the advance of the Medes,
the Gimerai (Gen. 10. 2), and the tribes from the
north-east against Nineveh in the reign of Hsar-
haddon IT. (8.c. 625). To this period also belong
tablets dated in the reign of Sinsar-iskun, the
Saracus of the classic writers.
Babylonian Captivity.—Of the period of the
Babylonian Captivity several important records have
recently been discovered :—T wo valuable terra cotta
cylinders, bearing inscriptions of Nabopalassar, the
Assyrian general who usurped the throne of Babylon
after the fall of Nineveh (B.M.). Of Nebuchad-
nezzar II. (B.c. 606) there are an almost unlimited
supply of records. The two rock-cut inscriptions,
the one at the mouth of the Nahr-el-kelb, the an-
cient Lycus, near Beyrout, and the similar inscrip-
tion on the rocks at Wady Birsa, in the Lebanon, |
testify to the presence of the great king in Syria. |
The latter of these is a most valuable record, as it is |
situated within sight of the town of Riblah, the
ancient Libnah, where the camp of Nebuchadnezzar
was pitched during the siege of Jerusalem (2 Kings |
25. 4), and where the eyes of Zedekiah were put
out (2 Kings 25.7). It is also to be noted that the |
Wady Birsa, where this inscription is, was evidently
the place where the cedars cut in Lebanon were pre- |
pared for transport to Babylon (Isa. 14. 8). The |
inscriptions relating to the buildings of Nebuchad-
nezzar may be counted by hundreds, and the boast
of the king is amply confirmed (Dan. 4. 30), for no
mound throughout Babylonia has yet been explored
that does not contain bricks of this king. The prin-
cipal inscriptions relating to the public works of
Nebuchadnezzar are the India House Inscription
(India Museum), Cylinders in British Museum.
Jews in Babylon.—To this period belong an
important series of commercial inscriptions (about
30,000 in number, B.M.) which relate to the trans-
actions of a firm of merchants and bankers named
Egibi. There is a strong probability that these
traders were Jews, for their name, also written Ikibi,
corresponds exactly to Jacob, and although the men
bore Babylonian names, probably changed (Dan. 1.7),
the women had mostly Jewish names.
Hach of these documents is carefully dated, and
most valuable for chronology. Numerous contracts
| are found dated in the reign of Evil-Merodach
(Amil-Marduk) (2 Kings 25. 27), who released Jehoi-
achin. To the same period belong inscriptions of
Neriglissar (Jer. 39. 13) (B.M.)—who styles himself
Rab Emga, ‘‘ the chief interpreter,’”’ the Rab-mag—
who was succeeded in B.C. 555 by Nabonidus, who
was apparently of a collateral branch of the family
of Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 5. 18).
The documents of this period are of very great
importance, as they confirm in a most detailed man-
ner the Scripture story :—Cylinder of Nabonidus
(B.M.), in which Nabonidus mentions Belshazzar
as his eldest son—‘‘ Belshazzar my firstborn son’’
(Dan. 5.1). The Annal Inscription (B.M.), which
shows that as early as B.C. 649, the seventh year of
his father’s reign, Belshazzar was at the head of the
army. Tithe Inscriptions of Belshazzar (B.M.),
proving that as early as B.c. 548 he had his own
household and retinue, and took an active part in
the affairs of state, being styled ‘‘the son of the
king.’? The Annal Tablet also mentions the advance
of Cyrus in B.c. 538, and the capture of Sippara or
Sepharvaim on Tammuz 14th, and of Babylon on
Tammuz 16th without fighting. The Calendar Tab-
let (B.M.) shews that Tammuz 16th was the great
feast of the Marriage of Istar, and would be cele-
brated as described by Daniel (5). Other important
inscriptions of this period are Cylinders of Nabonidus,
mentioning the overthrow of Astyages the Mede by
Cyrus in B.c. 550, and the capture of Ecbatana (Hzra
6. 2); here Cyrus is called the little servant of
Merodach (Isa. 46. 1). Belshazzar is never men-
tioned after the capture of Babylon by Cyrus, and
was doubtless slain. To this period belongs the
Cylinder of Cyrus (B.M.), mentioning his restoration
of the temples of Babylon (Isa. 46.1). But few in-
scriptions of Cyrus have been found, and none of his
successor Cambyses. Darius (B.c. 521) has left two
great monuments—his great inscription on the rock
of Behistun, in south-west Persia, and the so-called
Tomb of Darius at Naksh-i-Rustan. Of Ahasuerus,
or Xerxes, there are inscriptions at Vau, and remains
of his palaces at Persepolis and at Shushan (Neh.
1. 1), recently explored by M. Dieulafoy, and the
sculptures from which are in the Louvre. With the
fall of the Persian rule the monuments confirming
the Bible become scarce, and of little importance.

II. For the chronology of tHE HEBREW KINGDOMS
AFTER THE DISRUPTION there are several independent
lines of evidence, and as these, taken together, form
a continuous series to the Christian Hra, we are
enabled to substitute the computation B.C. for the
uncertain Anno Mundi.
1. The Books of Kings and Chronicles carefully
state the number of years in each reign, with cross-
references between the annals of Israel and of
Judah, shewing the mutual synchronisms. It is
true that these do not always tally one with another.
For example, by adding together the numbers of
the respective reigns from the Disruption to the fall
of the northern kingdom in the sixth year of Heze-
kiah, we reach a total for Judah of 259 years, for
Israel of only 242, thus :—
JupAH: Rehoboam 17, Abijah 8, Asa 41, Jehosha-
phat 25, Jehoram 8, Ahaziah 1, Athaliah 6,
Joash 40, Amaziah 29, Uzziah 52, Jotham 16,
Ahaz 16, Hezekiah 5—Torat 259.
IsRAEL : Jeroboam I. 22,.Nadab 2, Baasha 24,
Elah 2, Zimri, Tibi, Omri 12, Ahab 22, Ahaz-
tah 2, Jehoram 12, Jehu 28, Jehoahaz 17,
Jehoash 16, Jeroboam II. 41, Zachariah and
Shallum 1, Menahem 10, Pekahiah 2, Pekah 20,
Hoshea 9—Torat 242.
Various expedients have been employed to explain
the discrepancy, that most generally accepted being
the supposition of an interregnum after the reign
of Jeroboam II., and another after that of Pekah.
Some chronologers prefer to add the intercalated
years to the two reigns respectively. But neither
expedient has any direct support in Scripture.
Others, instead of lengthening the Israelitish period,
shorten that of Judah, by supposing, in two in-
stances at least, that, a son having been regent for
his father, the same years were assigned to both.
- We know that Jotham was regent for Uzziah, and
Jehoshaphat may have been associated in a similar
way with Asa. Other critics, again, suggest a series
of corruptions in the Hebrew text; and in some in-
stances there is certainly an error (ep. 2 Kings 1.17;
8.1; 8.16). It cannot, however, be said that these
methods of explanation are altogether satisfactory ;
and the problem must still be regarded as unsolved.
One tact that somewhat lightens the difficulty is
that in Jewish chronology parts of years are counted
as years complete. In an enumeration, therefore,
like the above, some years are entered twice oyer,

9. Soon after the Disruption, again, there begins
a series of synchronisms with the annals of other
countries, which throw much light upon the Hebrew
chronology. The histories of Egypt and Assyria,
and afterwards of Babylon and Persia, fix several
important dates; and, while elucidating, also con-
firm the Bible narrative. The first of these syn-
chronisms is furnished by Egypt, whose king
Shishak or Sesonchis invaded Judah in the fifth
year of king Rehoboam (1 Kings 14. 25). This Shi-
shak is shown by the monuments to have been the
founder of the 22nd Hgyptian dynasty; and his
accession is placed by Hgyptologers about B.c. 980.
On a wall of the great temple at Thebes, this
Egyptian king is depicted as wielding his terri-
ble club against the representatives of conquered
peoples, the Jews among the rest. From an in-
scription in the Silsilis quarries, this part of the
structure and its inscriptions are assigned to the
20th year of Shishak (Brugsch’s Egypt), or about
B.C. 960, so that the capture of Jerusalem must be
placed earlier than that date. The date, again, of
Zerah (Osorkon II., fourth king of the 22nd dynasty)
corresponds with that of Asa (2 Chron. 14. 9).
Turning now to Assyria, the ‘* Eponym Canon,”
discovered by Sir Henry Rawlinson in 1862, and
existing with more or less completeness in four
forms, contains a list of eponymes, or officers of the
kingdom, appointed yearly, from B.c. 909 to 640.
The correctness of this Canon was strikingly shown
by the verification of a solar eclipse, June 15, B.c.
763,* as well as by other coincidences ; and it is now
accepted by Assyriologists. The adjustment of this
Canon with the Bible chronology is undoubtedly
difficult, and the preceding paper by Professor Sayce,
“The Bible and the Monuments,’’ II. (6), gives
some dates which are irreconcilable with the num-
bers in Kings and Chronicles. Various suggestions
have been made to lighten this difficulty ; the most
important being that of the late George Smith, that
the “ Ahab of Zirhala,’? and the ‘‘ Jehu, son of
Omyri,’’ mentioned in the Assyrian inscriptions,
were not the kings of Israel, but others bearing
similar names.t If we are to identify them, the
whole scheme of Biblical chronology must be
altered, from Solomon downward, as the death of
Ahab, king of Israel, is assigned by the ordinary
computation to B.c. 897, whereas “Ahab of Zir-
hala’ is represented in the inscriptions as fighting
on the side of Syria against Shalmaneser, B.C. 853:
a difference of more than 40 yea “ The differences
between the two accounts,”’ s Dr. Edersheim,
“may depend on something as yet to us unknown,
and which, if known, might establish a harmony
between the two chronologies.’”? When we reach the
period of the destruction of Samaria by Sargon,f
and the downfall of the Israelitish monarchy (B.c.
722 or 721), the chronologies absolutely agree, and
this may be taken as an established date. The
chief remaining difficulty in the comparison of the
Assyrian with the Biblical records is, that the
former place the invasion of Judah by Sennacherib
in the days of Hezekiah, about B.c. 701, or 12 years

text has undergone some corruption, or the Assyrian
monuments have been misread. ‘The ‘‘ Canon of
Kings,’’ preserved in the works of the mathema-
tician Ptolemy (2nd century A.D.), starts from the
era of Nabonassar, B.C. 748, and gives the duration
of the reigns in the Assyrian, Persian, Macedonian,
and Roman empires down to his day. This also
furnishes invaluable help in determining the chro-
nology, fixing for instance the fall of Jerusalem at
B.c. 586. The Greek authorities concur in all the
principal dates, from the institution of the Olym-
piads (B.c. 776) downwards. On the whole, in
reviewing these several branches of information, it
may be said that while there is unquestioned
difficulty in fixing the details, there is a general
concurrence as to the order of events, strikingly
confirmatory of the Scripture record. In fact, from
the rise of the Babylonian empire onwards there is
practically no difference between chronologers. ‘The
dates of Cyrus, of Darius, of Xerxes (the Ahasuerus
of Esther), and of Artaxerxes Longimanus (Hzra 7),
are all clearly determined by Greek and other
authorities; and here the Old Testament history
ceases.
III. The chronology of the New TrsTAMENT is
associated with that of the early Roman empire,
and may be accurately determined, almost from
year to year. The ‘‘ Harmony of the Gospels”’ has
naturally enlisted much thought and research for its
elucidation; and, although certainty is unattain-
able, the labours of Greswell, Dr. Robinson, Tisch-
endorf (in his Synopsis Evangelica), with a host
of others, have brought out valuable, and in the
main concurrent, results. A main question is that
of the feast referred to in John 5. 1, which, with
the majority of critics, we take to be the Passover.
The dates in the Acts are chiefly determined by the
time of Herod Agrippa’s death, A.D. 44; with the
annals of the Roman emperors and procurators.
IV. It only remains to note the relation between
the two eras, A.M. and B.c. In the earlier part of
the Table it will be seen that the date of man’s
Creation is placed by Ussher at 4004 B.c.; by Hales
at 5411. The former reckoning makes exactly 4000
years between the Creation and the birth of Christ
(4.B.c.); the Christian Era, as adopted from Diony-
sius Exiguus, a Scythian by birth, who became @
monk in Rome in the 6th century, having been
placed, as it is now generally agreed, four years too
late. Partly, perhaps, the Jewish notion that the
world is to last through 6000 years of conflict and
1000 of peace, these millenniums corresponding
with the six days.and the sabbath of Creation, has
led to an arrangement so suspiciously symmetrical ;
the advent of the Saviour thus coinciding with the
dawn of the “fifth day’? of the world’s history.
The estimate of Dr. Hales rests on no such & priort
ground, but is taken simply from the comparison of
dates. Perhaps the question is one that cannot be
even approximately determined. If, however, we
take the LX X. reckoning (in the main, as adopted
by Dr. Hales) of 8763 years from the Creation to
the Exodus, while we find that the Exodus (480
years before the commencement of the Temple)
probably took place 1494 years B.c., we have 5257
years from the Creation to the Christian Bra; and
this is as near to a positive’ determination as we can
arrive. De Vignoles, in the preface to his Chrono-
logy of Sacred History, asserts that he collected
upwards of two hundred different calculations, the
shortest of which reckons only 3483 years between
the Creation and the beginning of the Christian
Hra, and the longest 6984.

to respect human life. He promises never again to destroy the earth by water

Noah blesses Shem and Japheth for filial conduct; but curses Canaan, fourth son

Abram and Lot return into Canaan, to Bethel. Their stock exceeding the pasturage
and water-supply (cp. Num. 22.3, 4), Abram magnanimously offers Lot the choice
of country; Lot selfishly and recklessly chooses the tropical and well-watered
valley of the infamous Pentapolis of the Plain of the Dead Sea, and settles in Sodom.
Abram receives the third Promise—an emphatic repetition and enlargement of the two
former. He encamps by the Oak (A. V. plain) of Mamre, near Kirjath-arba (Hebron).
Lot, captured in Sodom by Chedorlaomer, is rescued at Laish (Dan) by Abram and
his allies, Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. Melchisedek (? a faithful Canaanite patriarch,
ep. Job, Jethro, &e.) meets Abram (see Heb. 7. 1-4). Lot returns to Sodom.
Abram, lamenting his childlessness, receives the fourth Promise, viz. of a son whose
seed, numberless as the stars, shall inherit Canaan from the River of Egypt (Wady
el Arish) to the River Euphrates [fulfilled under Solomon]. Adopting as a sign or
pledge the customary covenant-sacrifice, God also reveals the intervening 400 years
of exile from Canaan and of bondage in Egypt, and the return of Abraham’s seed
from Egypt with great wealth into the Land of Promise in the fourth generation,
when the cup of Canaanite iniquity should be full.. Abram believes (see Rom. 4. 3)
—but Sarai gives to Abram Hagar her handmaid [whose child would reckon as
Sarai’s, ch. 80. 3, &e.]. Next year, Hagar bears Ishmael, whom even Abram regards
as the promised heir (ch. 17. 18).
In Abram’s 99th year God makes the “ everlasting covenant ” with Abram and his seed,
ordaining circumcision as its perpetual national sign. God confirms the Promises
and changes significantly the names of Abram and Sarai to Abraham and Sarah.
God promises Sarah a son, Isaac, to be heir to the new “everlasting covenant”;
and reveals Ishmael’s future. Abraham immediately adopts circumcision.
Abraham [still at Mamre] entertains three angels unawares, who repeat to him and
Sarah the Promise of a son. God reveals the doom of the five cities of the “ Plain
of Jordan” (ch. 18. 10); Abraham intercedes for Sodom (see Heb. 18. 2).
Two angels urge Lot to flee from Sodom. Lot is permitted to intercede for Bela,
i.e. Zoar, and escapes thither, but his wife perishes on the way. The other four
cities are destroyed. Lot and his two daughters leaving Zoar dwell in the moun-
tains (see Luke 17.29 ; 2 Pet. 2. 6-8; Jude 7), the future home of Moab and Ammon,
Lot’s descendants by his two daughters [and so kinsmen and future neighbours, but
generally foes, of Abraham’s seed ].

Moses, of Levi’s family (ch. 6. 16-21), the younger brother of Aaron and Miriam

Moses, aged 40, enquires into the oppression of his people. He slays an Egyptian
and takes refuge in Midian with Reuel the patriarchal priest, marrying his daughter
Zipporah, who bears a son Gershom (Acts 7. 23-29; Heb. 11. 27).
The Hebrew Nation—“ The LORD, the God of the Hebrews”
(Jehovah).—The Exodus.
After nearly 40 years, God responds to the prayers of the Israelites.
God reveals Himself to Moses in Mount Horeb from a burning bush as the God
revealed to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, now purposing to deliver His people and
to transplant them into Canaan [1913]. God commissions Moses to conduct the
Exodus, promising, as a pledge or earnest, that Israel shall leaye Egypt and
worship Him in that range. God bids Moses deliver this message to the assembled
elders, ¢.e. chiefs, of Israel, further encouraging him with a fuller revelation of
Himself as JEHOVAH=I AM=the Eternal Self-existent, A. V. the Lorp (see Var.
notes, R. V. marg.), and with signs confirmatory of his mission—to be repeated before
Pharaoh. Moses hesitates, and Aaron is assigned to be his spokesman (see Acts 7. 30-35).
Moses returns to Egypt; Gershom is circumcised, and Aaron meets Moses in Horeb.
The elders joyfully accept God’s message ; but when Pharaoh—scorning the God of
the Hebrews and His demand that His people should go three days’ journey out of
Egypt (i.e. to Mount Horeb) to sacrifice to Him—adds to their burdens, the elders
reproach Moses, and he God. Then God further reveals Himself to Moses as Israel’s
future Covenant-God, and promises to manifest His Godhead (1) by delivering His
people amid wonders discrediting the gods of Egypt, and (2) by bringing Israel
into Canaan according to His promise. The disheartened elders disbelieve. God
sends Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh to repeat the demand, and commissions them
(aged 80 and 83) to conduct the Exodus.
Moses. and Aaron revisit Pharaoh ; but the Egyptian magicians imitate their credential
miracles, and Pharaoh is obdurate. Though shaken by each of 9 progressive
plagues upon Egypt and its people—viz. (1) the Nile turned into blood, (2) Frogs,
(3) Lice, or Gnats (the magicians’ imitations cease), (4) Flies, (5) Murrain, (6) Boils
(the magicians suffer also and retire), (7) Hail, (8) Locusts; (9) Darkness, and by
the threatened Death of the firstborn—Pharaoh refuses to let Israel go.
The Passover is instituted for the 14th of Abib, henceforward the first month
(May 4), to commemorate the sparing of Israel’s firstborn and the Deliverance from
Egypt (see Heb. 11. 28).—On the 15th at midnight (plague 10) all the firstborn of
the Egyptians and their cattle die.

and covers their night march through the Red Sea, miraculously divided. On the
Arabian shore, the nation gives thanks for its deliverance from Egypt and Pharaoh’s
pursuit (see Ps. 106. 11, 12; Heb. 11. 29).
The Hebrews march southward along the shore of the Red Sea (Gulf of Suez)

Sinai, on the 15th of the second month after the Exodus began.

Aaron... God provides quails, and a supply of manna, daily (the Sabbath excepted),

The Covenant Nation._The Law given at Mount Sinai.
In the third month, Israel encamps “before the Mount” in the wilderness of Sinai.
God offers through Moses a Covenant (conditioned on obedience), and on the third

Moses, as intermediary between the terrified people and God, receives further ordi-
nances for the regulation of civil life and elementary religious observances called

of the New Covenant. (See Heb. 9. 17-20.) Moses, Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and
70 elders, are permitted to see God’s glory and to hold the Covenant feast (“ eat and
drink”) in the mountain.
| Moses summoned up the mountain receives the Tables of Stone, the Law, and other

and the people (A.V. tabernacle of the congregation) and its furniture; (2) the

The people’s faith failing during the withdrawal of the Shechinah and of Moses
into: Mount Sinai, the Covenant is forfeited by (Ps. 106, 20) a heathenish worship

God reveals to Moses this relapse and His purpose to destroy Israel, and make of
Moses’ seed another Covenant-nation ; but Moses’ intercession is accepted, and he
returns (with Joshua). Seeing the festival afar, Moses in righteous indignation drops

faithful to execute the faithless. The tribe of Levi responding slays 3,000 men,
thus earning the privilege of the Holy Tribe to be accepted in lieu of the dedicated
firstborn. Moses returns into the Mount, and God accepts his intercession for the
people, but sends plagues, and announces that His Angel and not He Himself would
henceforward be their guide. But the people’s mourning is accepted, and, at Moses’
intercession (in the Mount), God promises to resume His personal leadership; and
permits Moses (as visible evidence) to see His glory.
God summons Moses again intg the mountain with two new Tables of Stone. At
Moses’ intercession, God renews the broken Covenant between Himself and Israel,
and promises to displace the Canaanites if Israel make no terms with them and
generally will be faithful. During this second absence of 40 days, Moses is in-

return, a dazzling reflection of God’s glory irradiates his face, as on subsequent
interviews with God in the Tent of Meeting (see 2 Cor. 3. 13-16).
Moses invites contributions of materials and labour towards a Tent or Tabernacle of

wanderings. On the 14th of Abib, the Passover is kept.

A prophet rebukes Israel. An angel inspires Gideon, a Manassite, to deliver Israel
and, after destroying his father’s sanctuary to Baal and Asherah (A. V. “the grove”)

Midian, capturing the kings Zebah and Zalmunna beyond Jordan, while Ephraim
captures the princes Oreb and Zeeb at the fords (Isa. 9.4 and 10. 26; Ps. 88. 11, 12).
Judgeship of Gideon 40 years. Gideon refuses an hereditary sovereignty; but, to
promote the service of Jehovah, mistakenly (cp. Micah) sets up a sanctuary and an
oracle (“ephod”’) in Ophrah.
After Gideon’s death, Baal-worship revives in connexion with a local confederacy at
Shechem (Baal-berith, 7.e. Baal of the League). Abimelech, Gideon’s youngest son
by a Canaanite concubine, murders Gideon’s 70.sons, Jotham alone escaping, and is
elected by the Hivite and Israelite population chief of the confederacy at Joshua’s
pillar in Shechem. Three years later, in a counter-revolution, Abimelech is slain
ignominiously when assaulting Thebez.
Judgeship of Zola of Issachar in Ephraim 28 years.
Death of Tola. Judgeship of Jair of Gilead 22 years.
General apostacy of Israel (Ps. 78. 56-59). Eli high priest and judge. Samuel born.
Eli’s sons, in his old age, by cupidity and immorality profane and discredit the
Tabernacle service at Shiloh. A prophet announces the doom of Eli’s family, the
forfeiture of the high priesthood, and the death of Hophni and Phinehas on one day.

20 years. The Philistines, after seven months of plagues, send back the Ark to

Death of Jephthah. Judgeship of Jbzan seven years, and of Elon 10 years—both of

Judgeship of Abdon of Ephraim eight years. Betrayal and death of Samson. On
Israel’s repentance the prophet Samuel conducts a national reformation at Mizpeh,
and repulsing the Philistine invasion at Ebenezer, frees Dan. The Philistine sub-
jection ends. Judgeship of Samuel; his yearly circuits to Bethel, Gilgal, and
Mizpeh ; his home, justice-seat, and sanctuary at Ramah.
The Monarchy.—Saul and David.—The Promise to David [to be fulfilled
spiritually. See Isa. 55. 8-5, cp. Ps, 18. 48-45; Jer. 23. 5, 6, cp. 88. 14-18;
Isa. 9. 7, cp. Luke 1. 88; Acts 2. 29, 30].
Corrupt administration by Samuel’s sons, his deputies in Beer-sheba, in his old age.
Relapse of Israel and its renewed oppression by the Philistines. The people demand
a king to administer justice and lead them in war, especially against the Philistines
and a threatened invasion by Ammon, Samuel’s protests are finally overruled ; and
Saul, a Benjamite, is indicated by God, and being anointed privately by Samuel, is
chosen king by the sacred lot in a national assembly at Mizpeh (ep. Josh. 7. 14, &e.).
Samuel declares and records the new constitution. Saul relieves Jabesh-gilead,
surprising the Ammonites, and the constitution is solemnly ratified at Gilgal.
Samuel. formally resigns his civil judgeship.
Saul forms a small standing army, the Philistines having disarmed the Hebrews.
Jonathan begins a war of independence. Saul’s three characteristic failures—(1) At
Gilgal, at the outset of the war, the king offers sacrifice instead of awaiting the
prophet’s arrival; Samuel pronounces Saul’s rejection—(2) Saul’s rash curse mars
Jonathan’s victory and makes Israel to sin—(3) Saul neglects to fully execute God’s
commission against Amalek; Samuel repeats the sentence of rejection, and ceases to
visit Saul.

Judah also revives, Joash’s successors, Amaziah, Uzziah, and Jotham being, like him,
generally faithful, although the “high places” remain. But general demoralisation
underlies the material prosperity.
Amaziah re-conquers Edom [889] unaided, and capturing Selah [Petra?] calls it
Joktheel. Puffed up by this success, he silences a prophet’s rebuke of his adoption of
Edom’s idols, and persists in provoking war with Israel. Jehoash, invading Judah,
captures Amaziah at Beth-shemesh, breaks down 400 cubits of the north wall of
Jerusalem, takes all the sacred and other treasures [839], and returns to Samaria with
hostages. Amaziah outlives his conqueror 15 years [passed over in silence].
JEROBOAM II. upholds the worship of the Calves, yet is permitted to realise Jonah’s
prophecy and deliver Transjordanic Israel [884] from Syria to its original frontiers
(Num. 34. 12); he also re-conquers [895] Moab (Amos 6. 14), and subdues Damascus
[now weakened by wars with Rimmon-nirari, grandson of Shalmaneser 1H Esdle
Amaziah flees from conspirators, who kill him at Lachish. The people make his son
UZZIAH (Azariah, Kin.) king, aged 16. Faithful whilst Zechariah lived, he is
“marvellously helped.” He rebuilds Elath (lost with Edom, 889), and he extends
Judah to its frontiers under Solomon (i.e. as far as Egypt) by conquest of the Philis-
tines, Arabians, and Mehunims (Meunim, 7.¢. Maonites of Mount Seir, 887, 912), and
by Ammon’s submission [758], developing the pastoral and agricultural districts of
the west, south, and east, thus subjected. He re-organises and equips the army, and
repairs the walls of Jerusalem [826], adding towers and novel artillery.
In Jeroboam II.’s reign and onward, Amos and Hosea announce the Ten Tribes’
forfeiture of God’s respite by abusing their recovered prosperity to increase their
religious, moral, and social corruption. They foretell the destruction of Jehu’s
dynasty [772] and of Israel’s strength (“bow”), and the extinction of the nation
(with her calf-worship, &c.) by captivity into Assyria; bidding Judah be warned.
Amos is denounced to Jeroboam and treated as a false prophet by Amaziah, the
Israelite high priest, at Beth-el; he foretells Amaziah’s dishonour and captivity.
Jeroboam II. dies. [An anarchical interregnum of 11} years occurs (Ussher) ].
ZACHARIAH, son of Jeroboam II. and fifth of Jehu’s dynasty, succeeds, and God’s
promise is fulfilled. Zachariah follows the example of his predecessors, and is mur-
dered six months later by SHALLUM; Jehu’s dynasty thus ending violently as
foretold. Shallum having reigned a month is slain by MENAHEM, who buys his
confirmation in the kingdom of Put, ¢.e. Tiglath-pileser Il. [the first (mentioned )
Assyrian invader of Israel], for 1000 talents of silver. ‘
Uzziah, proud of his wealth and power (Isa. 2. 7-16), persists in usurping the priest’s
office, and becomes leprous in the Holy Place. Jotham his son is made regent.
PEKAHIAH succeeds his father Menahem. PEKAH, a general of Pekahiah, murders
and succeeds him. [Pekah seems to have rebelled against Tiglath-pileser. ]
Uzziah dies. God in glory reveals to Jsaiah the captivity of Judah, but the inde-
structibility of “the holy seed.” Judah prospers for Jotham’s faithfulness, but
formalism and idolatries, injustice and erimes, luxury and wantonness increase,
and Isaiah and Micah urge her to avert God’s wrath by repentance. JOTHAM
completes the defences of Judah and Jerusalem, strengthening Ophel and the upper,
i.e. northern, gate of the Temple. He puts down a revolt of Ammon [810], exacting
a special tribute of silver and corn. ‘Toward the end of the reign, Rezin king of
Syria and Pekah combine to put down the Davidie dynasty in Judah.
AHAZ, Jotham’s son, aged 20, reigns 16 years. Weak and foolish (Isa. 3. 12), he
re-introduces [840] the Israelite Baalism and Ammonite worship of Moloch (1 Kin.
11. 7). He sacrifices a son (Chr. children) to Moloch (see Mic. 6. 7), and worships
at the “high places.” Rezin and Pekah invade Judah to set the “son of 'Tabeal ” on
David’s throne. After two crushing victories, the allies carry thousands captive—
Rezin to Damascus and Pekah to Samaria (where Oded causes their restoration)—
and besiege Jerusalem.
Isaiah, sent to encourage Ahaz, predicts their failure, and Syria’s captivity [732*] and
Israel’s obliteration by Assyria—Judah also to be overrun and desolated, except Jeru-
salem [713]. He gives—Ahaz refusing to choose—a sign confirmatory of God’s aid,
viz. the birth of a child, the Messianic King, type of virgin-born IMMANUEL (see
Mie. 5. 2,8). Rezin deprives Judah finally of Klath [810]; and the Edomites and
Philistines invade Judah. Ahaz, surrounded by foes, hires Assyrian aid, volunteering
vassalage, and seeks help of the Syrian gods. TicuaTu-pineser captures Damascus,
and removes the Syrians to Kir, and Naphtali and Israel east of Jordan with Gentile
Galilee (Heb. the district, ¢.¢. the border, Isa. 9. i) to Assyria. Ahaz, through the
high priest Urijah, replaces Solomon’s brazen altar by a copy of one at Damascus.

ZEDEKIAH. Jeremiah opposes a general restlessness, fostered by false prophets in
Chaldza and Judah, who predict the Chaldean Empire’s speedy fall, and the restora-
tion of Jehoiachin, the exiles, and the vessels of the Temple. Zedekiah vacillates,
but following the national party brings ruin on himself and on the relics of Judah,
as foretold (Jer. 27. 17 & 38. 17-23). Jeremiah, in a letter (by Zedekiah’s embassy),
bids the exiles settle down, promising the restoration of a converted remnant at the

writes urging his punishment as a false prophet. In Zedekiah’s third or fourth year,
embassies from his neighbours concert a rebellion; Jeremiah replies (‘yokes ”),
declaring Nebuchadnezzar’s irresistibility ; the death of Hananiah as predicted by
Jeremiah discredits his own counter-predictions. Zedekiah visits Babylon in his
fourth year, and Jeremiah sends, by Seraiah, his prophecies of Babylon’s fall, the
preliminary of the Restoration (by Cyrus, Isa. 44. 28; 2 Chron. 36. 20-23).

lon ;—and in the seventh, Nebuchadnezzar’s advance; foretelling the overthrow of
David’s throne “ wntil he come whose right it is.”
Zedekiah, in the eighth year, breaking his oath, allies himself with Egypt [Horura]
and rebels. The Chaldeans advance; Judah’s late allies, especially Philistia, and
Edom (denounced by Obvadiah), join them. In the ninth year, only Lachish,
Azekah, and Jerusalem hold out; Zedekiah asks God’s aid through Jeremiah, but is
bidden to submit. In the 10th month, Jerusalem is invested ; a fact at once revealed
to Ezekiel (24). On the approach of an Egyptian army, the Chaldeans raise the
siege: the Hebrew freedmen are re-enslaved, and Jeremiah, again invoked, denounces
this breach of faith and predicts the return and success of the Chaldeans; he is
imprisoned as a traitor. Zedekiah consults him secretly, and transfers him to the
quarters of the royal guard (court of prison), where, in the 10th year, amid the
horrors of a protracted blockade, he foretells the Restoration (redeeming Hanameel’s
field as a sign), and the fulfilment of all God’s Promises in a sprout from Dayid’s
stem when apparently dead, Jenovan our Ricurrousness. Jeremiah collects in a

starve in Malchiah’s dungeon ; Ebedmelech, an Ethiopian, rescues him; Zedckiah
guarantees his life, but fears to adopt his urgent counsel to save Jerusalem by sur-
render. Jeremtah remains in the guard house till released by the Chaldeans.

escapes, but is captured (Ezek. 12.12) near Jericho, and taken with his sons to
Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, where he is tried and blinded. He dies in prison at
Babylon (fulfilling Ezek. 12. 18).

the residue of the sacred vessels. He assigns lands to a remnant; Jeremiah choosing
to remain is consigned to Gedaliah the governor. Jeremiah writes Lamentations.
Refugees gather round Gedaliah, but Ishmael of the blood-royal murders him (in the
7th month). The remnant of Judah fearing Nebuchadnezzar’s vengeance consult
God through Jeremiah ; bidden to remain, they deny Jeremiah’s inspiration, and flee
into Egypt, taking him and Baruch by force. In Taphanes, and after their disper-
sion, Jeremiah warns them that, unless they abandon idolatry, a consuming punishment
shall overtake them when Nebuchadnezzar conquers Egypt (probably fulfilled in
568 B.c., of. Ezek. 29. 17-20); as a pledge, he predicts Hopura’s deposition.

EBUCHADNEZZAR, though warned by the dream of the tree, interpreted by
Daniel, is puffed up by his victories over Egypt, Judah, and Western Asia, and by
the magnificence of his buildings at Babylon, and is smitten with madness (/ycanthropy).
After seven years (‘times’) spent almost as a beast of the field, his understanding
returns, and he humbly acknowledges God’s power and goodness; and is confirmed in
his kingdom. A few years later he dies, having reigned about 43 years.
Evil-merodach his son succeeds in the 87th year of Jehoiachin’s captivity, and in his
first year releases and pays the highest honour to this last earthly king of Dayid’s
line.
([Evil-merodach reigns two years, and after Neriglissar’s usurpation, &c., the line of
Nebuchadnezzar is restored in Nabonadius (or Nabonedus), the last king of Babylon,
with whom his son Belshazzar is latterly associated as king. He commands in
3abylon while Nabonedus takes the field against Cyrus.] In the first year of Bel-
shazzar’s reign in Babylon, Daniel has the vision signifying the four universal
empires, and of God (‘‘the Ancient of Days”) judging the fourth, and delivering
all power and sovereignty to the “ people of the saints of the Most High.”
Belshazzar makes in his palace, during the siege of Babylon, a great feast to 1,000
nobles, and sends for and uses the vessels of the Temple [599, 588], to the glory of
his idols and dishonour of the true God. A hand appears writing on the wall.
At the queen’s (queen-mother’s ?) suggestion, Daniel, the former chief of the wise
men (Dan. 2. 48), is summoned, and reads and interprets the writing: Mene, 7.e.
numbered; Tekel, t.c. weighed; Upharsin, i.e. and they are dividing! (with a play
on the word Persians): and is proclaimed the third in the kingdom. The same
night Belshazzar is slain and Babylon is taken by Cyrus; the empire passing, as
foretold, to the Persians and Medes.
In Belshazzar’s third year [probably soon after Babylon’s capture], Daniel at Shushan
(Susa), the Persian capital, has the vision of the ram and he-goat; the angel Gabriel
explains the former part, of the destruction of the Persian Empire by Alexander
the Great and his four successors;—the latter is usually interpreted of the future
Greek king of Syria, Antiochus Epiphanes, the persecutor of the restored Jews and
their religion [170-167].
Darius the Mede, aged about 62, “ took the kingdom.” [The most probable opinion is
that Cyrus, while completing his conquests, made Astyages, the king of Media de-
posed by him, civil governor of the Perso-Median Empire, with full regal power.]
The Perso-Median nobles [as if offended at their supersession by a Chaldwan Jew],
intrigue to ruin Daniel through his piety, finding his management of affairs
unimpeachable. They move the king to decree, that for 30 days no petition be made
to god or man, but to himself only, on pain of death by the lions. Daniel, by his
customary prayers, places himself in the power of his enemies, but is miraculously
delivered. Darius decrees that all his subjects shall acknowledge the God of Daniel.
Towards the end of the first year of Darius the Mede, reckoned from the fall of the
Babylonish Empire, the 70th year of the Captivity begins, the last,as Daniel now
“ understood by the books” (Var., so R.V.), ¢.e. by the writings of Jeremiah and the
prophets (cf. Ezra 1. 1; in Isa. 40—66 the exiles are encouraged to confidently
expect deliverance: Cyrus, pursuing his conquests, is to enter Babylon and release
the Jews, chs. 40. 1-11 & 41. 1-3 & 43. 14-20 & 44. 2446. 4, 18, &c.].—-Danie/
prays fervently for the promised restoration of all Israel and Jerusalem, and Gabriel
announces God’s command to that effect, and the prophecy of the 70 weeks.
The first (imperial) year of Cyrus (he reigned over the Persians 29 years) begins with
Darius’ death—Darius’ two years being included in the nine assigned to Cyrus in the
Babylonian annals. Cyrus now issues his wonderful edict (cp. Isa. 44. 28 with
Ezra 6. 8) for the rebuilding of the Temple at Jerusalem, probably under Daniel’s
influence (Dan. 1. 21, marg.). He permits ali the people of Jehovah to return, with
their property, and any offerings of well-affected neighbours for themselves or the
Temple.
Cyrus also restores to Zerubbabel (Sheshbazzar, successor to Jehoiachin through
Shealtiel), as the recognised lineal head of the House of David, the 5,409 (2,499, text)
vessels of the Temple, and grants cedars from Lebanon and money for the building.

1 Chron. 3 | It is, however, clear that during this period the Jewish nation made marked progress
17-20 towards the great change which distinguishes the nation of the Old Testament from
Lu. 3 23-31| that of the New. (1) The house of David lost its restored pre-eminence under
Zerubbabel, and sank or was sinking into obscurity; and the sacerdotal tribe of
Levi took the place of the royal tribe of Judah. (2) The study of the Law and
Prophets, which had been collected and revised by Ezra, and the supplanting of
the ancient Hebrew, “their own language” (see Prologue 2 to Kcclesiasticus), by
the current dialect and alphabet of Syria (Aramaic or Chaldee), called into
existence interpreters, teachers, and copyists of Scripture, and thus laid the
foundation of the later Rabbinical schools and political-religious sects. And (3) the
influence of the high priests and of the tribe of Levi, increased by the guardianship
and knowledge of the Law, was becoming at once enlarged and corrupted by the
Jos. Ant. accession of temporal power. The single historical fact of the period, viz. the
sified murder of his brother Joshua by the high priest JonaTHan, on suspicion of aiming
at the high priesthood by Persian influence, indicates that Judah was practically
ruled by the high priest, and that the civil power of the Sacred office had already
made it an object of political ambition; and foreshadows the jealousies and crimes
of the priestly families, which, taking the place of similar quarrels in ruling
families elsewhere, hereafter gradually undermined the fabrie of Jewish inde-
pendence which was erected by the faith, genius, and heroic devotion of the
Aaronic family of the Hasmonzans, otherwise called the Maccabees.
The religious revival, which is the main feature of the post-Captivity Period, is
traced in the Book of Tobit (written probably during this century), which shews
the great reverence in which the Mosaic Law was already held. Indeed, the nation,
prompted by Ezra the priest the learned Scribe, the second founder of the Jewish
Commonwealth, and influenced especially by the two Books of Chronicles, had
cp. John 21| formed itself into a hierarchy on the basis of the Law (and the Service of the
48 Temple). The Davidiec monarchy being abolished, and prophecy suspended, the
Acts 6 13 | Law alone survived to be “a distinctive pledge of nationality, and a sure guide
to truth.” The knowledge of the Law had been disseminated and its observance
inculeated—after the example of Ezra (Neh. 8. 1-8, 13, 18)—by the Services of
the Synagogue, in which the Pentateuch was read through and interpreted in
public once a year, a section on each Sabbath-day, and was also expounded in
sermons (cp. Acts 15. 21; Luke 4, 16-32; Acts 13. 14-44); for a synagogue had
been established in every Jewish community of any size. And the growth of a
zeal for the Law is shown by the distinction drawn, at an early date, between
the Zaddiktm or Righteous, ze. the observers of the written Law, and the
Chasidim [167] or Pious, who voluntarily superadded rigorous observances handed
down by tradition—parties which foreshadowed those of the Sadducees and Phari-
sees. Thus moulded, the Jewish character must have soon assumed the austere exclu-
siveness, social and religious, which, being the logical outcome of a jealous adherence
to the letter of the Mosaic covenant, separated the Jewish nationality—whether in
Judah or dispersed in Babylonia and Media—from all others [see B.c. 226].

remove them into Judea. Meanwhile, Judas’ captains in Judea disobeying orders
take the offensive, and are defeated by Gorgias, governor of Idumza and Philistia,
before Jamnia. But Judas dismantles Hebron, the capital, and the fortresses of
Idumeea—and overruns Philistia to Azotus (Ashdod), abolishing idolatry.
Antiochus Epiphanes, foiled in his attempt to plunder the Temple of Nanza, é.e.
the Persian Venus, in Elymais, a district of Susiana [166], and hearing of the
successes of Judas and his consequent military strength and wealth, hastens home-
wards to make Jerusalem “ the Jews’ burying place”; but is stricken with a

(2 Mac.) with loathsome disease (eaten of worms, ep. Hdt., 4. 205; Acts 12. 23),
which he recognises as a judgment for his treatment of the Jews and their Temple.
After making his foster-brother Philip regent during his son’s minority, he dies on
his way to Babylon at Tab, in Persia, B.c. 164-3. But Lysias on hearing of his
death proclaims Antiocuus V. (Kupator), aged nine [or twelve], king, and
assumes the regency.
Judas besieges vigorously the Syrian garrison of Jerusalem [165] in the citadel :
warned of its danger, Lysias invades Judea from Idumea with 120,000 men
(including Greek mercenaries) and elephants bearing wooden towers, and lays
siege to Bethsura ; Judas attempts its relief. In the battle of Beth-Zacharias,
Eleazar the Maccabee kills the largest elephant, supposing it to be the king’s, and
is crushed by it; but Judas is defeated, and retreats to Jerusalem, followed by
Lysias. It being a Sabbatical year, victuals fail; Bethsura capitulates, and the
army of Judas melts away: indeed, the magazines of the garrison of the Temple
were almost exhausted, when Lysias, who was besieging it, hearing that Philip had
assumed the regency at Antioch, induces the young king and the princes to make
peace with Judas, and to regrant to the Jews all their ancient privileges, as they
had enjoyed them before the Edict of Antiochus Epiphanes. Thus the Maccabean
revolt is crowned with success just when it seemed about to be crushed. The
‘Romans confirm the treaty and Antiochus Eupator in the kingdom. But the
Syrians dismantle the fortifications of the Temple, on seeing their strength, before
departing, and so far break the treaty.
Lysias captures Antioch, and Philip (2 Mac. 9. 29) flees into Egypt.

attended him into Judea, hoping to be restored to office—and makes ALCIMUS,

to be (2 Mae. 14. 7), but was not, of the high-priestly lineage (Josephus); the
succession, indeed, ended with Onias, son of Onias III., who, being thus deprived
of his birthright, retires into Egypt. Among the numerous Egyptian Jews, Onias
would revive the pure worship that had been paganised by the Hellenizing party
at home during the nsurpations of the high priesthood by Jason and Menelaus and.
“the mingling” ; [see B.c. 187; cp. 158}.
The Roman commissioners (/egat?) in Syria (1) oblige Antiochus V. to reduce his fleet
and elephants to the amount stipulated after the battle of Magnesia in B.c. 189.
(1) The influence of Rome in the East.—This was enormous, while as yet Reme possessed not a rood of ground in
Asia [7.e. before B,C. 133]. Continual embassies were passing between the Senate and the kings and potentates of
Asia Minor, Syria, and
Egypt, through which Rome, te a great extent, directed the course of events in the East as
she thought best for her own interests, None of the states could afford to quarrel with the great power of the West;
the moment any community obtained her protection, or any prince her alliance, the respect of all the neighbouring
states and princes was
at once secured.—Prof. Rawlinson.

Judea to Syria. Ptolemy assassinates Simon and his sons Judas and Mattathias,
but fails to seize Jerusalem and the Temple (now its citadel), and Gazara, and to
kill Simon’s surviving son, John (Hyrcanus), who occupies Jerusalem and succeeds
his father [143; 141]. Ptolemy sends to Antiochus VII. for an ‘army, offering,
in return, to surrender Judea to him; but is obliged to take refuge with Zeno, the
prince of Philadelphia (Rabbath Ammon), see B.c. 101.
Antiochus VII. overruns Judea, and JOHN HYRCANUS, driven into Jerusalem, is
obliged to surrender the city nine months after Simon’s murder ; he retains Joppa,
Gazara, and a few other Maccabean acquisitions outside Judea proper, but only
as a tributary of Syria, and buys off the restoration of the Syrian citadel and
garrison in Jerusalem. The advisers of Antiochus urge him to extirpate the
Jewish nation, but in vain; and for his moderation in victory and toleration of
the Jews’ religion he acquires the title of Euszpus, i.e. the Pious. But he destroys
the fortifications of Jerusalem.
The Romans acquire their first province in Asia (i.e. the western and the greater
part of Asia Minor), henceforward called “the Proper Asia” (see B.c. 75 & 62), by
bequest from Attalus, king of Pergamus; they occupy it after four years of war.
Hyreanus, as the ally of Antiochus VIL., aids him in his war against the Parthians
for the release of Demetrius [141]; Antiochus re-conquers Babylonia and Media;
whereupon the other provinces east of Euphrates revolt to Syria, Phraates retaining
the original kingdom of Parthia only. Hyreanus returns home.
Demetrius is released and sent into Syria by Phraates; but the Parthians destroy
Antiochus VII. and his army soon afterwards. The consequent disturbances in
Syria enable Hyrcanus to extend his dominions and to throw off finally the yoke
of Syria. He amasses wealth, and hires mercenary troops and fortifies the palace
Baris in Jerusalem [see B.c. 141, the Antonia of Herod, Jos. Ant. xviii. 4. 3].
Hyreanus begins the conquest of the Transjordanic districts [94] by taking Medaba
in N. Moab, (1) destroys Samaritan Stchem and the temple of Mount Gerizim
[see B.c. 883, note], and conquering the Jdwmeans he merges them by compulsory
proselytism in the Jewish nation.
Hyreanus renews the treaty with the Romans [141], and they abrogate his treaty
with Antiochus [135]; thus Judea regains its independence, as under Simon.
Henceforward, the Jews maintain their independence in alliance with Rome, and
prosper—lgypt and Syria being enfeebled by wars of succession or by the luxury
and folly of their kings, and the Parthian Empire being yet undeveloped.
The two half-brothers, Antiochus Grypus and Antiochus Cyzicenus, divide the
kingdom of Syria, the latter becoming king of Damascus (Cele“Syria and
Phenicia). The Jewish prince, profiting by their weakness, attacks Samaria [832],
and his sons Aristobulus and Antigonus capture the city, notwithstanding the

800 of his captives; 8,000 of his opponents go into exile, and peace ensues,

obscure. Babylonian Rabbi of Aaronic family, ANANEL, passing over Mariamne’s
brother Aristobulus, the sole male heir of the Hasmoneans, as being under age.
But Mariamne’s importunity and the intrigues of her mother, Alexandra, the
daughter of Hyrcanus II., and widow of Alexander son of Aristobulus II., with
Antony and Cleopatra, cause Herod to depose Ananel and appoint Aristobulus,
aged 16-17, The enthusiastie welcome of ARisropunus III. by the Jews arouses
Herod's jealousy, and he causes the murder of the young high-priest (while
bathing), whereupon Alexandra appeals through’ Cleopatra to Antony, who
summons Herod to Laodicea; but Herod unexpectedly wins over his judge,
though Cleopatra pressed for Herod’s life and kingdom, as part of her scheme
for recovering the Syrian territories of the first Ptolemies. Ananel resumes the

But Herod's mother, the Arabian Cypros, and his sister Salome, whom the haughty
Mariamne had alienated by taunting them with their low birth, disclose to the
king the designs of Alexandra upon the ¢rown during his absence, and also make
him suspect the fidelity of his beautiful wife. Thus began the fatal division of
Herod’s family into Herodian and Hasmonzan factions. [29.]
But otherwise the Jewish kingdom reaches a climax of prosperity under Herod,
although his subjects, and especially the Rabbinical Schools of the Pharisees, hated
him for his connexion with the Gentiles (Rome) and his claim to be the successor
of David and of the Maccabees. In the Roman civil war, the king would have
fought for Antony, but he, at Cleopatra’s instigation, sends Herod to inyade the
kingdom of Arabia in her interest, to enforce her right of tribute over part of it,
which he does after some reverses, with eventual success. Octavianus Cesar defeats
Antony and Cleopatra at Actiwm [31]; they take refuge in Egypt.
Herod puts Hyrcanus II. (aged 80) to death, and, finding Antony deaf to his advice,
he meets Octavianus at Rhodes, and wins his friendship; for the victorious Cesar
was anxious to deprive Antony of Herod’s aid. Cwzsar and the Senate confirm
Herod in his kingdom, and Herod assists the former to invade Egypt. Mariamne,
on Herod’s return, betrays her alienation from him, and. the king’s mother and
sister again stimulate his anger and suspicions.
The Roman civil wars are terminated by Cvsar's conquest of Egypt, and by the
deaths of Antony and ‘Cleopatra; Egypt is then made a Roman Province, and the
Macedonian kingdom of the Ptolemies in Egypt ends, having lasted about 290 years.
Hearing of Cesar’s success, and of Antony’s death, in Egypt, Herod hastens to meet
(at Ptolemais) the victor of the world, accompanies him to Antioch, and becomes one
of his chief friends—for Rome needed his alliance against the disaffected in Egypt,
Arabia, and Syria, ever ready to conspire with the Parthians (the Arabian desert
and the river Huphrates being the frontiers most open to attack), and his experience
in dealing with Orientals, the Kast having been since the days of Pompey a blot on
Roman diplomacy. Czxsar restores to Herod the balsam-region of Jericho (given by
Antony to Cleopatra B.c. 35-34, and farmed of her by Herod), and adds to his
kingdom some of the chief independent cities established and fortified by Pompey
and Gabinius, 7.c. Gadara, and Hippos (with the adjoining parts of Decapolis), and
Samaria inland, and Gaza, Anthedon, Joppa, and Strato’s Tower on the coast
(another gift of Antony’s to Cleopatra). Herod’s kingdom thus includes all Idumea,

I,—The Kenites.
We read of ‘‘ Kenites”’ among the inhabitants of
Canaan in the days of Abraham (Gen. 15.19). The
name (like our Smith) seems originally to have de-
noted a worker in metals (Gesenius, Thesaurus, sub
voce), and may have arisen from some specialty of
the tribe in work or warfare. ‘They were evidently
a nomad race, and we next meet with them in the
land of Midian, the Sinaitie peninsula; Jethro, the
Midianite priest, whose daughter Moses espoused
(Exod. 8. 1), being also a Kenite (Judg. 1. 16).
For a time, then, the Kenites had cast in their lot
with the descendants of Keturah ; but they after-
wards followed the destinies-of Israel, influenced no
doubt by their connection with the great lawgiver.
Balaam in his prophecy refers to the Kenite tents as
on the outskirts of the Israelite camp (Num. 24. 21).
Jethro himself declined to follow his son-in-law to
Canaan, but his son Hobab seems, after some hesi-
tation, to have remained with Moses (Hxod. 18. 27;
| gipsy race.
Num. 10. 29, 82); and _ the clan eventually occupied
‘“the wilderness”’ in the south of Judah, dwelling
in tents, although in close and recognised alliance
with the Israelite community—in fact a kind of
As circumstances might dictate, they
would pass from spot to spot; and we meet with a
Kenite settlement in the uplands of Naphtali, to the
north, mentioned in the history on account of Jael’s
exploit (Judg. 4, 11, 17); while in after days men-
tion is made of Kenites as dispersed among the
Amalekites of the Negeb or South Country (1 Sam.
15. 6; see also 27. 10).. They ranked among the
friends of David when a fugitive from Saul (1 Sam.
30. 29); and through all changes were faithful to
the religion of Israel.
II.—The Rechabites.
_After the days of David we read no more of the
Kenites under that name; and the foregoing notices
of their existence and virtual incorporation with
Israel might have escaped attention but for a re-

markable offshoot of the clan in the family of
Rechabites. In 1 Chron. 2. 55, certain families of
Kenites dwelling at Jabez (probably in Southern
Judah) are described as descendants of one He-
math, ‘‘ father of the house of Rechab.’? Whether
Rechab is a proper name, or an appellative signify-
ing “‘ rider,” and denoting the habits of the com-
munity, is not quite clear. No personage of the
name is mentioned elsewhere in Scripture; but
Jehonadab or Jonadab the son (or descendant) of
Rechab appears in the days of Jehu’s great uprising
against the family of Ahab, as taking a stern and
decisive part in the suppression of idolatry (2 Kings
10. 15, 23). As we learn from Jer. 35, Jonadab
reorganized the Kenites, or a portion of them, into
an ascetic community, pledged by stringent vows
neither to dwell in cities, to build houses, nor to
cultivate land, but to maintain a nomad life, and
especially to abstain from wine and strong drink.
In the days of Nebuchadnezzar, however, the ap-
proach of the Babylonian armies compelled these
Rechabites to escape from their tents for safety
into Jerusalem. For the sake of a lesson to the
Jewish people, Jeremiah was directed to test the
fidelity of the Rechabites. Driven from their wan-
dering life, might not the disciples of Jonadab sup-
pose themselves discharged from their ascetic vows,
or at any rate seize the opportunity of release ?
Vessels of wine were set before them in the Temple,
and they were bidden to drink. They firmly refus-
ed; and the prophet takes occasion to impress upon
the people of Judah the much-needed lesson of
faithfulness to principle, adding at the same time
the promise of Jehovah that the Rechabites should
““stand before Him’ continually, in other words,
should minister in some capacity in His Temple.
The nature of this ministry we can only conjec- |
ture. In 1 Chron. 2. 55 the Rechabites appear as
““seribes’’; in the LXX. inscription to Psalm 71,
they are given rank among the sweet singers of
Israel. It appears certain that from the era of the
Captivity the nomad life was to some extent re-
nounced, seeing that a son of Rechab is found
co-operating with the priests and rulers in rebuild-
ing the wall of Jerusalem (Neh. 3. 14). It may be
added that at a much later period the historian
Hegesippus, as preserved by Husebius, in describing
the martyrdom of St. James the ‘‘ brother of the
Lord,” writes that ‘‘ one of the priests, the sons of
Rechab, who are mentioned by Jeremiah the pro-
phet,”’ cried out against the crime (see Smith’s |
Dict. Bible, art. ‘‘ Rechabites,’’ by Professor Plump-
tre). On the whole there seems satisfactory evi-
dence that a place in the sanctuary itself was given
to these descendants of an alien and wandering
people. The subsequent history of the Rechabites
is unknown; the reports of travellers who profess
to have discovered their traces are hardly conclu-
sive, while warranting further research into this in-
teresting bye-way of Scripture history.
III.—The Samaritans.
During the later age of the separate kingdom of
Israel, the name of Samaria, its capital, was often
employed to denote the nation (Isa. 7.9; Jer. 23.
13; Ezek. 16. 46, &e.). When, therefore, another
community had usurped the place of the Ten Tribes,
it was natural to apply to them the name of “ Sa-
maritans.’’ The word, however, is found only once
in the Old Testament (2 Kings 17. 29). This com-
munity was in its origin in great part heathen, con-
sisting—at any rate chiefly—of immigrants from five
provinces of Assyria, sent by Hsar-haddon (probably |
under the convoy of one of his generals, Asnapper,
Israelites had been deported. In the earlier period
of their residence, the land which had long been
waste and unpeopled was ravaged by lions. This
the settlers interpreted as betokening the anger
of the unknown tutelary “‘God of the land,’’ and
in answer to their solicitations a captive priest
was sent from Assyria to instruct them. He fixed
his abode at Bethel, but taught them no more
than to combine the worship of Jehovah with
that of their own ancestral idols. ‘‘ They feared
the ee and served their own gods’’ (2 Kings
17. 33).
This motley religion endured for some gene-
rations, but the worship of the old Assyrian and
Babylonian deities seems gradually to have died out,
partly, no doubt, from the influence of the Israelitish
remnant still scattered through the land—such men
as, after the destruction of Jerusalem a century
later, came ‘‘ from Shechem, from Shiloh, and from
Samaria’? to worship and to mourn at Mizpeh with
their brethren of Judah (Jer. 41. 5; cp. 2 Chron. 84.
6, 9). Notwithstanding the arguments of Heng-
stenberg and others, the opinion that the survivors
of the Ten Tribes in the course of time coalesced
with the descendants of the Assyrian settlers, and
that the Samaritans had in part an Israelite
origin, seems defensible on all rational and Scrip-
tural grounds.
When*the decree of Cyrus restored Jerusalem
to the Jewish exiles in Babylon, they found a con-
siderable community in the northern part of the
kingdom who claimed to worship the God of Abra-
ham, and proffered their assistance to Joshua and
Zerubbabel in the erection of the Temple. The
Jewish leaders decisively repulsed them, feeling the
danger of admitting rs mixed a community into
the commonwealth of Israel. Their alliance being
thus refused, they became thenceforth the bitterest
adversaries of Judah (Hzra 4. 1-5). This hostility
broke out in the days of Nehemiah, when Sanballat
of Beth-horon (a Samaritan city near the frontier),
with Tobiah, an Ammonite slave, long harassed
the Jews with malignant opposition of every kind ;
ending all, however, after Nehemiah’s departure,
by specious advances towards reconciliation. For
the good and patriotic governor, returning, found
to his amazement that Tobiah was installed in
lodgings within the Temple precinct, and that San-
ballat had given his daughter in marriage to a
grandson of the high priest. It was impossible
for Nehemiah to come to terms with the former
enemies of God’s people. For an Ammonite to
be established in the sanctuary was a profanation.
Tobiah and the high priest’s grandson (Manasseh,
Jos. Ant. xi. 7, sec. 2) were summarily expelled
(Neh. 18. 4-9, 28, 29), and the breach between Jews
and Samaritans became irreparable. [But Josephus
makes Manasseh brother to Jaddua high priest,
placing him in B.c. 333, a second Sanballat being
Manasseh’s father-in-law. ]
Manasseh now assumed the priesthood in Samaria
(about B.c, 408), establishing there an organized
religious community. Mount Gerizim, in time long
past held in honour as one of the ‘‘ holy places’? in
Palestine, was selected as the centre of the new
worship; and, by permission of the Persian king
Darius Nothus, a temple was there reared to Je-
hovah. Soon this was declared to be the place
which God had chosen, and dexterous alterations of
the Pentateuch were made to favour the assump-
tion. The Law of Moses, without the after his-
tories or the prophetic books, was taken as the
text-book of the Samaritan faith; and, breaking
by degrees from the old idolatrous admixture, this
Ezra 4. 10), to colonize the districts from which the | schismatic community laid claim to a stricter wor-

When Antiochus Epiphanes (about B.c. 175) made

the Jews, the Samaritans revealed the spuriousness
of their faith by their ready submission to the
tyrant (Jos. Ant. xii. 5, sec. 5). This placed them
in deadly opposition to the Jewish patriot party,
which, under John Hyreanus, the Maccabee, de-
| stroyed Samaria and the temple of Gerizim, B.c, 130
(Jos. Ant. xiii. 9, sec. 1). But the altar remained,
the spirit of the sect was unbroken, and the old
animosity subsisted in all its force down to the
