Judea, no Jew, if he could help it, would pass
through Samaria, but would take the road on the
eastern side of the Jordan. When members of the
two communities met, angry strife was sure to arise
(Luke 9. 52-54), often leading to bloodshed. No
name of scorn was more bitter in Jerusalem than
that of Samaritan (John 8. 48), All this gives point
to our Lord’s repeated lessons of brotherly-kindness
(Luke 10. 33, &c.) ; and it is interesting to find that
one of the disciples who was for calling down fire
from heaven to destroy the Samaritans who rejected
Christ, himself preached the Gospel afterwards in
many Samaritan villages (Luke 9. 54; ep. with
Acts 8. 25).
Through all generations and amid eyery change
the Samaritans have remained in their ancestral
abode of Nablous (Neapolis, the ancient Shechem),
with their altar and their sacrifices upon Mount
Gerizim. They are now ‘‘the oldest and the
smallest sect in the world’’ (Dean Stanley), con-
sisting of from forty to fifty families. ‘They pre-
serve their edition of the Pentateuch, in its old
Hebrew characters, with religious care. There has
been much discussion as to this relic of antiquity ;
and if, as seems most probable, it. represents the
Law as handed down among the Ten Tribes from
the days of the disruption under Jeroboam, the fact
effectually disposes of modern theories as to the late
origin of the ‘‘ Five Books.” The subject is one
that cannot here be discussed, but it deserves and
will doubtless receive further elucidation,
IV.—Nazarites.
More correctly ‘‘ Nazirites,” as in R. V.
Strictly speaking, the Nazirites (from Heb. nazar,
“to separate’’?) formed no community, their vows
and obligations being distinctly personal. The rules
for this kind of separation are given in Num. 6;
and from the manner-of their introduction, seem
to recognise the order as already existing. Some
have thought, but on scarcely sufficient authority,
that it was borrowed by the Jews from the Egyptians.
The principle of the Nazirite vow evidently was that
of consecration to God ; the temporary and outward
“ separateness’? testifying to the life-long universal |
obligation. The symbolic accompaniments of the
yow were extremely simple, demanding no seclusion
nor engrossing observances, and in no way inter-
fering with the ordinary duties of life. To abstain
from strong drink, as well as from the fruit of the
vine in every shape, to allow the hair to grow, and
not to approach the dead—such was the threefold
JEWISH SECTS, ORDERS, AND SOCIETIES. 169
rule for man or woman; and the long hair would
be the only very noticeable token of the vow. The
“days of separation’? might be many or few,
according to the wish or conscience of the Nazirite.
Jewish writers tell us that the usual period was
thirty days, but. vows were occasionally made for
sixty or a hundred days, and even for a longer time
(see the case of Helena, queen of Adiabene; Smith’s
Dict. Bible, art. ‘‘ Nazarite’’). At the expiration
of the vow, the Navzirite had to present himself at
the altar with a complete series of offerings; he
parted also with his locks, which were burned im the
fire of the sacrifice. The meaning of this ceremonial
was twofold, including on the one hand release from
the special restrictions to which he had been sub-
jected; but on the other, that dedication to a life
of piety and holiness of which all sacrifices were the
symbol.
In the Nazirite vow, accordingly, there was a
sacramental consecration of all life to God; it was
peculiarly appropriate therefore to youth; and
scanty as are the details furnished by Scripture on
the subject, there are hints that this was the period
of life usually chosen for the vow. See Amos 2. 11;
also the touching lament of Jeremiah (Lam. 4. 7) :
“Her Nazirites* were purer than snow, they were
whiter than milk, they were more ruddy in body
than rubies, their polishing was of sapphire”’ (cp.
Ps. 144. 12, ‘that our daughters may be as corner
stones, polished after the similitude of a palace’’).
A striking similarity exists between the symbols of
Nazirite and those of high-priestly dedication (Lev.
21. 10-12, where the word rendered crown is the
same as that used in Num. 6. 19 for the long hair of
the Nazirite). The separated one would thus be
reminded of the great ideal of a holy life—a priestly
self-dedication to God. See Exod. 19. 6; Isa.
61. 6.
A distinction is made by Jewish writers between
a ‘‘Nazirite of days”? and a ‘‘ Nazirite for life.”
The latter were those dedicated from infancy, for a
special purpose, to a life-long observance of the
Nazirite vow. Such were Samson (the only one
actually called ‘‘a Nazirite”’ in Scripture (Judg. 18.
7); also Samuel (1 Sam. 1. 11), and John the Bap-
tist (Luke 1. 15). James “the Lord’s brother”’ is
represented by tradition as a Nazirite. Whether
this particular form of dedication was customary in
earlier or later times we are not able to decide on
the authority of Scripture. ‘‘ Hwald supposes that
Nazarites for life were numerous in very early times,
and that they multiplied in periods of great political
and religious excitement.”’ ‘The referencesin Scrip-
ture and the Apocrypha (Amos 2. 11, 12; 1 Mace.
3. 49), seem to refer to the ‘* Nazirites of days.” In
the history of the Apostle Paul we read of four
persons of this class, in whose votive observances he
himself took part (Acts 21. 28, 24, 26); while the
vow at Cenchress (Acts 18. 18) was evidently of
another kind.
It is scarcely necessary to mention that the words
Nazirite and Nazarene have no relation to each
other. The letter ‘‘z’’? in the two is radically
different in Hebrew (? and ¥). ‘‘ Jesus of Naza-
reth’’ was not ‘‘a Nazirite,’’ as He Himself sug-
gests (Matt. 11. 18,19) in contrast with His fore-
runner John.
* Or perhaps the word here used (a somewhat different
form from that usually rendered Nazérite) means “sepa-
rated” in dignity—* princes” (R. V. “nobles” : “ Nazir-
ites” in margin). The same word is used (Gen, 49. 26;
Deut. 33. 16) of Joseph.

JEWISH SECTS, ORDERS, AND’ SOCIETIRS.
PHARISEES, SADDUCEES, AND ESSENES.
(The Chasidim.)
The era of the Jewish captivity, writes the late
Emanuel Deutsch, was ‘“ one of the most mysterious
and momentous periods in the history of humanity.
What were the influences brought to bear upon the
captives during that time, we knownot. But this
we know, that from a reckless, lawless, godless
populace, they returned transformed into a band |
of Puritans.’’ One result of this revival of the
Israelite faith, was the firm and organized stand
henceforth made against the efforts of their suc-
cessive heathen rulers to denationalise and paganise
the nation. It is true that some in high places
were unable to resist the seduction. Thus, under
the influence of Antiochus Hpiphanes, king of Syria
(B.c. 175-164), the very high priest, Jason by name,
introduced Pagan rites into Jerusalem, and sent
offerings to Hercules, the god of Tyre. This dis-
graceful period was afterwards appropriately spoken
of as the time of “‘the mingling.” But the heart
of the nation was true, and the noble struggles of
the Maccabees against the tyrant are familiar to all
readers of Jewish history. In connection with the
prolonged contest we meet with a fraternity under
the name of Assidxans, described as ‘‘ mighty men
of Tsrael,”’ “‘ voluntarily devoted to the Law”? (see
1 Mace. 2. 42; 7. 13; 2 Mace. 14. 6). Evidently
this appellation is a Graecised form of the Hebrew
Chasidim, ‘* Pious,’’ or, to'adopt a modern term,
‘* Pietists.”” From this fraternity, whose common
bond of union was a resolution to devote their lives
to the upholding of the Law in its integrity, appear
to have sprung, directly or indirectly, the three
great “‘sects’’ of after time—the Puarismns, the
Sappvucwns, and the Hssenus. Widely as these
eventually diverged from one another, and bitter as
were their mutual controversies, they all started
from the same point—a firm adherence to the na-
tional faith. But while the Pharisees, laying their
chief stress’ wpon exact obedience, were led to for-
malism and an exaggerated estimate of the autho-
rity of the Fathers, the Sadducees, taking morality
as their watchword, lost all sense of the superna-
tural, while the Exssenes, whose great principle was
self-control, were led into a mystical and unprofit-
able asceticism. Only the two former sects are
mentioned in the New Testament, although there
are clear traces of the third: Josephus has much to
say upon them all.
V.—The Pharisees.
In opposition to the ‘mingling,’ of which we
have spoken above, arose the brotherhood of the
“ Distinct’? or “ Separatists ’’ (perushim,* whence
comes the Greek form of the word ‘‘ Pharisees.’?
The name which they themselves assumed was
Chaberim, or ‘“ Associates”). When or how the
fraternity assumed its shape, we cannot accurately
tell. ‘The word ‘‘ Pharisee” is not found in the
Old Testament or Apocrypha; its earliest occur. |
rence being in Josephus, in the annals of Jonathan
the high priest (B.c. 144), and of John Hyrcanus
(B.c. 109), when the body was already powerful and
of great repute (Jos. Ant. xiii. 5, sec. 9 and 10, 5.
See also xviii. 1, 3, and Wars, ii. 8, 14). Two
points were held by the Pharisees as of high impor-
tance, and on each of them a pledge was exacted as
* From parash, Heb. to separate or distinguish, almost |
like nazar. See Nazarite above.
was the obligation to pay all tithes before the use
or sale of any commodity, nothing being allowed to
be eaten with regard to the tithing of which there
was any doubt. The other point related to the
avoidance of all uncleanness, in regard to which a
multitude of rules were laid down, many of which
were minute and puerile. T'o these two character-
istics of Pharisaism our Lord alludes (Matt. 23. 28,
25). But the chief point of distinction lay in the
regard paid by the Pharisees to the oral law, a
series of unwritten interpretations of the Divine
oracles handed down from doctor to doctor, and
forming an elaborate system extending to every
detail of worship and of life. The “‘ traditions of
the elders” thus spun around God’s Word a web of
intricate refinement; and while purporting to ‘‘ fence
the Law,” or to lessen the risk of breaking it, these
traditions became in the multiplicity of subtle dis-
tinctions and vexatious rules an oppression to the
conscience. ‘Formalism was substituted for spiri-
tual religion, and the ‘‘ separateness’? of this
fraternity, as evinced by their long robes with
fringe and tassels, their broad phylacteries, their
long prayers publicly recited by the highways at
the customary hours, as well as by the casuistry of
their teachings and the inconsistency of their lives,
proved their piety to be in great measure an affec-
tation. Very terrible is the indictment brought
against the Pharisees by our Lord, as reported in
Matt, 23, Mark 7, Luke 11. They were in fact
the principal obstacle to the reception of Christ
and His Gospel. It was impossible for them to
accept the spirituality of His doctrines, or to de-
scend to the humility of those who would follow
Him. Their spirit was that of self-sufficiency and
pride. When John the Baptist preached the baptism
of repentance in the wilderness, the Pharisees for
the most part (Luke 7. 30), although not entirely
(Matt. 3. 7), held aloof. They thanked God that
they were not ‘‘as other men” (Luke 18. 10) ; yet
while exalting themselves in their own esteem to
heaven, they verily became the ‘‘ children of hell”?
(Matt. 23. 15).
Undoubtedly there was another side to the Phari-
saic character. They held certain great doctrines,
as that of a resurrection and future life, with a
tenacity unknown to the people at large; while
their strictness on points of religious observance
served as an antidote to prevailing laxity. The
| Apostle Paul regarded it as a distinction among
the professors of Judaism to be a Pharisee, the son
of a Pharisee (Acts 23. 6; cp. Phil. 3. 5). Like
the Jesuits in the Roman Church, the Pharisees
proved the utmost capabilities of their religious
system, if, like them, they found it wanting. . The
best and the worst of the people were Pharisees* ;

VI.—The Sadducees,
The antagonism between the Sadducees and the
Pharisees in New ‘Testament times was so pro-
nounced as to suggest that the former sect origi-
nated in a reaction from the strictness of the latter.
More probably, however, as already observed, both
arose from the desire on the part of the most
faithful among the Jews to preserve the purity of
the national religion when threatened by heathen
oppressors. Josephus, in his first mention of the
Sadducees, in the history of Jobn Hyrcanus (Ant.
xiii. 10, 6), simply says that their ‘‘ notions are
quite contrary to those of the Pharisees.” A
current Jewish tradition ascribes their origin and
their name to one Zadok, disciple of Antigonus
(B.c. 200-170), who, it is said, taught that virtue
was to be cultivated for its own sake, without
calculation of consequences or hope of future re-
compence. An ennobling thought! although after-

The origin of the Sadducees is the key to much
of their history. Schools of morality are sure to
decline from the simplicity of their primitive prin-

true pleasure, and the Hpicurean became a mere

MONEY AND COINS.
GENERAL REMARKS.—In the Old Testament, no
real coins, i.e. pieces struck under an authority, are
mentioned previous to the Captivity, although various
allusions of earlier date—e.g. Josh.7. 21; 1 Sam. 2. 36;
Ps, 68. 30—indicate, as the prescribed payments un-
der the Mosaic Law imply, a currency of pieces of
rough silver of fixed weight ; the A. V. adds ‘‘ pieces”
or “ shekels’’ to Hebrew numerals in sundry places,
e.g. 2 Kings 5. 5, where a weight, whether of gold or
silver, is probably intended. Of actual coins the
first mentioned are ‘‘drams”’ of the time of Cyrus,
B.C. 588 (Hzra 2. 69), probably the gold staters, i.e.
standard coins of the reformed coinage of Croesus,
king of Lydia (B.c. 568). The second are ‘‘ drams ”?
of the time of Artaxerxes Longimanus, son of the
Ahasuerus of the Book of Esther, i.e. Xerxes (Hzra
8.27; Neh. 7.72); these would be the Daric staters
or standard Persian gold coins of the reformed coin-
age of Darius, son of Hystaspes (B.c. 521-485), which
circulated extensively in Persia in Artaxerxes’ reign.
In the Apocrypha, the drams mentioned are a
fraction of the Attic talent, which [varunt, II. ]
Alexander the Great’s succession rendered nearly
universal, In B.c. 189, Antiochus VII. (Sidetes), of
the Graeco-Syrian dynasty, granted special permis-
sion to Simon Maccabeus to coin money with his
own stamp (1 Mace. 15. 6), and the first Jewish coins
(silver shekels and half-shekels) were issued by
Simon in B.c. 141.
The Asmonwan dynasty issued a copper coinage,
gradually showing Greek tendencies to the time of
Antigonus, the last prince, and the numerous coin-
age of Alexander Jannzous (B.c. 105-78) doubtless
circulated even in N.T. times. The Idumwan princes,
commencing with Herod I. (surnamed the Great),
continued a copper coinage with Greek legends,
which circulated in Judea (as well as a coinage
minted by the Roman ‘‘ governors” of the province
of Judea, A.D. 6-59) till the death of Agrippa IT.
(Acts 25. 18; 26. 2, seg.) in a.p. 100.
In the N. T. period, therefore, the coins current in
the Holy Land would be of gold, silver, copper, and
bronze (“‘ brass,’’ Matt. 10. 9)—partly Jewish (espe-
cially the bronze and copper coinages of Alexander
Jannzus [mire] and of the Herods), but chiefly
Greek and Roman. Of these foreign coins, some
would be imperial, i.e. of Alexander the Great and
his successors, and of the Cxsars, viz. Augustus,
Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, and Nero;—others
would be local, i.e. of the great commercial cities
of Syria and Pheenicia, and of the Roman procu-
rators of Judea. The current gold coin was the
Roman Awrews, equivalent to 25 denarii [PENNY],
and worth about £11s. The bulk of the silver
currency consisted of tetradrachms, i.e. 4-dram-
pieces or staters of the Attic standard [PIECE oF
MONEY, TALENT IT. struck at Antioch on Orontes,
Tyre, &c., but chiefly of Roman denarii [PENNY], a
quarter of the weight of the stater.
As Jewish money only could be brought into the
Holy Place, the presence of ‘‘ money changers’? in
the outer courts of the Temple was necessary to
convert this motley currency into Jewish coin.
The following coins are mentioned in the post-
captivity books of the O.T., in the Apocrypha, and
in the N.T. :—
Drachm (2 Mace. 4. 19; 10. 20; 12. 43; Tobit 5.
14), v.e. the earlier Attic drachm (8.c. 338), worth
nearly 10d.; the later, about 8d., English. See
PENNY and PIECE OF SILVER.
Dram (Hzra 2.69; 8.27; Neh. 7. 70-72; 1 Chron.
29.7; Heb. Adarkon and Darkemon), a standard gold
coin, viz. the Persian daric, worth a guinea or 22s.
Farthing renders (1) Assarton (Matt. 10. 29;
Luke 12. 6, i.e. Gk. for the Roman as or assarius),
probably a Greek coin of bronze (‘‘ brass,”? Matt.)
minted at the Syrian Antioch, and worth 35 of a
denarius [PENNY], or about 8 farthings English ;
(2) KopDRANTES (Matt. 5. 26; Mark 12. 42, i.e. Gk.
for the Roman quadrans, 4th part of the as), worth
about ¢ of an English farthing. See mire.
Half Shekel (Exod. 30. 13, 15, Heb. bekah) =
1s. 4d. English.
Mite (Mark 12. 42; Luke 12. 59; 21. 2), Gk.
lepton, a small Greek copper coin worth half the
original quadrans [¥ARTHING (2)]. But as the
““mites’? must have been Jewish coins, they were
probably two of the small coins struck by Alexander
Jannzus, equal to-a quadrans, and worth 2 of an
English farthing each.
Penny (Matt. 18. 28; 22. 19, &c., Gk. denarion,
Lat. denarius). Roman denarii formed the bulk of
the silver coins current in Palestine during the N. T.
period [see PIECE OF MONEY]. <A denarius (value
83d.) was the regular pay of a day labourer (ep.
Matt. 20. 2-13), as in the Middle Ages. It was also
the tribute [TRIBUTE MoNEY] payable by the Jews
to the Emperor after Judzea became a Roman pro-
vince. Nero reduced its value to 73d.
Piece of Money, in Matt. 17. 27, is the Gk.
stater = standard coin, t.e. the Attic tetradrachm,
or Greeco-Syrian piece of 4 drachme (= denarii or
““pence”’), which, with the denarii [see PENNY],
composed the silver currency of Palestine during the
ist and 2nd centuries 4.D. Being equal to the
shekel, this stater represented the sacred tribute
[TRIBUTE MONEY] for two, our Lord and St. Peter.
Piece of Silver in the O. T. represents ‘‘ shekel
of silver’? in weight, except in 1 Sam. 2. 36;
Ps. 68. 30; Josh. 24. 32; Job 42. 11, where it may
mean uncoined money. In the New Testament it
renders (1) drachme, i.e. the Attic drachm (Luke
15. 8), equivalent in St. Luke’s time to the Roman
denarius [PENNY], and to the quarter shekel, and
worth 8d.—8id. English; (2) argwrion, in Matt.
26. 15, &c., where the ‘30 [pieces] of silver,”
usually taken to be denarii or “‘pence,’’ are pro-
bably shekels (see the parallel, Zech. 11. 12, 13,
and cp. Exod. 21. 32), i.e. Syro-Greek tetradrachms
or staters [PIECE OF MONEY]; and also in Acts 19. 19
(Vulg. “denarii,” no doubt correctly).
Shekel. A Hebrew word used in the O. T. only,
signifying “‘ weight,’ and also an ingot of fixed
value (Exod. 30. 13) [see WEIGHTS], but used later
for money uncoined and coined. Its divisions are

(1) the half shekel, Heb. bekah [see We1cHTS] ;
(2) the third part, which the Jews who returned
from the Captivity paid yearly towards the main-
tenance of the Temple service (Neh. 10. 32, 33), |
instead of the half shekel contributed before the |
Captivity (Exod. 30. 18; 38.26; cp. 2 Chron. 24. 6), |
and again at a later date [vRrBUTE mMoNEY, IT. ]; |
(3) the fourth part, Heb. rebah (1 Sam. 9. 8), worth |
about 8d.; and (4) the twentieth part, Heb. gerah |
(Exod. 80.13), worth about 14d.

WEIGHTS.
GrNERAL ReMARKS.—No ancient measures, but
some specimens of Assyrian, Babylonian, Egyptian,
and Greek weights have been discovered, and some
very striking successes have consequently been
achieved; yet we cannot hope to reconstruct the
primitive systems; and least of all the Hebrew
system, of which no specimen survives, with the
| elaborate tabular detail and decimal precision too
| often attempted. Some writers rely upon informa-
tion obtainable from Hebrew literature, but, as
| regards the shekel at least, monumental and other
| evidence disproves the Rabbinical distinction be-
tween the Mosaic and the later shekel.

| A.V. translation of maneh ; in Gk.mna (LXX.); in

| the Hgyptians, Phoenicians, Hebrews, and Greeks
with the use of the Babylonian weight-talent ‘‘ of the
| king”? [wanent, I.]. It is found in 1 Kings 10. 17
(Solomon’s golden shields of ‘‘ three pounds” each ;
ep. 2 Chron. 9. 16) ; in Ezra 2. 69 and Neh. 7. 71, 725
and in the obscure passage of Hzek. 45.12. In the
| Apocrypha, viz. in 1 Mace. 14. 24; 15.18, and 1 Esdras
| 5. 45, it is the A. V. translation of the Gk. mna; as
also in the New’ Testament, in the Parable of the
Pounds (Luke 19. 13-25). The maneh was zo of a
| talent. For its weight and value in the three talents
| in use among the ancient Hebrews, see TALENT, I.
Il. In the New Testament, except in Luke 19.
| 18-25 (‘‘mna’’), ‘pound’? renders litra (John
12. 8; 19. 39), a word used by the Greeks of Sicily

Shekel (Heb. weight) occurs in the O.T. only,
viz. first as a weight, by which numerous objects,

Talent. I. In the Old Testament ‘‘ talent ’’ (Heb.
kikkar, ‘a circle” or ‘‘ globe”’), the largest Hebrew
weight for metals, occurs first in Exod. 25. 39,

metals’ mentioned are gold, silver, brass, iron, tin,
lead (Num. 31. 22) among the spoils of Midian. In
Ezek. 27. 12 these metals (gold, LX X.) are men-
tioned as imports of Tyre, with precious stones
(ib. v. 22). In Job 28. 1-11 (see Var. note on v. 4)
mining is described.
Antimony is mentioned (2 Kings 9. 21; Var. note,
ep. Hzek. 23. 40) as used, like the modern Kohl,
to give effect to the eye.
Brass, in Hebrew necosheth (copper, Var.), prob-
ably denotes both copper and its alloys, i.e. bronze
and brass; of the alloys, bronze must have been in
very early times familiar to the Hebrews, and in
more modern times brass would also have been
known to them. Cyprus, always famous for its
copper, was one source of supply; other sources
being the Lebanon (Asher, Deut. 8. 9 & 33. 25)
and Asia Minor (Hzek. 27.13, Javan=lIonian Greece,
and Tubal and Meshech=tribes of Hastern Cappa-
docia). Mefka, in the Sinaitic peninsula, was a
source of the copper employed by the builders of
the Egyptian pyramids.
Gold has six Hebrew names, of which four, in-
cluding the gold of Uphaz or Ophir (according to
some ancient Versions), occur in Job 28. 15-19.
Gold of Parvaim (2 Chron. 3. 6) came perhaps from
Farw4, in South Arabia, perhaps from the far Hast
(Piroa=LHastern in Sanscrit).
Tron is mentioned as a product of Asher, and was
plentiful among the Canaanites (see Judg. 1. 19 &
4, 3). The “‘northern iron,” apparently famous for
its hardness (Jer. 15. 12; see Var. notes), may have
come from the Chalybes, the great iron workers of
Armenia.
Lead is a symbol of weight in Exod. 15. 10 &
Zech. 5. 8, and it is mentioned as used for separat-
ing precious metal from dross (Isa. 1. 25; Jer. 6. 29;
Haek. 22. 18), and to make an indelible writing tablet
(Job 19. 28, 24).
Silver seems to have served as the chief medium
of exchange; Spain was probably one of the chief
sources of supply (1 Macc. 8. 8).
Tin was found amongst the ornaments of the
Midianites (Num. 31. 22), and, in Homeric times,
it ranked with gold and silver for ornamental pur-
poses. It was used with copper to make bronze.
The Phoenicians obtained it from Spain certainly,
and probably from the Malay Peninsula, but prob-
ably not from Cornwall in very early times. Italy
also appears to have afforded a source of tin,
PRECIOUS
THE Precious Stones of the Bible are spoken of
generally as imported into Tyre from Sheba and
Raamah (Ezek. 27. 22), and are chiefly of interest
| in connection with the breastplate of the High
| Priest, and the New Jerusalem (Rev. 21. 11, 18-21),
and the vision of Ezekiel (1. 4, 16, 22, 26). The
| twelve stones of the breastplate and the two stones
on the shoulder-ornaments have been the objects
of a considerable amount of literature from the
4th century.
But even at the date of the Septuagint transla-
| tion, the stones to which the Hebrew names apply
could not be identified, for the LX X. renders the
same Hebrew name by different words; so also
does Josephus, although he believed that he had
seen the actual stones. In short, it is hopeless to
try to identify the stones by the light of any existing
translations.
The only method open to us is to study the sur-
viving stones once accounted precious in Egypt,
Assyria, and Mesopotamia, and to try and identify
the Hebrew names with some of them.
The following stones are found among Egyptian,
Babylonian, and Assyrian ornaments :—chalcedony,
sard, carnelian, plasma and sapphirine (green and

ANIMAL
FISHES AND FISHERIES.
Fishes.—The creation of fishes is placed in Genesis
in the fitth day with that of marine monsters, or
whales, of reptiles and birds, and so prior to that of
the inhabitants of the dry land; geological science
strikingly corroborates this or der ot sequence.
Little is said about fishes in Holy Writ. The
Law (Lev. 11. 9=12) recognises only the distinction
between clean, i.e. those that have fins and scales,
and the unclean, i.e. those which have neither.
No Hebrew name of any fish has survived, although
the number and variety of the fresh-water and
salt-water fish of Palestine is extraordinary. Fresh-
water fish swarm in the streams of Palestine; those
of the Jordan-system are distinct, and approximate
to the fishes of the Nile and its lakes; those of the
streams from Lebanon approximate more to those
of Asia Minor and of the Euphrates.
The animal-worship of Egypt included the worship
of fishes, which is prohibited in Deut. 4. 18, and
Dagon, the Fish-God (dag = fish and the stump
in 1 Sam. 5. 4=/fishy part), was the Philistine
national deity.
Fisheries.—The Hebrews, with their single port
of Joppa and their pastoral and agricultural pro-
clivities, had little inducement to a seafaring life
or to sea-fishing, but doubtless the Lake of Galilee,
with its marvellous shoals of fish, was never with-
out its fishermen and the important trade in fish,
of which we read in Roman times. The sea-fisheries
were from time immemorial in the hands of the
Pheenicians of Tyre and Sidon, and later, also, of
their congeners, the Philistines (see Neh. 13. 16,
&c.). The fish for market would be salted or sun-
dried.
The fishing implements referred to in the Bible
are the draw-net, or seine (Gk. sagéné, Matt. 13.
47-50) ; the drag of Hab. 1. 15, set and drawn from
a boat (Isa. 19. 8); the casting-net (Gk. amphi-
bléstron, Matt. 4. 18 and John 21); the spear
(Job 41. 7), and the hook and line (Isa. 19. 8;
Hab. 1. 15; Job 41. 1; Matt. 17. 27). In Beypt,
fish, though forbidden to the PIICEtS, was a starle
food of the masses (Num. 11. 5; ep. Isa. 19. 8);
fishes were kept alive in stews, and allusions to a
like practice amongst the Hebrews occur in Cant.
7.4; Isa. 19.10; cp. Job 41. 2.

INVERTEBRATE ANIMALS.
The creation of creeping things of the land, 1.e. of
all the species of invertebrate animals and of insects,
is placed in Genesis in the sixth day. These also
were studied by Solomon, but the references to
them are rare, except to the locust.
Naturalists divide the order of insects termed
Orthoptera, to which the locusts belong, into the
Runners (Cursoria) and Leapers (Saltatoria), sub-
dividing the latter into families, of which the cricket,
grasshopper, and migratory locust are respectively
types.
The Locust Tribe. The Law treated all the
Runners as unclean; of the Leapers, four species
are mentioned in Lev. 11. 22 as permissible for food,
A.V. the locust, bald locust, beetle, and grasshopper
(Heb. chagab), and though unidentifiable, they were
doubtless various species of locusts (or grasshoppers,
R.V. marg.). By the palmer-worm, cankerworm,
and the caterpiller in Joel 1. 4 (R. V. as A. Y.),
locusts are also meant, and, perhaps, by the grass-
hopper in Amos 7. 1 (Heb. gob) [GRASSHOPPER |; but,
although Pusey holds decidedly that the Hebrew
of the three former words and of ‘‘ locust ’’ (Heb.
arbeh) in Joel describes four species succeeding one
another, and that the Heb. gob, i.e. the Creeper,
alone represents the locust in its wingless state, we
hold from local observation that different stages in
the locust’s existence are denoted by at least the
‘pnalmer-worm’’ and ‘‘canker-worm”’ also (so R. V.
marg.). The locust is the worst scourge of the
East. The Hebrews had good reason to observe
it, and the habits of the migratory locust are de-
scribed with moderate accuracy in all the allusions,
but notably in the imagery of Joel 2. 2-9, 20, and
in the narrative of the 8th plague of Egypt (Wxod.
10. 5, 6, 18, 15, 19; Heb. arbeh). To this day,
clouds of locusts (Acrydiwm peregrinum and Bdipoda
migratoria), borne on the wind from the Arabian
wilderness into Palestine, darken the air, and porish
only when a strong wind drives them into the sea
(cp. Ps. 109. 23). Alighting nightly, they cover the
ground and devour every green thing, swarming
even up the trees, and leave a desert behind them;
nothing bars their orderly and relentless march
(Joel 2. 7-9; ep. Exod. 10. 6). Moreover, they
deposit in the soil a er op of eggs, whence a new
swarm hatches out, no less destructive in its cater-
pillar and pupa stages, and after destroying all
vegetation around, it attains to the winged state
and flies away (Nah. 8. 16, 17) to destroy and
multiply elsewhere.
Locusts are still eaten in the Jordan valley and
wilderness of Judah (Matt. 3. 4), where, like the
“wild honey,’ they always abound; stewed in
butter, Arab fashion, they taste somewhat like
shrimps, but with less flavour.

The Land of Israel as possessed, as distin-
guished from the Land of Promise (Gen. 15. 18),
was bounded on the west by the Great Sea, ¢.e. the
Mediterranean ; on the north by Lebanon, w hich sepa-
rates it from Phoenicia; and on the east by Mounts
Hermon and Bashan, and the desert, to the River
Arnon. Thence, the’ southern boundary ran along
the eastern shore of the Dead Sea, and from its
southern end across the wilderness of Zin past
Kadesh-barnea, to the ‘‘ River of Hgypt,’’ ¢.e. the
Wady-el- Arish. It was named Palestine, or Syria-
Palestina, from the Philistines, who occupied the
rich maritime plain between Joppa and the Desert
of Shur;—Judxa, from Judah, which after the
Captivity represented the Hebrew nation ;—and the
Holy Land, because there Christ was born, pr eached,
and taught, confirming His ‘‘ good news,”’ @.e. the
Gospel, by miracles ; ; and laid down His life for man-
kind. It is about the size of Wales or Portugal,
being less than 140 miles in length, and from 70 50
miles in breadth (including the smaller section east
of Jordan). It consists of a mountainous region (with
few distinct ranges), which broadens and lowers
southward from Lebanon and Hermon, and is bisect-
ed by the extraordinary depression of the Jordan
valley. The western section is broken transversely
by one plain (Hsdraelon), and again lowers to form
the ‘‘ South,’’ between Judah and the Wilderness.
The climate of Palestine is, during a great part
of the year, very hot. The east winds are peculiarly
dry, though they are sometimes tempestuous; and
those which are westerly are attended with rain.
The first rains, as they are called, generally fall
about the beginning of November; and the latter
rains in the month of April. See Calendar, and
especially the Note on the Seasons.
Geology.—The surface rocks of Palestine—except
a small voleanic section in the north-east between
Hermon and the River Yarmuk, which extends west-
ward across the Lake of Tiberias to Tabor—are of a
soft limestone containing many fossils, and remark-
able for numberless caverns and excavated cisterns,
and for fountains issuing as small brooks from the
solid rock. In spite of the destruction of the forests,
and diminution of cultivated and other vegetation,
the water-supply yet justifies Moses’ description
(Deut. 8. 7). The whole country is seamed with
perennial streams or winter torrents.*

tamia, used to be exported for embalming the dead.
Its bed being often 2,600 ft. below the sea-level,
this depression is the deepest in any continent; and
having no outlet, the water is so intensely salt that
nothing can live in it, and. swimming is rendered
nearly impossible by its buoyancy. The drift-wood
from the Jordan is soon bleached and petrified.
The Lake is about 46 miles long, and 10-11 miles in
extreme width. On the west, the riven mountains
of the Wilderness of Judza—and on the east, the
ravine-pierced wall of the plateau of Moab rise
abruptly from it, while at the southern end (beyond
a level plain) a line of cliffs close the basin; all
barren alike. In the south-west corner, the Jebel
Usdum, an isolated range of rock salt, rises in
fantastic pinnacles. The Lake was formerly sup-
posed to cover the oasis of the four cities, Sodom,
Gomorrha, Admah, and Zeboiim (Bela or Zoar
being spared), but this is unsupported by Biblical
or scientific evidence. No sign of any such recent
geological change is to be found. Some place these
cities in the plain at the southern end; some (especi-
ally Grove) in the plain at the northern end of
the Lake.*
Jericho, or the city of palm trees, was an oasis in
the final plain of Jordan, irrigated from the moun-
tains of Judea by aqueducts, &e., whose ruins are
yet traceable, and by its famous springs now marked
by the only vegetation that breaks the dreary ex-
panse. Its nearly tropical climate and adequate
water-supply made it a perfect garden (cp. Gen.
13. 10), famous for its balsam and other products,
wnence a revenue resulted worthy of Cleopatra’s
acceptance from Mark Antony. Herod bought it
from Cleopatra, and built a winter palace there (see
Josh. 6; 1 Kings 16. 84; Luke 18, 85—19. 27).
The sea coast of Palestine is singularly deficient
in ports, but small hollows with moles added, and
creeks sufficed for early navigation. The only bay
is that of Akka (the Accho of Judg. 1. 31; and
Ptolemais of Acts 21.7), formed by the single pro-
montory, Mount Carmel. The Hebrews could not
take Accho from the Phenicians. The city stands in
a fertile plain connected by a narrow pass with the
great transverse plain of Western Palestine, Esdrae-
lon, and is traversed by the Rivers Belus and Kishon.
The Knights of St. John settling at Akka gave it
the name of St. Jean d’ Acre.

half-way between Carmel and Joppa, was the capi- |
tal of the Herods, and of the Roman governors of |

Joppa (now Jaffa) in Dan, is yet the port of Jeru-
salem. Thence Jonah sailed for Tarshish; here the
pilgrims disembark. It is an unprotected roadstead,
and landing is often impossible.
The Plains.—Between the coast and highlands a
strip of plain intervenes, divided (Deut. 1. 7) into
“The Seaside’—between Mounts Lebanon and
Carmel—assigned to Asher, but retained by the
Phoonicians; and “The Vale.” The latter, ex-
tending from Carmel uninterruptedly to the neigh-
bourhood of Gaza, is divided in the Bible into (1)
Sharon to the north and (2) Philistia to the south of
Joppa. Sharon is the narrower (average 10 miles
wide) and more undulating, and formerly (Josephus
and LXX.) shared the wooded character of Carmel
and of the valleys between it and the vale of Shechem.
Into Sharon descend the passes of Manasseh: from
the plain of Hsdraelon (see below), the commanding
links in the chief military and commercial route be-
tween the valleys of the Euphrates and Nile. Phi-
listia is broader (average 15-16 miles), and nearly
level, and forms in its season a continuous corn-field,
the brown soil being apparently inexhaustible. As
the district best known to travellers and merchants,
especially through its ports, Joppa and Cesarea,
Philistia gave to the western division of the Holy
Land the name Palestine, now extended to the whole.
The plain of Hsdraelon (i.e. Jezreel) alone divides
the western highland, and thus connects the plain of
the coast with the Jordan valley and the plateaux
east of it. The spring pasturage and water-supply
of Esdraelon—now called Merj-ibn-Amir, or the
Meadow of the Prince—formerly attracted the
nomad ‘“‘children of the Hast,” i.e. the pastoral
tribes of Amrhon and Moab, as it yet attracts their
successors the Bedouin. The level surface of this
unique highway made it the natural battle-field of
nations whose strength lay in chariots of iron, and
from such associations St. John quotes the Hill of
Megiddo (Ar-Mageddon) as the type of the never-
ceasing battle between good and evil. But little
elevated above the sea level, its southern end is
swampy; being surrounded by hill countries, it is
scored by winter torrents that a single storm can
fill, though the Kishon, in which all unite, is in
summer but a string of pools; its bed, hollowed in
the alluvial soil, is treacherous, and the fords shift
with every flood (Judg. 5. 21, 22).
West of the watershed—which crosses the plain
(15 miles wide) from north to south past Endor—
Hsdraelon forms a triangle with its apex in the pass
below Carmel by which Kishon enters the plain of
Accho (Acre), the north side being about 12 miles
and the south about 18 miles in length. Hast of the
watershed, Tabor, Moreh (Little Hermon), and
Gilboa,* parallel to the Jordan, divide the plain
into three branches, by which famous routes lead (1)
north-east to Tiberias, west of Merom, and Damas-
cus; (2) east down the valley of Jezreel, past Beth-
shan to Aphek, or to Gadara in Decapolis, the
centre of the Roman roads; and (3) by Engannim,
south to Shechem, Bethel, Jerusalem, and Hebron,
along the rising watershed.
The Hill Countries.—The plateaux east of
Jordan—the forest and pasture lands of Pales-
tine — are divided into Bashan and Gilead. *
The western highlands comprise the ‘‘ mountain ”’
(1) of Naphtali, (2) of Ephraim, (3) of Judah (Deut.

3rd, Judea; of the N.T. The ranges of Upper
(4,000 ft.) and hills of Lower Galilee (1,800 ft.)
resemble Gilead in water-supply and forestal cha-
racter, but contrast strongly with the bare white
hill-country south of Hsdraelon. This plateau
rises steadily to’ Hebron (3,000 ft.), with an_hori-
zontal profile as seen from the sea coast, though
really studded with rounded hills and riven east and
west by torrents, whose heads—often overlapping—
leave only a sinuous and narrow backbone on the
Jordan side of the centre. As the Jordan sinks
while the plateau rises, the eastern ravines are
the deeper, and increase in wildness south till the
Kedron between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea falls
4,000 ft., and west of the Dead Sea the ** Wilderness
of Judwa’’ becomes a labyrinth of savage. gorges,
aptly called “‘the rocks of the wild goats’’ (1 Sam.
| 24, 2)—the time-honoured retreat of outlaws and
hermits.
The Towns and Villages stand on natural or
artificial eminences, even on the plains. In Galilee
and Samaria, they occupy knolls in the charac-
| teristie basin-like plains which diminish south in
extent and number; in Judea, they often stand on
the ends of the ridges (or projections of the high-
land) between the ravines; of such, Jerusalem is a
type.
Nazareth, on the southern edge of the hills of
Galilee which overlook the plain of Esdraelon, lies
on one of a series of converging slopes likened by a
medieval traveller to the petals of a rose.
North of Sharon is Samaria (now Sebastiyeh,
from Sebaste, the name given to it by Herod, and
the Beth-khumri= House of Omri, of the Assyrian
monuments)—the capital substituted for, Shechem
and Tirzah by Omri, Ahab’s father. Its isolated
ridge rises from a fertile basin, and is covered with
ruins and gardens.
About 8 miles to the south-east is Shechem, the
present Nablous, upon the watershed between the
parallel ridges of Hbal and Gerizim.* It has always
been famous for its springs, and divides the palm of
beauty and fertility with Samaria. ‘'Tirzah formerly
surpassed both,
Jerusalem is nearly encircled by ravines, so as to
seem situated in an amphitheatre ; little remains of
the city as it appeared in Christ’s time, the situa- |
tion being changed; for Mount Sion, the highest
part, was cut down by the Maccabees, and is almost
excluded : while the places adjoining Calvary are
nearly in the centre. The city occupies a rocky
plateau about 3 miles round, on the end of a ridge |
which was protected by walls only; by this ridge,
t.e. from the north, Titus, and (apparently) former
conquerors, captured the city.
Bethlehem, i.e. House of Bread, also called
Ephrata, now Beit-lahm, is a small village on a
highly-cultivated ridge 6 miles from Jerusalem, and
east of the main route thence to Hebron.
Hebron, or Kirjath-Arba (Josh. 14. 15), one of
the oldest cities in the world, stands on the culmi-
nating point of the watershed of the hill country
of Judah, exactly half-way between Jerusalem and
Beersheba. It is now called Hl Khalil (7.e. “‘ the
friend’? of God), in memory of Abraham. <A
mosque covers the cave of Machpelah. It was the
royal city until the citadel of Jebus was taken by
Joab, and Jerusalem became ‘‘ the city of David.”
The South Country.—South of Hebron, the
plateau descends in a series of terraces to that of
the Wilderness of Paran (average 2,000 ft.), forming
the pastoral ‘‘ South Country,” Heb. Negeb (Gen,
13. 1, &e.) ; between the mountains of Judah and the
edge of the Desert of Paran. ‘The Negeb occupies
a middle position both topographically and physi-
cally between the rich soil of Central Canaan, and
the sandy wastes of ‘‘ that great and terrible wilder-
ness.”’ In the Bible it is subdivided into.(1) ‘‘the
South of the Kenites,’’ south-west of the Dead Sea
(Judg. 1. 16) ;—(2) ‘‘ the South of Judah,’’ nearly
=Simeon’s allotment (2 Sam. 24. 7) ;—(8) ‘“‘the
South of the Cherethites”’ (i.e. Philistines, 1 Sam.
30. 1, 14, 16), south-west of Beersheba to the river
of Egypt, z.e. the Wady el Arish,—a fine pastoral
region which constituted the Philistine kingdom of
Gerar in Abraham’s time; it is remarkable for
many ruins and old wells (Tristram). After the
Captivity the whole Negeb was overrun by the
Edomites, and was merged in their kingdom known
by the Grecised name of Hdom, i.e. Idumea, Con-
quered and forcibly proselytised by John Hyrcanus
in B.c. 125 (1 Mace. 5. 65, 68), Idumea was ruled
by Jewish governors, one of whom, Antipater, a
native, became by the favour of Julius Cesar the
first Roman Procurator of all Judea. His son was
made by Augustus the first “‘ king of the Jews”
since Nebuchadnezzar abolished David’s throne.
The Wilderness of the Wanderings and the
Sinaitic Peninsula,—The Desert of Ht Tih, 7.e. of
the Wandering, an arid and nearly waterless mass
of limestone, is the ‘‘ great and terrible wilderness ”’
of Deut. 1. 19, across which the Israelites seem to
have made their first and direct approach to Canaan
in the second year after leaving Egypt, i.e. by Ka-
desh, as far as ‘‘ the mount of the Amorites.”’
It is bounded by mountain ranges on its other
sides also: especially. south-west by the range of
Shur, the boundary of the wilderness of that name
traversed by the high road from Palestine to Hgypt;
and south by the range Et Tih, which divides it
from the belt of sandstone, Debbet er Ramleh (i.e.
sand). Beyond this belt—which is ‘‘a rocky but
not a sandy desert,”’ and luxuriant with pasture in
the spring—the triangle of the Peninsula of Sinai
(between the Gulfs of Akabah and of Suez) is filled
by the ‘‘ terrific granite groups”’ of the Tir (=rock)
—hbroken into horns and aiguilles, and likened “‘ to
a stormy sea suddenly petrified ’’—which is known
in the Bible as Mounts Horeb and Sinai. The
latter has been identified by the recent Ordnance
Surveyors with Jebel Miisa—and its spur Ras Suf-
safeh, at the head of Wady er Raha (the sleeve-like
extension of the Wady esh Sheyk), with the ‘‘ Moun-
tain of the Delivery of the Law.”
The Arabah, Edom, Zin, &c.—The great de-
pression which divides the country perpendicularly
from Antioch to the eastern gulf (Akabah) of the Red
Sea, and contains the system of the Jordan, reaches
its lowest depth in the Dead Sea. The basin of
this sea is closed by a line of low cliffs (? the
ascent of Acrabbim, Josh. 15. 3), about 10 miles
south of its southern end. ‘Thence the Arabah
rises for about 75 miles to a watershed 781 ft.
above the Red Sea (Wilson, R.H.), and about 25
miles from the head of the Gulf of Akabah. The
ancient character of this watershed satisfies modern
geologists that the Dead Sea had never any outlet
into the Red Sea. The precipitous sides of the

Arabah are a continuation of the mountainous
region which forms the “retaining walls” of
the Jordan valley. On the west the horizontal,
blanched, and bare plateau of limestone bounds the
“South Country,”? with which two chief passes
communicate, and the wilderness Ht Tih. On the
east the range of Edom (=Red), the Mount Seir of
the Horites, Esan’s inheritance, prolongs the downs
of Gilead and Moab to the Red Sea; but it is lofty
and rugged, and of red sandstone streaked with
various reddish and _brownish-yellow colours; in
this range Petra is situate. The valley is an un-
dulating waste, corresponding generally to the
upper plain of the Jordan, and similarly seamed
north of its watershed, but to a much less extent,
by torrents converging into the inner hollow of the
Wady el Jib, which enters the Dead Sea from the
south. This dreary desert of loose gravel and
stones, furrowed by torrent beds and studded with
water-borne blocks of porphyry, is little known,
being only traversed by a few caravan routes ; but
the western edge, which, with the adjacent highland
probably formed the Wilderness of Zin, is much
less barren, and would have supported part of the
Israelites and their cattle. 'To the north-west of
Edom (Num. 33. 37), and on the southern bank of the
Brook Zered, overlooking’the Arabah and the Dead
Sea, rose Mount Hor, probably above Petra.*
The Arabah was traversed by the Israelites (i.)
after their first failure to enter Canaan, as far as
Hzion-Geber on the Gulf of Akabah; (ii.) when
they returned thence to the Wilderness of Zin, i.e.
Kadesh (Num, 33. 35, 36) ; (iii.) on their final march
from Mount Hor ‘‘ by the way of the Red Sea’?
round the land of Edom, to enter Canaan from the
south-east by the gap providentially made by the
conquests of Sihon the Amorite in the territory of
Ammon and Moab, the kindred nations whom they
were forbidden to attack (Deut. 2.5, 9,19). The
Arabah is 14-16 miles wide opposite Petra, but
diminishes to 2-4 miles near the gulf. About 200
years before Christ, the Nabathawan Arabs, who had
occupied Petra when the Edomites moved west (see
“the South Country’), formed out of Edom proper
the kingdom of Arabia Petraea, whose monarch
Aretas had captured Damascus when St. Paul
arrived there after his conversion (2 Cor. 11. 32 ;
Acts 9. 25). Petra (the Greek, as Selah is the
Hebrew name for a cli’) lies in a perfect ‘nest in
the rock,”’ approached by the twisting defile of the
Sik (=cleft), between deep-red sandstone cliffs and
temples and tombs hewn in their face, which Stanley
terms the Street of Tombs, or Petra’s Appian Way.
This well-watered resting-place of the Arabian
caravans has given the name of Arabia Petrea (i.e.
of Petra) to the adjacent region.
Elath (or Eloth) and Ezion-Geber commanded
the trade with Sheba, &e. (and perhaps with Ophir)
by sea, as Petra by land. Hence Jewish Hastern com-
merce depended on the conquest of Edom (2 Sam.
8. 14), which controlled the passes to the sea and
these two ports on the head of the eastern gulf,
Thus the loss or re-conquest of Hlath and Edom
mark important vicissitudes in Hebrew history
(1 Kings 9. 26; 2 Kings 8. 20; 14. 22; 16. 6).
The Present and Future of Palestine.—It
should be noted, in conclusion, that the climate of
these lands has, been greatly modified by neglect and
waste on the part of its inhabitants and governors,
and especially by the Saracens and the Turks who
followed them. Its forests are gone—the surface
soil has yielded to the plentiful rains (as in Greece
and other limestone mountain-regions) for lack
of the trees whose roots retained the soil—the
rock-hewn cisterns are disused, and even threatened
with destruction, and the network of water-pipes
for irrigation connected with them are become
faintly-traceable ruins;—the terraces which — sus-
tained and supplemented the scanty soil of the
rocky slopes are fallen. Only in favoured spots
are seen the remnants of those works ‘‘ whereon
they had spent no labour’’ into which the Israelites
entered, which are amply illustrated by the wonder-
ful terrace cultivation still surviving on the western
slopes of Lebanon. But, inasmuch as the climate
in its essential elements remains unchanged—capi-
tal, industry, and good government could yet repair
the waste and neglect of centuries, could utilise
Palestine’s highlands and lowlands, with their cli-
mate varying from the sub-Alpine to the subtropical,
and make the “desert springs of water’’ and the
‘“ wilderness blossom like a rose.’

olive trees in the open spaces round the villages.

wheat, barley, millet, peas, beans, and lentils, fol-

esculent vegetables.

THE HEBREW CALENDAR.
THE YHAR’S DIVISIONS.
In Scripture (until the Captivity at least) dates are
often fixed by a reference to the Seasons, and to
Agriculture, because the Hebrew year was divided
according: to natural phenomena exclusively. It
combined therefore the solar and lunar year. The
months began with the new moon, but the first
month was fixed (after the Exodus and by the
necessities of the Passover) by the ripening of
the first corn (barley). Watchmen announced to
the priests at Jerusalem the first appearance of the
new moon (Jer. 31. 6), which, being duly attested,
was proclaimed by a blast of trumpets, and beacon
fires. (N.B. Three ears, from two at least of the
northern, central, and southern districts of Pales-
tine, were required for the determination of the
Passover month.)—The lunar month averaging 294
days, a year of 12 months of 30 and 29 days alternately
naturally resulted; ‘but this involved a variation
of 11 and 22 days alternately in 18 out of 19 years.
To reconcile this lunar year with the year of the
seasons, a 13th month must be inserted about once
in three years. This the Jews probably intercalated
before the first month; 2.e. in what would seem a
backward season,—for they now call it Veadar, or
the 2nd Adar; but it is not mentioned in the Bible.
Thus their practice approximated roughly to the
Metonie cycle (adopted by the modern Jews about
A.D. 360), in which a year of 18 months is inserted

THE SEASONS—WEEK—SABBATICAL YVEAR—JUBILEE.
THE SEHASONS.
The harvest in Hgypt occurs from one month to
six weeks earlier than in Palestine—i.e. the flax and
barley harvest in March, the wheat and spelt harvest
in April. The sub-tropical regions of the Jordan
valley, and especially the nearly tropical region of
Jericho and.the Dead Sea, correspond nearly to
Kgypt and parts of India in climate, seasons, and
vegetation. The harvests of the highland plains of
Palestine (averaging 2,000 feet above sea-level) are
about a month later; the coast plains of Philistia
occupy an intermediate position. Hyerywhere the
barley precedes the wheat harvest by about three
weeks, and the crop is reaped about four months
after sowing. Palestine comprises by nature a series
of climates so extraordinary that an overruling Provi-
dence could easily cause the stages of agriculture
to overlap from-sheer abundance (cp. Amos 9. 18).
Its climate varies: from the sub-Alpine to the sub-
tropical as the joint result of elevations and depres-
sions of the surface (equivalent, if taken together,
to a maximum of 7,000 feet), and of ravines infinitely
varied in depth, aspect, and shelter, The rainfall,
though probably less. irregular when the forests yet
stood, and when the soil was retained by terraces
and tilled by a teeming population, would suffice
for irrigation if duly husbanded in cisterns and
channels; and its regularity was guaranteed to
Israel, if faithful. The parching winds from the
eastern deserts, which yet yellow the exposed wall
and evaporate the vital warmth till death super-
venes, had their counterpoise in the moist sea
breezes which pass the Jordan. And until May
the shepherd can yet pass ‘‘ from winter to summer
in an hour,” and elsewhen give his flock from month
to month suitable temperature and pasturage by
moving from the valley to the glen, and thence to
the lofty steppe, and back again.
OTHER DIVISIONS OF TIME—THE WHEK, THE SABBATICAL YEAR,
AND THE
The Week of seven days is traceable in the record
of the Creation and the Deluge (Gen. 8. 10), and it
is mentioned in the agreements between Laban and
Jacob (Gen. 29.27). The consecration of the seventh
day as a day of rest is expressly attributed by Moses
to God Himself (Gen. 2. 3), who in the Mosaic Law
developed the institution by appointing years of rest
to be observed by His people after their settlement
in the Land of Promise. At the end of every week
of years, t.e. every seventh year—or ‘“‘ year of re-
lease,’’ now termed a Sabbatical Year—the Hebrews
and their land were to ‘‘ keep Sabbath,’ the soil
remaining untilled, the vine unpruned (Lev. 25. 2-7),
the oliveyard undressed, while the self-produced
crops were abandoned to the poor, to the stranger,
and to the wild animals. Debtors were to be
released (made to rest) from their debts (Deut.
15. 1-18), and domestic slaves of Hebrew blood
from their servitude, unless they chose deliberately
to remain in slavery (Hxod. 21. 1-11; Jer. 34. 14).
The Law was to be publicly read (Deut. 31. 10-13) ;
the leisure of the year would promote its study,
religious progress, and education.—Towards the
close of the seventh Sabbatical year, or week of
week-years, i.e. on the great Day of Atonement
(10th of first month of the civil, and seventh of the
sacred year, see Calendar) the Year of Jubilee
began. Its first three months coincided (less 10
days) with the last three of the outgoing Sabbatical
year, and it ended on the Day of Atonement of the
year following. ‘To the observances of the Sab-
JUBILEE.
batical year were added (1) the restoration of all
lands and houses in unwalled or Levites’ houses
even in walled towns (Lev. 25. 30, 38), free of all
debt or mortgage, to the heirs of the original
allottees at the time of Joshua’s Settlement ;
(2) the release of all bondmen of Hebrew blood,
and especially of those who had sold themselves
and families (with or without their land), or had
been seized for debt, and become agricultural slaves
or serfs (Lev. 25. 839; 2 Kings 4.1). The alienation
of land, &c., was thus absolutely limited to a period
of 49 years. No mention is made of debt or debtors
in connection with the Jubilee, probably because
both should have disappeared in the preceding nine
months of the seventh Sabbatical year. The Jubilee
year ended just before the commencement of the
uncertain and often long-protracted seed time of
Palestine (see Calendar). Thus the Hebrews were
ever reminded that the land was God’s, and they
but His tenants; oppression was checked and
pauperism limited; the accumulation of land in a
few hands was prevented, and the integrity of the
tribes and their allotments assured; while the
necessity of proving tribesmanship and heirship at
intervals of half a century tended to insure the
accuracy and preservation of the family genealogies,
by which the descent of the Promised Seed of the
woman and the fulfilment of the promises to David
by the coming of the Redeemer (Messiah) must be
recognised. in the fulness of time. [Ep.]

ihe HET OF DAY—HEBREW RECKONING.
THE DAY AND ITS DIVISIONS.
By Rev. C. Hous, M.A.
I—IN THE OLD TESTAMENT.
The natural day, from sunrise to sunset, which
varies in England from about eight to sixteen hours
according to the season of the year, is more uniform
in the lower latitude of Palestine, where it varies
from about ten to fourteen hours. The calendar
| day, or civil day, extending always and everywhere
| through the twenty-four hours, may commence
variously. When reckoned, as with us, from mid-
night to midnight, it has the advantage of including
the entire daylight in one business day; whereas by
any other computation, as from noon to noon, from
sunrise to sunrise, from sunset to sunset, common
events would far more frequently have double dates.
The following texts are adduced to show that
the Hebrews reckoned from ‘sunset to sunset :—
“The evening and the morning were the first day ”’
(Gen. 1.5); ‘‘ from even unto even shall ye celebrate
your sabbath”? (Ley. 28. 32); ‘‘ unto 2,300 days”
(Dan. 8. 14; marg. ‘‘ evening-morning ’’).
The sub-division of time into exact intervals re-
| quires mechanical inventions. When we consider
how obvious is the determination of noon by the
shadow, and bear in mind such easy contrivances as
| the out-flow of sand or water, or the sinking of a
| perforated vessel placed in a vessel of water, it is
hard to think that so intelligent a people as the
| Israelites had no simple mechanism for measuring
time. » An agricultural race would be satisfied with
very rough calculation, and every household might
measure by the intervals most convenient to itself.
The preciousness of time is felt only in the activities of
an artificial civilisation, whence alone would arise the
necessity of public standards and uniform measures.
This would account for the general absence of precise
divisions of time in the O.'T., while the incidental
reference to the “‘dial’’ or ‘‘sun-dial’’ of Ahaz
(2 Kings 20.11; Isa. 38. 8), the nature of which is
only a matter of conjecture, leads us to infer that
time-measurers of some kind were in use. Other-
wise, unless roughly by the stars, the midnight point
could not be determined. The ‘‘ hour,’ necessarily
| an artificial space of time, appears to occur once
only in the O.T., ‘‘astonied for one hour’’ (Dan.
4.19); but the Hebrew word thus translated (shddh)
| signifies no more than an indefinite interval. ‘The de-
scriptive terms, dawn, morning, noon, heat of day,
cool of day, evening, twilight, night, are of common
occurrence and always intelligible. Attempts have
been made to arrange the Hebrew originals it a
| graduated scale, with very doubtful success, and
with no real gain to any of the narratives. Thus,
“heat of the “day ” (Gen. 18.1; 1 Sam. 11. 11) is
placed about 9 a.m., and “‘ cool "of the day’? (Gen.
| 3. 8) before sunset. But even if reliance could be
placed upon such interpretations, they would not
help the English reader, as the A. V. does not
| translate the Hebrew uniformly; one word being
rendered both as twilight and dawn, another both
as morning and dawn. While the ever-varying day
| furnishes so many descriptive and natural terms, the
| dead level of night’ can only be artificially divided,
and for this the relays of guardians or watchers of
the public safety would furnish a scheme. Doubtless
the Temple was placed under nightly watch, and it
is considered that Ps. 184 contains the salutations
that passed at the reliefs. ‘‘ Night watches’? thus
became a current expression, and hence the question
in Isa. 21. 11, “‘ Watchman, what of the night ?”
In the O. T. three distinct watches are discernible :
(73
Il.—_IN THE NEW TESTAMENT.
(1) “‘the beginning of the watches’? (Lam. 2. 19),
supposed to have ended at midnight; (2) ‘‘ the
middle watch,’ supposed to have commenced at
midnight ; (8) ‘“‘ the morning watch’? (Exod. 14, 24),
considered to have ended at sunrise. Such watches
of the night would correspond generally with the
three main divisions of the day recognised in Ps. 55.
17, ‘‘ At evening, morning, and at noon will I pray.”
II. In the New Testament we recognise Roman
computation in Time as well as in Money, Weights,
and Measures; and here at length the word ‘hour?
occurs with the proper meaning: ‘‘ Are there not
twelve hours in the day?’’ (John 11.9). We may
conclude, from the known usage of that period, that
the natural day is the one meant; the hour, there-
fore, would vary in length with that of the daylight
to be sub-divided. ‘Tio compute any given hour of a
Jewish day in modern terms is thus a matter of some
complication, as only one hour of the Jewish day,
that of noon, would always correspond with one
hour of our day. The Jewish sixth hour would end
at our 12 at noon; but the Jewish first hour, which
began at sunrise, would correspond with our 6 a.m.
only at the equinoxes, when alone the Jewish twelfth
hour at sunset would coincide with our 6 p.m. The
following hours are named in the N. T.: i
(Matt. 20.3; Mark 15. 25; Acts2.15); sith (Matt.
20. 5; 27. 45; John 4. 6; 19. 14; Acts 10. 9);
seventh (John 4. 52); ninth (Matt. 20. 5; 27. 45,
46; Acts 3.1; 10. 3); tenth (John 1. 39); eleventh
(Matt. 20. 6), i.e. the last of the working day.
single passage indicates that the night also was
divided into hours, ‘‘the third hour of the night’’
(Acts 23. 23), the usual notation being by ‘‘ watches.”’
The ordinal number prefixed (which was never the
case in the O. T.) shews that the N. Tl’. watches—
whatever the O. T. might have been—were four in
number, corresponding with the Roman reckoning ;
and the following are mentioned—second and third
(Luke 12. 38), fourth (Matt. 14. 25). In only one
passage the night season is described in another set
of four terms, evening, midnight, cock-crowing,
morning (Mark 18. 35), which are thought to have
corresponded respectively with twilight to 9 p.m.,
9 to 12, 12 to 3 a.m., 3 to day-break.

Scripture method of computing time is to reckon a

(Jer. 25. i); t.e. two full years a ‘and the fragments of
two others. In like manner may be explained the
expressions used of our Lord’s resurrection, “the
third day’? (Matt. 16. 21; Luke 24. 21); Ce after
three days”? (Matt. 27. 68; Mark 8. 31); ‘“‘three

in the grave on Friday before the Sabbath com-

so that whether the day was reckoned as beginning

was another Hebrew form of speech meaning the

THE primary object of the following list is to promote

New and almost all those in the Old Testament.
Strict accuracy is no doubt unattainable. In some cases
(e.g. Moses, Aaron, Solomon, Isaac, Samuel, Jeremiah)
the forms adopted by the Authorised Version are bor-
rowed from the Septuagint through the medium of the
Vulgate. Here the correct pronunciation would require
an alteration of familiar names, which would be quite
intolerable. But even where the current forms ar
derived from the Hebrew, a strictly accurate pronunciz
tion would offend by introducing a dissonance into the
rude but real harmony of our Knglish speech. Besides,
that quickness of ear which is necessary for reproduc-
ing foreign sounds is conspicuously wanting to most
atives of England. Still the prevalent system of
pronouncing Biblical names seems unnecessarily wide
of the mark. ‘There is asion to offend so
gratuitously against the laws Hebrew sound and
composition as we do at present. Not a few of our
mispronunciations of Hebrew names impede the com-
prehension of their me aning, especially in the case of
names of religious significance, where the meaning is
most fully fraught with instruction.

tent mispronunciation is surely feasible, and
this which has been attempted in the following

shifted so as to bring the religious significance of the

The meanings of names not of a religious character
may sometimes appear strange and unnatural; but it
does not follow that their interpretation is fanciful or
supported by insufficient evidence. ‘lhe selection of a
name was, and still is, in the East, often dictated by
some accidental circumstance, as by a word spoken at
the birth of a child, or by some object which chanced
to meet the eye of the mother. So Rachel called her
last-born Benoni, the son of my sorrow, while his
father called him Benjamin. It would almost appear
from Luke 1. 60-62 that the mother was the first to
give a name, subject to correction by the father. None
of the meanings here given are arbitrary, and yet
they are by no means equally certain, (1) because the
original form of the names has sometimes become
modified, and (2) because the old Hebrew lite is

entire word-store of the Israclites, that it ‘is
nec iry to call in the aid of the kindred di

scholars will often come to different results; but the
majority of the meanings here given have at least a
high degree of probability. The most doubtful ones
have the sign of interrogation attached.
